By the Queen: A Proclamation, for dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling of another.

ANNE, R.

WHEREAS we have thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Tuesday,

---

the TueotyTeventh Day of this instant April; we do, for that Knd, publish this our royal Proclamation, and do hereby diffoive the said Parliament accordiugly: And Uie Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burge lies, Coromiftioners for Shires and Burghs, of the said Parliament, are discharged from their meeting on the said Twenty-seventh Day of April. And to the Intent our good Subjects may perceive* the Confidence we have in their A tied ions, and how desirous we are to meet our People, and have their Advice, by their Kepresentatives, in Parliament, we do hereby make known to oUr laid Subjects, that we do intend, in i’ome short time, to give Directions to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to cade Writs to be issued, in due Form of Law, for the calling a new Parliament.

---

Given at our Court at Kensington, the Fifteenth Day of April, in the Seventh Year of our Reign.

God save the Queen.

By the Queen: A Proclamation.

ANNE, R.

---

WHEREAS by our royal Proclamation, bearing Date the Fifteenth Day of this instant April, we did dissolve the last Parliament, which then flood prorogued to Tuesday, the Twenty-seventh of this instant April, and did thereby declare, that, in lonie ftiort time after, we did intend to give Directions for the calling of a new Parliament; we do by this our royal Proclamation, publish and declare, that, with the Adviceof our Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to issue out Writs in due Form, for the summoning, and holding, a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Tejle the Twenty-sixth Day of this instant Aprils and to be returnable on Thursday, the Eighth of July next ensuing the Date hereof.

Given at our Court at Kenfignton, the Twenty-second Day of April, 1708, in the Seventh Year of our Reign.

God save the Queen.

ANNE, R.

By the Queen: A Proclamation, giving notice of the holding the Parliament, and requiring the Attendance of the Members of both Houses of Parliament.

ANNE, R.

WE being desirous, that the Members of both Houses of Parliament may have convenient Notice of the Time, when their Attendance in Parliament shall be requisite, have, with Advice of our Privy Council, thought fit to illiie this our royal Proclamation, hereby declaring our Pleasure, that our Parliament, which now itauds prorogued to Thursday, the One-aml-twentieth of this inltant October, shall be further prorogued unto Tuesday, the Sixteenth Day of November next entiling the Date hereof: And our Purpose being, that our

laid Houses of Parliament shall not only meet upon the said Sixteenth Day of November, but shall then fit for the Di(patch of divers weighty and important A ft airs; we do hereby charge all the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burge fils, Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, to give their Attendance at fi eji-minster, on the said Sixteenth Day of November, accordingly.

Given at our Court at Kensington, the Sixth Day of October, in the Seventh \ ear of our Reign.

God save the Queen.

Then the Lord Chancellor said.

My Lords, and Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

BY virtue of h<er Majesty’s Commissioni, now read, to fcs (among other Lords) directed, we let you know, it is her Majesty’s Pleasure, we should not declare the Causes of calling this Parliament, until there be a Speaker of the House of Commons: And therefore it is her Majesty’s Pleasure, that jou, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, repair to the Place, where the Commons usually lit, and there chuse a fit Person to be your Speaker; and that you prpfent him, whom you shall ehul'e, to her Majesty’s Commissioners here, for her Majesty’s royal Approbation by the said Coiqiiuffioners, on

The House being returned;

The Serjeant at Arms brought the Mace, and laid it under the Table.

And the Right honourable the Lord acquainted the House, that the Person, he should name to be ttieir Speaker, wanted nothing to recommend him: That he was of great Experience, and had served his Country with Integrity in the most difficult and worst of Times: And therefore it was his Motion, that Sir Richard Onslow, Baronet, may take the Chair, as Speaker.

And Sir Wm, Strickland acquainting the House, that the Gentleman, which had been prpposed by the noble Lord, was a very fit Person, considering all his Qualifications; being a Person of great Experience in Parliament, and one, who had ffiewed his Justice and Integrity in all Times; and therefore he seconded the Motion, that Sir Richard Onslow might take the Chair:

And the honourable Colonel Henry thirding

the Motion; for that the Person proposed had a very good Estate in his Country, and was every way qualified:

And the House generally calling upon him to the Chair:

Sir Richard Onslow, in his Place, desired, that the House would please to excuse him, in respect of the many Difficulties, that attended the Discharge of so great a Trust; declaring, that his Intercession to them proceeded from a real Sense of his own Inabilities, left the Service of the Publick might receive any Prejudice by his Incapacity; withal, giving the House his humble Thanks, for the great Honour they had done in proposing him.

Upon which the House unanimously calling upon him to the Chair;

The Lord Wm. Powlett and Sir Wm. Strickland conduced him from his Place to the Chair: But upon the first Step he again said, that he was obliged to give them the Trouble of a Second Request,* that they would be pleased to excuse him* and out of the great many present to elect 9 more able Person for so great a Service; alluring them, that it proceeded not lb much from Form, as the Sense of his own Inabilities; and that it would be an insupportable Trouble to him, if the Publick should suffer by any Defects of his; and therefore again most earnestly desired to be excused.

But the House cried, " No, No."

And thereupon he fat down in the Chair.

And the Serjeant at Arms came up, and laid the Mace upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Thursday Morning next. Nine a Clock.

Jovis, 18° die Novembris; Anno 70 Annas Reginte, 1708.

THE House being met j and Mr. Speaker elect having taken the Chair;

A Message was brought by Mr. Aston, Deputy Gen-tleman-ulher of the Black Rod:

ML Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate attendance of this lionou/able House in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, that they had, in Obedience to Command, been at the House of Peers; and that he had presented himself; and that the Lord Chancellor had declared her Majesty’s Pleasure to approve of the Choice, \he House had made of their Speaker; acquainting them, that it was a Testimony of the great Esteem the Queen had for them.

That he did, in their Name, demand Liberty of Speech, that their Debates might be free, the better to enable them to make suitable Provisioqs for the Service of the Publick; also Freedom from Arrests for themselves, and Servants, that their Properties might not be disturbed; and also Aqcels to her Majesty’s royal Person, that they might lay before her a true State of their Proceedings, when it should be necessary for the Publick Service.

That he demanded, and bad obtained, as ample a Grant of them, as ever was made to any preceding Parliament; believing, no Prince ever had a more loyal House of Commons, or more deserved to be intrusted with those Privileges: And, withal, he desired, that his involuntary Errors might only be imputed to the unfortunate Author: And again returned the House his Thanks, for the Ho. pour they had done him; giving them Assurances, to use his utmost Endeavours to deserve the Continuance of their Favours, and to supply his many Defers by a faith* ful and deligent Application to the Dispatch of those great and arduous Affairs, for which this Parliament was now convened.

And (in regard some Liberty had been taken, in a late Pifeourse, concerning some Carriages of those, who had been formerly in the Chair) further said.

That he was by Birth intitled to Liberty and Property, and by Education taught so to value the Constitution and Government of England, as by the several Laws established, both in Church and State, that he would rather chuse to expose himself to Egyptian Bondage, than be a Prostitute in this his native free Country j and, whenever he swerved from this Resolution, their Admonitions would be a Favour, or, if they proved ineffectual, their fevered Censures; But, so long as he endeavoured to discharge his Duty, he hoped, he might intirely depend upon their Support; and that he asked the same with the greatest Earnestness, believing, the Chair never had a greater Occasion: And, as an Inducement, desired Leave to assure them, that no Person was ever placed in it with a better Disposition to discharge the Duty of it; and that he should esteem himself very happy, could he prevail with them to enter upon the Dispatch of publick BufiDels more early in the Morning, and with that Decency, and good Order, as becomes ib great a Senate.

And then Mr. Speaker alone took the Oaths, and repeated the Declaration, or Tell, and the Oath of Ab: Juration, and fiabferibed the lame, according to the Laws for that Purpose.

And afterwards many other Members took the Oaths, and repeated the Declaration, or Test, and the Oath of Abjuration, and subscribed the fame, according to the Laws for that Purpose.

And then the House adjourned till To-morrovr Morning, Nipe a Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported, that when he, with the House, went to the House of Peers, the 18th instant, at the Desire of the Lords Commissioners, appointed by her Majesty under the Great Seal of Great Britain, for opening, and holding this present Parliament, the Lord Chancellor (being one of the said Commissioners) made a Speech to both Houses; which being very long, and

Vol. 16.

of great Importance to the Publick, left any Part thereof should be mif-recited, or omitted, he had obtained a Copy thereof; which he read to the House, and is as follows; vie.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In pursuance of the Authority given us by her Majesty’s Commission utlder the Great Seal (among other tiling1') to declare the Causes of her Mai.fly’s calling this Parliament,

We are, by her Majesty’s Command, in the First Place to obf.rve to }<'u, that the extraordinary Length of this Year’s Campaign hath obliged her Majesty to defer your Meeting longer, than otherwise she would have done, that you might be informed, with the greater Certainty, of the State and Pollure of the War, in order to your Resolutions for the ensuing Year.

This necessary Delay hath now so far shewn us the Success of Affairs abroad, as that, whether you consider the Places acquired by the Allies, or the farther and continued Proofs, given this lad year, of their fu peri or Courage and Conduit (which, as to the future Part of the War, is equal to all other Advantages) we may, with Thanks to God, and Justice to those he hath been pleased touie as Instruments in this great Work, conclude, that, upon the Whole, wc arc brought much nearer, than we were the last Session, to the End of our undertaking this War, the reducing the dangerous Power of and settling such a Peace, as may secure itself from being violated.

Her Majesty therefore commands us to assure vou, fhc hath not the lead Doubt, but that this Parliament will be of the fime Opinion with her last, as to the vigorous Prosecution of the War, 3nd the Ends of it; believing it importable, the Representative of the British Nation can endure to tlunk of losing the Fruits of all our past Endeavours, and the great Advantages we have gained, particularly in this present Year, by fub.nitling at lait to an in secure Peace.

And therefore, since, probably, nothing can hinder our Success abroad for the time to come, but Misunderstand-ings among ourselves at home, we have it in Command to conjure you, by your Duty to God, and to her Majesty, your Zeal for the Protestant Religion, your Love fur your Country, and the Regard you cannot but have for the Liberty of Europe in general, to avoid all Occasion of Divift ms; which are ever hurtful tc the Pubflck, but will more especially be so at this Juncture, when the Eyes of all our Neighbours are upon you, with a very particular Concern; and your Unanimity, and good Agreement, will be thegn-atell Satisfaction, and Encouragement to all our Ahu s.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

You cannot but be convinced, that the several Parts of the War, which were provided lor by the last Parliament, will require your Support, at lead, in the same Degree: But in Flanders, the Nature of the War is much altered, by the great Advances made there towards entering into France; which hath so far alarmed our Enemies, that they are drawing more Troops daily to that Side, for the Defence of their own Country: And therefore her Majesty hopes, you will luve lo right a Sense of our present Advantages, as to enable her Majesty to make a considerable Augmentation, for preserving, and improving them j which, by the Continuance of God’s Blcfiing on our Aims, mull hn n put a glorious Period to this long and expensive War.

As to the Condition of the Fleet, we have it in Command from her Majesty to acquaint you, that the con-slant and remote Services, in which the Ships have been employed, have made a greater Sum, than usual, requisite, as well for the extraordinary Repairs, as the budding of new Ships; and the taking of Port Mahon, as ic huh afforded the Means of having a Part of the Fleet operate with more Readinels and Eftelt on the Enemy, or wherever it may be ulelul to the common Cause, in those Parts, so the making such Provisions, at so great a Distance, as will be proper for that Service, mull of ne-

teffity, cause some extraordinary Expences; all which her Majesty recommends to your serious Consideration; de-firing you to provide timely and effectual Supplies for those Ends, and likewise for the carrying on such Fortifications, for the Security of our Ports, and extinguishing the Enemies Hopes of profiting by Disturbances in Scotland, as you shall think fit.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Union is esteemed by her Majesty to be so happy and great a Part of the Successes of her Reign, and her Majesty hath so much at Heart the confirming and improving it, that (he is pleased to command us to remind you of preparing such Bills, as shall be thought conducing to that End; and particularly, to make the Laws of both Parts of Great Britain agree, as near as may be, for the common Interest of both People, especially as to those Laws, which relate to criminal Cafes, and Proceedings, and settling the Militia on the same Foot throughout the United Kingdom.

Her Majesty is graciously pleased, we should also af-sure you, that if you can propose any Means for the Improvement of our Trade or Manufactures, or better Employment of the Poor, her Majesty will take the greatest Satisfaction in enacting such Provisions; there being nothing (he so earnestly desires as that God will blel’s her with more and more Opportunities of doing all possible Good to so well-deserving a People, so firm and affectionate to her Interests.

And, as her Majesty does not doubt, by God’s Blessing, and your good Affections, to continue to defeat the Designs of the Pretender, and his open or secret Abettors; so her Majesty will always endeavour, on' her Part, to make her People happy, to such a Degree, as that none (except of desperate Fortunes) shall enter into Measures, for the Disturbance of her Government, the Union, or the Protestant Succession, as by Law established, without acting at the same Time manifestly against their own true and lading Interest, as well as their Duty.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, to congratulate the glorious Successes of her Arms, and those of her Allies, this present Year; and to allure her Majesty of our utmost Endeavours to enable her to carry on a vigorous War against the common Enemy, until the Liberties of Europe may be secured by a safe and an honourable Peace; and also to support and defend her Majesty, and the Succession, as by Law established, in the Protestant Line, against the Pretender and all his open, and secret Abettors.

as shall or may come in Question, touching Privileges, and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinion therein, to the House, from Time to Time; and they have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and if any Thing shall come in Question, touching the Matter of Privilege of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate.

Ordered, That only Two Counsel of a Side be heard Usual Orders, at the Bar of the House, upon the Matter of controverted Elections.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, take this first Opportunity of expressing to your Majesty the deep Sense we have of the great Loss, your Majesty and this Kingdom have sustained in the Death of his Royal Highness Prince George of Denmark; whose tender AffeCfit n to your Majesty, and Love to our Country, had gained him the Hearts of all your good Subjects, and will render his Memory ever dear to them.

We humbly beseech your Majesty to moderate the Grief, so justiy due on this fad Occafian, since it cannot be indulged, without endangering the Health of your royal Person, on whose Safety the Happiness of Great Britain, and the Liberties of do, under God,

depend.

Your faithful Commonsthink themselves obliged(more particularly at this Time) to allure your Majesty of their inviolable Fidelity to your Person and Government, and of their firm Resolution effectually to support your Majesty against all your Enemies, both at home and abroad.

Sir Wm. Strickland reported from the Committee, to

whom it was referred to draw up an Address, to be presented to her Majesty, to congratulate the glorious Suc-ceffes ofher Arms, and those ofher Allies, this present Year; and to assure her Majesty of our utmost Endeavours to enable her to carry on a vigorous War against the common Enemy, until the Liberties of Europe may be secured by a safe and honourable Peace; and also to support and defend her Majesty, and the Succession, as by Law established, in the Protestant Line, against the Pretender, and all his open and secret Abettors; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was twice read, and is as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to congratulate the glorious Successes of this Year, gained by the Arms of your Majesty, and those of your Allies.

The great and signal Advantages, that have been so wonderfully obtained, so vigorously prosecuted and improved, and upon all Occasions so happily accomplished, are repeated Instances, that noDifficulties are insuperable to your great Commanders, and no Force of the Enemy able to obstruct the Progress of your victorious Arms; which gives us good Grounds to hope for further Success before the Conclusion of this long and active Campaign.

Your Majesty’s good Subjects, through the whole Course of this War, have most chearfully granted the necessary Supplies, forsupporting and carrying it on with Vigour, and have seen such good Fruits of their former Zeal, that your Majesty may be allured, this House will never be wanting in their Duty to your Majesty, or the Interest of those they represent; but are determined to give such Supplies, as, by the Blessing of God, may be most effectual, for redyeing the Power of the common Enemy, and forcing him to accept such a Peace, as your Majesty, in Conjunction with your Allies, shall think honourable, and lading.

' The Union is so great a Glory to your Majesty, and Advantage to all your People, that we shall do every thing on our part to (Lengthen and improve it; but, above all, it shall be our utmost care to defend your Majesty’s sacred Person, to support your undoubted Title to the Crown, todisappoint the hopes and designs of the Pre.

tender, and all his open and secret Abettors, and to main tain the Protestant Succession, as by Law established.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Address, to be presented to her Majesty.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure, when lhe will be pleased to be attended with the said Address, and in what Manner.

And the Petition of William Palmes, and William Strickland, Esquires, being also read; letting forth, that the Petitioners were duly elected Burgesses, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Mahon, in the County of York, and were so declared, and returned, by Nathaniel Harrison, Gentleman Bailiff* of the said Borough; yet one Wm. Answer to Mr. Secretary Biyle reported to the House, that her Addreiies. Majesty having been attended with their Address, To condole with her Majesty, on the Death of his Royal Highness Prince George ot Denmark; and to desire her Majesty to take Care of her royal Person, upon whose Health the Happiness of this Kingdom, and the Liberties of Europe, do lb much depend; and to allure her Majesty, that the Commons of Great Britain will support her Majesty again!! all her Enemies, both at home and abroad; her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious An liver; viz.

That Ihe thanks you very kindly for this Address and that the Concern, which the House has expressed for her Affliction, is very acceptable to her Majesty.

Mr. Secretary Boyle also reported to the House, that her Majesty having been attended with their Address, To congratulate the glorious Success'es of her Arms, and those of her Allies, this present Year; and to allure her Majesty of our utmost Endeavours to enable her Majesty to carry on a vigorous War again!! the common Enemy, until the Liberties of Europe may be secured by a lafe and honourable Peace; and also to support and defend her Majesty, and the Succession, as by Law established, in the Protellant Line, against the Pretender, and all his open and secret Abettors; her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer; viz.

That Ihe returns you many Thanks for all the hearty Assurances you have given her in this Address, particularly for those of assisting her, in bringing this War to a lafe and happy ConduCon, which her Majesty Voi. 16.

does very much desire, for the Ease and Security of her People; and as she does intirely depend upon your Dispatch of the Supplies, necessary to that End, l'o she hopes, God Almighty will still continue to bids the Endeavours of her Majesty, and her Subjects, for the Good of the Common Caule.

A Petition of the Mayor, and divers Burgesses, of the ancient Borough of Wiston, in the County of Pembroke, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Burgesses of the said Borough, was read; setting forth, that is an

ancient Borough by Prescription, and the Mayor and Burgesses thereof, together with the Mayor and Burgesses, and Inhabitants, of Pembroke, and the Mayor, Burgesses, and Inhabitants of Tenby, in the said County, have a Right to vote at the Election of a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Pembroke, and ought to have publick Notice of every Election; which Right they have frequently exercised, and have had such Notice by the Mayor of Pembroke: That Sir Arthur Owen, Baronet, with Intent to gain the Government of Pembroke wholly into his own Hands, and deprive the Petitioners of their said Right at such Elections, procured himself to be elected Mayor thereofin 1704 (though, by their Charters, he was not qualified so to be) and continued Mayor for Two Years (though not legally admitted) making great Numbers of his Friends, Tenants, and Servants (many not living within the Liberties of broke) to be Common-council-men, contrary to the Charters of the Borough: That, the better to effect this unjust Design.Sir Arthur Owe afterwards procured one Jabez Rickfon (a mean Person and no Householder within the Borough of Pembroke) to be elected Mayor; and he also irregularly admitted great Numbers of the Friends and Tenants, Dependants and Servants, of Sir to be Burgesses of Pembroke; and he solicited on Sir Arthur's, behalf, when the Time of Election for this Parliament was drawing near, and proceeded to the Election, without giving Notice to the said Borough of IViJion; and some of the Petitioners (being by Accident at the said Election) were denied their Votes by the said Mayor; whereby, and by otherundue Practices, the said Sir Arthur Owen procured himself to be elected, and returned, and the Petitioners are in danger of losing their said just Right of Election, unless relieved by the House: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Merits of the said Election, and Return, be heard upon Saturday, the 23d Day of next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty thousand Men be employed in the Sea Service, for the Year 1709, including Eight thousand Marines.

Rtfohed, That it it the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding 4 a Man be

allowed for maintaining the said Forty thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds, be allowed for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year 1709.

Rtfohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Forty thousand Men, which were raised, to ad in Conjunction with the Forces of her Majesty’s Allies, be continued for the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Nine hundred and One thousand Eight hundred Twenty-seven Pounds, Thirteen Shillings, and Six-pence, be granted to her Majesty, for maintaining the said Forty thousand Men for the Service of the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committe, That the additional Forces, of Ten thousand Men, be continued for the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Seventy-seven thousand Five hundred Eleven Pounds, Three Shillings, and Six-pence, be granted to her Majesty, for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men for the Service of the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That her Majesty’s Proportion of Three thousand Palatines, formerly taken into the Service of her Majesty, and the States General, be continued for the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-four thousand Two hundred Fifty-one Pounds, Thirteen Shillings, and Four

g:nce, be granted to her Majesty, to defray her Majesty’s roportion of the Charge of maintaining the said Three thousand Palatines, for the Service of the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That her Majesty’s Proportion of Four thousand Six hundred Thirty-nine Saxons, taken into the Service of her Majesty, and the States General, in the Year 1707, be continued for the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-three thousand Two hundred Fifty-one Pounds, Twelve Shillings, and Sixpence, be granted to her Majesty, to defray her Majesty’s Proportion of the Charge of maintaining the said Four thousand Six hundred Thirty-nine Saxons, for the Service of the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That her Majesty’s Proportion of s Regiment

of Dragoons, conlifting of Eight hundred Men, taken into the Service of her Majesty, and the States General, in the Year 1707, be continued for the Year 1709.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceedingNine thousand Two hundred Sixty-nine Pounds, Sixteen Shillings, and Six-pence, be granted to her Majesty, to defray her Majesty’s Proportion of the Charge of maintaining of the said Regiment of Dragoons, for the Service of the Year 1709.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, Nemine tontradicente.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine a Clock.

The humble RETURN of the principal Officers and Commissioners of her Majesty’s Navy to the Order of the honourable House of Commons, of the 26th Instant, for laying before the House the Names of the Commissioners, employed in the Out-ports, and Copies of the Warrants for such their Employments, and an Account of the Allowances made to them:

That George St. Loe, Esquire, is employed in the Port

of Chatham;

Isaac Town fend, Esquire, at the Port of Portsmouth: William Wright, Esquire, at the Port of Plymouth:

Lawrence Wright, Esquire, at the Port of

At the Salaries of £. 500 per Annum each: And, Thomas Jennings, Esquire, at Lisbon, at the Salary of £. 1,000 per Annum, whilst he continues there.

And on the other Side is humbly presented a Copy of his late Royal Highness’ Warrant to William Wright, Esquire, to repair to the Port of Plymouth, and reside

there, as a Commissioner of the said Port, being all of that Kind wc find entered in this Office.

Cha. Sergifon,

W. Lee, B. Tyme well.

Geo. TollDan. Furzer.

His Royal Highness Prince George of Denmark, &r. Lord High Admiral of Great Britain and Ireland, &c and Generalissimo of all her Majesty’s Forces, L?c.

WHEREAS I think it necessary for her Majesty’s Service, that one of the Members of the Navy-board should be sent to her Majesty’s Yard at Plymouth, to reside there, in the room of Henry Esquire,

since lately deceased; you are therefore hereby required, and directed, forthwith to repair thither, and make your constant Abode in the Dwelling-house, usually enjoyed by the Commissioner at Plymouth Yard, and fee to, and take care of, the faithful, vigorous, and frugal Management of all Matters and Things, relating to her Majesty’s naval Service there, in the same manner, aS either the said Commissioner Greenhill, or any other Commissioner of the Navy, did, or ought to have done, who resided at that Place: And the rest of the principal Officers and Commissioners of her Majesty’s Navy are hereby required to take notice hereof accordingly. Given under my Hand this 20th of Ju/y, 1708.

GEORGE,

A P ETI TI ON of the Merchants, Clothiers, and others, concerned in the Woollen Manufactures in and about the Town of Leeds, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Trade in the Woollen Manufactures is greatly decayed, by reason of the Exportation of our Wool } whereby Foreigners set up Manufactories of their own, whoused to be supplied by the Petitioners: And praying the House to consider of some Law, that may more effectually hinder this evil Practice, than the Law's now in being.

Ordered, That the Confederation of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Encouragement cf those who are Manufacturers of the Woollen, Iron, and Linen Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for the more easy Recovery of Wages, due for the working up the said Manufactures, and to Day-labourers, is committed.

A Petition of the Owners of the Marsh Grounds in the Levels of Havering and Dag in the County of Essex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by an extraordinary Spring Tide 1707, a Breach was made in their Marsh-walls, adjoining to the River of Thames, whereby above 1,000 Acres of Land in the said Level were overflowed, and have ever since continued so, although the Petitioners have been at great Expence to regain the fame; and the great Quantity of Ground, which is fallen into the said Riyer, hath raised a great Part of the Channel, which is likely to obstruct the Navigation thereof; and there is no Likelihood of recovering the said drowned Lands, without a far greater Charge upon the Petitioner* Lands in the said Level, which already is taxed by the Commissioners of Sewers at £ 5. 1 or. per Acre, for repairing the said Breach; and, although they make no Profit of the drowned Lands, they pay the Land Tax at the Rack Rent, as assessed before the Inundation: And praying, that the House will take their deplorable same into Consideration, and grant them Relief therein, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That it be referred to a Committee, to examine the Matter of the said Petition, and report the same to the House.

And it is referred to Sir Gilbert Mr. Lowndes,

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt in her Majesty’s Prison of the Fleet, on behalf of themselves, and other poor Debtors in the several Prisons in and about the City of London, was presented to the House, and read;

setting forth, that by an Act, made in the first Parliament of his late Majesty King William, in , Sessions

the Sixth, for Relief of poor Debtors, it was enacted, that such poor Prisoners for Debt, as then were, or should be, in Prison, upon Complaint to the Magistrate for Want of Maintenance, the Creditor, or Creditors, of such poor Prisoners is to find him the fame, but, in Default thereof, the said Magistrate is empowered to set such poor Prisoner at large: That the Petitioners, who are many Thousands, are reduced to a starving Condition, and divers of their Families kept by their respective Parishes: And praying, that they may have the like Law, as in Scotland, or be otherwise relieved, by their serving in the Fleet, or Army, or finding a fit Person to serve for them.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Town Clerk, Boston Common Council, Vicar, Churchwardens, Gentlemen, Church, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Boston, in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that their Parish Church is an ancient and large Fabrick, wdiofe Tower is very and is a uftfol Sea-mark, and requires a great yearly Sum, to keep it in repair, and Handing within 16 Yards of the Haven, the Parishioners (to preserv the Foundation thereof) are obliged to maintain a Bank, about 20 Foot deep, and 300 Foot long, to keep off a violent ebbing and flowing Water: That the Method of railing Money for those Repairs, and others, common to all Churches, has been by aftelfing the Inhabitants according to the respective Seats they fit in; but this Method, having been about Six Years since contested, was adjudged unwarrantable in the Court of Delegates, though the Parish had before prevailed in Two inferior ecclesiastical Courts; and the Parish fearing, Suits will be commenced, if they /hould aflels after the said usual Manner (though they are desirous, that a Law may be made for the more effectual laying, and colletfting the said Assessment, the Church now wanting great Repairs) they pray, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling them to make Assessments, for repairing, and keeping in repair, the said Church of Boston, and the Bank, adjoining to the Haven there.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Bertie, Mr. Wynn, the Lord Willoughby, Colonel Whitchcot, and Sir Thomas Parker do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of the Merchants, Owners and Matters of Ships, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Whitby, in the County of York, was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, that in the Year 1702 an Act of Parliament patted, for repairing the Harbour of Whitby, and building and repairing the Piers there; for which Purpose several Duties were thereby laid, forraifing a Sum, not exceeding £.6,000 and to continue for Nine Years, if the Work were not finished before: That all the Money, raised by the said Act from the First of , 1702, to the First of May, 1708, being Six Years, amounts but to £. 1,940. 17 s. 4 d.and the Disbursements, already laid out, amount to £. 2,530. 5 s, 5} d. and the Piers are half finished, and the said Two Years to come, next May, will do very little more, than reimburse the Money advanced: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the said Act for repairing the said Harbour, and Piers.

The House proceeded (according to Order) to the heating of the Merits of the double Return of Sir Hugh Paterfone, Baronet, and Henry Cunningham, Esquire, lor the Shire of Sterling, and also the Merits of the said Election.

Preservation of the Trade to has been always held a Matter of high Importance to this Kingdom, and its Plantations; and that Fortsand Settlements are absolutely necessary for the Defence and Improvement of that Trac e, which, the Petitioners are of opinion, cannot be advantageously carried on without ajoint Stock, with Privileges to Support; and that no other Method can enable the British Subjects to serve the Plantations with Negroes at a moderate Rate: That, upon the Encouragement of a Charter, granted by King Charles the ad, in the 24th

Year of his Reign, the Petitioners raised* by Subscription, a considerable Sum of Money for ajoint Stock, and have since advanced several large Sums, great Part of which has been expended in purchasing, erecting, and maintaining, Forts, far Improvement of the said Trade; which . been by them only preserved to the Nation, without any Advantages to the Petitioners, notwithstanding their many great Lodes, during the last, and this present.

War, and the Attempts of foreign Nations to gain this Trade: That in the Year 1697 the Parliament (as a Means to preserve and support this Trade) thought fit to open the fame, by admitting all Persons tq trade to Africa, paying^. 10 per Cent, to the Company, upon their Exports, towards defraying the Charges of Forts and Settle-, merits there; but that Expedient hath not answered its Ends, the unbounded Liberty, given by that Ad to trade, without any Regulation, having lb divided the Interest of the British Nation, that the Natives of Africa impose what they please upon them: and this Difference has much lessened the Prices of Goods, imported to Guinea, and advanced the price of Negroes; and which is fomented by Foreigners, who hope thereby to eogrofe the Trade to themselves: That, notwithstanding all the Lolfes, Difficulties, and Discouragements, the Petitioners have sustained, they have paid several additional Sums upon their Shares in the said joint Stock, in order to preserve the said Trade, so beneficial to the Nation, and are ftiil willing tQ advance a further Stock, sufficiem to support and improve the said Trade in every branch thereof if they may have suitable Encouragement for carrying it;

On: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such needful Privileges, as may enable them effectually to preserve, support, and improve, the said Trade.

Ordered, That the Con side rat ion of the said Petition be referred to a Committee,

Ordered, That it be referred to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Fortnight,

Tefblve itself into the said Committee.

to the House, and read; setting^fortly-ahat the Pcti-» tioners being informed, that the Royal African Company, by their Petition to the lall Parliament, did allege, that the Trade to Guinea was attended with so many Difficul- ties, that it occasioned the Advance of the Price of Negroes, and, by reason of other Hard ships, that Trade was in Danger of falling into the Hands of other Europeans; that the Petitioners are deeply affected in that Trade, their constant Supply of Negroes, at moderate Rates, being the chief Support of whereby

able Damage to the Petitioners, and tends to the Ruin of their Trade, and lessening her Majesty’s Revenue, and the Navigation of Great Britain: And praying, that the British Interest on the Coast of Africa may be effectually preserved, and the Trade put on such a Foot, that the Petitioners may constantly be supplied with a sufficient Number of Negroes, at moderate Rates.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Recruiting Committee of the whose House, to whom the Bill for Land Force*, the speedy and effectual recruiting her Majesty’s Land Forces, and Marines, was committed, the Amendments, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That all Harvest-men shall be free from impressing, chat have a Certificate from the Parish, where they live, and allowed by the Justices of Peace.

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up: And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

For encouraging Deserters to come in.

And the same was twice read, with Blanks} which were filled up; and the Clause amended: And afterwards the same was, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Another Clause was offered,'- to be added to the Bill,

That the Commissioners for the County of Chester, and the Officers of the Town of Cudington, shall execute the Act in a Place called Threapwood, where many Deserters have been harboured.

And the same was twice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

For making good the Money to the Land Tax Credit again, that shall be issued for Recruits.

And the same was twice read, and upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Then several Amendments were proposed to be made to the Bill, Fol. 6, and 7.

And the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of Alborne, an ancient Market-town, belonging to the Duchy of Lancaster, in the County of Wilts, and Twelve Miles from Newberry, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there is a Bill depending in the House, for making the River Kennett navigable from Reading to Neivberry, in the County of Berks: The Petitioners are fully satisfied, the same (if effected) will be a^eneral Advantage to the neighbouring Country, and particularly to the Inhabitants of Alborne, who employ abundance of Poor, in making of Fustian; and it will be a great Ease to them, in conveying their Goods to and from London: And praying, that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Trades-men, dwelling in the Town and Parish of Lamborne, and Parts adjacent, in the said County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the River Kennett in Berkshire, is capable of being made navigable; and, if the same be done, it will be of publick Advantage, and very much tend to the Preservatiao of the Highways: And praying, that a Bill may pass for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making the River Kennett navigable from Reading to Newberry, in the County of Berks, is committed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, Freemen, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Whitchurch, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forthjthat there being a Billintended tobe brought into this House, for making the River Rennet navigable from Reading to Newberry, in the County of Berks, the Petitioners apprehend, that the doing thereof will be of publick Advantage, by promoting of Trade, and supplying the Country with Coals, and other bulky Commodities: And praying, that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Portreeve, Bailiff, Burgesses, and In- Kennett habitants, of the Borough and Parish of Great Bedwin, in Navigation, the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there being a Bill in the House, for making the River Kennett navigable from Reading to Newberry, in the County of Berks, the Petitioners conceive, the same will be a general Good, by rendering the Communication between the Cities of London, Bath, and Bristol, much more commodious, and the Conveyance of their bulky Goods (now sent by Land Carriage, at excessive Rates) more easy, the Roads between Newberry and Reading being almost unpassable: And praying, that the said Bill may pass.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Bailiffs, and other the Justices of the Peace, of the City of Gloucester, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held at Gloucester, for the same City and County thereof, the 10th Day of January, 1708, and in the 7 th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, was presented to the House, and read; lotting forth, that the drift Prosecution, lately commenced in the Exchequer against divers Distillers thereabouts, for a Duty of per Hogshead for the Cyder and Perry they at first buy to distil, under Pretence, they are Buyers and Retiilers thereof, within the Intention of an Act of the First Year of her Majesty’s Reign, for laying a Duty on Malt, Mum, and Cyder, is a great Hardship upon’ them; for that (although they bought their Cyder and Perry publickly) they were not charged with the said Duty, till after they had disposed of great Quantities of Spirits, nor had Notice thereof, and yet now are prosecuted, with a Retrospect of Five or Six Years, for the said Duty, which will amount to more, than many of them are able to pay; and for that the Justices, and the Petitioners, who apprehend themselves to have the Execution and Determination of the said Act lodged in them, (have upon Application) discharged the Distillers of the said Duty, the which (if exacted)will not only ruin the said Distillers, but greatly discourage the felling of Fruit, Cyder, and Perry, and the manufacturing thereof, whereby many Dealers therein maintain their Families, and pay their Taxes: And praying, that, upon the doubtful Construction of the said Act, the said Persons, and Trade, may not be ruined, but relieved by the House.

Mr. Watfotireported from the Committee, to whom Address ad-

it was referred to draw up an Address, upon their Resolu- Y'fm8 ^u*n tion of the 25th lnstant, to be presented to her Majesty; 10 m<irry’ _ that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at tho " Clerk’s Table; where the same was twice read, and is as followeth, viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most loyal and dutiful Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, being truly and deeply sensible of the many and great Blelfings we have enjoyed, during the whole Course of your Majesty’s most glorious Reign, do most humbly conceive, we should be unexcufably wanting to ourselves, and the whole Kingdom, if we should neglect to use our most zealous Endeavours, that those Bleflmgs may be derived down to future Ages; and therefore, with Hearts full of the most profound Respect and Duty to your royal Person, we most humbly beseech your Majesty, graciously to consider the universal Desires, and most humble Supplications, of your faithful Subjects, that your Majesty would not so far indulge your just Grief, as to decline the Thoughts of a second Marriage.

This would be an unspeakable Joy to your People, who would join their most fervent Prayers to Almighty God, to bless your Majesty with royal Hue; all of them concurring in this Opinion, that no greater Happiness can be desired for your Kingdoms, than that they, and their Children, may long continue under the gentle and gracious Government of your Majesty, and your Posterity.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address, to be presented to her Majesty.

Resolved, That the Concurrence of the Lords be desired to the said Address.

Ordered, That Mr. Watson do carry the Address to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors, Prisoners in her Majesty’s Gaol the Cattle of , was presented

to the House, and read; setting forth, that they are many in Number, and most of them imprisoned through vexatious Suits, and Attorneys extravagant Fees; and others of good Education; so that few or none of them (were they at Liberty) but could keep themselves, if not their Families, who are now kept by their Parishes: That many of the Petitioners are so distempered, by nauseous Smells of the Gaol, and for want of Necessaries to support Nature, that their Conditions are very deplorable: And praying the House to relieve them from their miserable Imprisonment, by some Ad of Grace, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the Ease of insolvent Debtors, shall be brought in.

The Queen’s most excellent Majesty in Council.

Christopher's in America, when the French invaded the said Islands in March 1705; and there being fokowife read at the Board a Report from the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, upon the Petition of Stephen Duport, of St. Planter, relating to the great Losses he has sustained there, Which the Petitioner humbly prays, may be considered in the same Manner, as is intended to those, who suffered there in the late Invasion; it is ordered by her Majesty, in bet Privy Council, that the said Returns, and Repo/T of the Commissioner* of Trade, which are hereunto annexed, be, and they are hereby, referred to the Right honourable the Lord High Treasurer, to consider the fame, and to report, what his Lofdship conceives, her Majesty may fitly do therein.

Prayers.

A PETITION of the Cottons, Serge-makers, and

» \ other Woollen Manufacturers, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, and many Hundreds of others, have been greatly supported, by making Goods, usually exported by the Royal African Company; which Trade is (as the Petitioners are informed) in danger of being loft to the Nation, to the Ruin of the Petitioners: And praying, that the Traffick of the said Company to Africa may be preserved, and encouraged, by such Means, as the House shall judge fit.

Ordered, That the Confederation of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of several Tradesmen, inhabiting in and about London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have been very much encouraged in their several Trades, by the Exports of the Royal African Company to; which Trade, from the great Discouragemenls the Company have met with under the present Establishment, has very much declined, and is in danger of being loft to . Nation, to the Prejudice of the Publick Good, and Loss of the Petitioners; And praying, that the Traffick of the said Company to Africa may be secured, and encouraged, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of Briftsl, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Traders and Artificers of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, since the Opening the Trade to Africa, the same has greatly encreased, by the Consumption of our Manufactures, the Increaft of Navigation, and the better supplying the Plantations with Negroes, inso much that they conceive, no Branch of Trade turns to a better Account to the British Nation; and, if the same should be confined to a select Number of Men, exclusive of all others, the contrary Consequences will attend it: And that the^. 10 fer Cent, paid to the African Company, towards Maintenance of Forts and Cadies, by the separate Traders, is found to be a great Discouragement to them, instead of a Security, as they were intended: And praying, that the Trade to Africa may befb settled under such Regulations,

as it may tend to the Benefit of all her Majesty’s Subjects.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants of the several Parishes within the Hamlets of the Tower of London, as

well in behalf of1 their respective Parishes, as of many thousand poor Families within the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Hamlets mostly consist of Seafaring Men, and Tradesmen depending on such, the greatest part of which Seamen are poor, and actually in her Majesty’s Service, and have been supplied withNeceflaries by such Tradesmen, upon the Credit of their Wages, who, by want of their Money, have been reduced to great Extremities; and, when they* or their Agents, have attended the Payment of several Ships at Chatham, Portsmouth, and Plymouth, at great Expence,

they have been at last obliged to return home without Payment, and many of the Seamen’s Wives have been forced to beg in their Way home; and sometimes such Tradesmen have been denied the Privilege of going on board the Ships, and the Seamen many times permitted to receive their Wages, though they had made Assignments to their Creditors; and frequent Payments have been made without publick Notice; and generally, when the Ships are ready to fail, so that such Seamen, as have been willing to fend up their Wages for the Subsistence of their Families, and Payment of their Creditors, have not Opportunity to do it, whereby the Money has been loft to the Enemy, or lpent in foreign Parts, and the Creditors never paid; which has so discouraged them, that they will give no further Credit; (b that the Wives and Children of Seamen in her Majesty’s Pay, and many Families of their Creditors, are become chargeable to their respective Parishes, which are greatly impoverished, and not able to relieve them: And praying such Redress in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, who are to examine the Accounts, which have been laid before this House, of what, Ships have been employed as Cruifersand Convoys, over and above the Ships for the Line of Battle, and for Convoys to remote Parts; and also the Estimate of the Debt of her Majesty’s Navy, as it flood, on the Heads mentioned in the said Estimate, the 30th of September, 1708; and that Mr. Barker, and all, that serve for the City of London, and County of Surry, be added to the said Committee.

according to the _ Will of Samuel Sainthill, Esquire, deceased, was committed; that they had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true 1 and that the Committee had directed him to report the same to the House, without any Amendment: And he delivered the same in at the Clerk’s Table.

A Petition of several Freeholders, and Inhabitants, in the County of Berks, within Five Miles of the City of Oxford, on behalf of themselves, and other Inhabitants within the Limits aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; Letting, forth, that by an Act, made -in the 18th Year of the Reign of Queen all Inhabitants, living within Five Miles of the City of (except Day-la--bourers, and hired Servants) being possessed ot one Yard Land, or upwards, or having, or using, a Cart, Plough, or Wain, should find-or fend, for the mending or repairing the decayed Bridges, or Ways, within one Mile of the said City, with all things necessary, as by the said Act is directed, under divers Penalties; and all this was to be done, in Consideration that the said Inhabitants were exempt from Purveyance, as the Ad recites: That by an Act, of the 12* Car. idi, no Sum of Money, or other Thing, should be takvn for Purveyance for his Majesty, his Heirs or Successors: That the Inhabitants within Five Miles of Oxon are charged towaids the repair of the said Highways, and Bridges, in a different Manner from all the red. of her Majesty’s Subjects, and yet have no greater Privilege, they being also exempt from Purveyance by t! e last mentioned Act: That the Petitioners are at very great Charge in repairing the Highways of -their Parishes, and also the Highways within a Mile of Oxon, to which they have been forced to submit, even inHarveft-time, being then summoned to do their Work by the said Act, although the Inhabitants of Oxon are much better able, and can with more Ease repair their said Highways, and Bridges, than the Petitioners; and yet are in a manner wholly exempt from the Charge and Trouble thereof: And praying, that Leave maybe given to bring in a Bill for repealing the Act of the 18th Year of Queen Eliz. intituled, An Act for the repairing and amending of the Bridges, and Highways, near unto the City of Oxford.

Alio another Petition of several Freeholders, and Inhabitants, in the County of Oxon, within Five Miles of the City of Oxford, on behalf of themselves and other Inhabitants within the Limits aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; being in the same Words, as the Petition last before-mentioned.

And the said Act being read;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petitions; and that the Lord Ryalton, Sir John Slonehouse, Sir Wheat, Mr. Mordaunt, Mr. Page, and Mr. Dolben, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Ordered, That the Lord Downe, and Sir Wm. Strickland, be added to the Gentlemen, who are to prepare, and bring in, the Bill for the better regulating the Manufacture of the broad Woollen Cloth, in relation to the Lengths and Breadths.

A PETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, together with other the principal Inhabitants, of the City of Bath, was presented to the House, and read; fitting forth, that there is a Bill depending in the House, for making the River Kennett navigable from Reading to Newberry, in the County of Berks, the doing whereof, the Petitioners apprehend, will be of publick. Advantage, to the Preservation of the Highways, Improvement of Trade, and Increase of Watermen: And praying, that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Importing A PETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen, Com-Inih \ am. mon Council, Freemen, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Dunhevod, alias Launceston, in the County of Cornwall, in behalf of themselves, and Hundreds in the Neighbourhood, Was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Trade of the said Town chiefly depends on the Spinning, and Sale, of Woollen Yarn, which is almost wholly the Employment and Maintenance of their Poor; which Trade is of late Years very much decayed, by the Importation of Irish Yarn, to the lluin of the Poor, the sinking the Petitioners Estates, in so much as to render them unable to relieve them, and pay Taxes,

if this mischievous Importation be not prevented: And praying, that the House will take some Method, to put a Stop to the Importation of Irish Yarn, and thereby prevent the Ruin of so many poor Families.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of she Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and of the Merchants and Traders, of the City of Exon, on behalf of diemselves, and many thousand others, employed in the Woollen Manufactures within the said City, and Places adjacent, is referred.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Cal-lingtm, in the County of Cornwall, on behalf of themselves, and many poor Families in their Neighbourhood, Was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that their chief Trade and Support depertdson the Spinning, and Sale, of Woollen Yarn; which Trade is very much lessened, by the visible Decay of their publick Markets, and almost the Ruin of their Poor, by the Importation of such Yarn from Ireland: And praying, that such effectual Methods may be taken, as may wholly put a Stop to the Importation of Irish Yarn, or lay it under such Duties, as may prevent the utter Ruin of their Poor, and Trade.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be 21

referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and of the Merchants and'Traders, of the City of Exon, on the behalf of themselves, and many thousand others, employed in the Woollen Manufactures within tire said City, and Places adjacent, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayer, capital Burgesses, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of in the County of

Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that many thousand of Families are ruined by the great Importation of Worsted Yarn from Ireland, being loid at much cheaper Rates, than it can be wrought in England: And praying the Compassion of the House, for their Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and of the Merchants and Traders, of the City of Exon, on the behalf of themselves, and many thousands others, employed in the Woollen Manufactures within the said City, and Places adjacent, is referred.

A Petition of Margaret and Mary Molhy was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, in 1705, did prefer their Petition to this House, praying, that they might be relieved in relation to an Estate of their Grandfather and Father’s in Ireland, sold as a forfeited Estate; which Petition was referred to Committee, who reported the Matter thereof, and came to a Resolution, as their Opinion, that the Petitioners had proved the Allegations of their Petition, and that they were real Objects of Companion, and jullly deserved the Favour of the House; but the Parliament was fcon after prorogued, and nothing was done for the Petitioners: That the Petitioners having obtained her Majesty’* gracious Recommendation, and renewed their Petition to the House the last Session, it was ordered, that the Consideration thereof should be referred to a Committee, to examine the Matter, and report the same to the House: That the Committee accordingly reported, that the Petitioners had fully proved the Allegations of their Petition, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; yet nothing is done for their Relief: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Petitioners Relief; in regard that, by their great Poverty, they are disabled from leeking any other lledress, but what they hope for from the Justice of the House.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House.

A Petition of the Right honourable Richard Lord Bellew was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that at the Election of a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Steyning, in the County of Sussex, in the room of the Lord Tunbridge (called up to the House of Lords) the Petitioner and Harry Goring, Esquire, flood Candidates; and the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to have been returned alone; but by Bribery, Menaces, and Partiality of the Constable of the said Borough, who polled several, who had no Right, for Mr. Goirng, and refused others to poll for the Petitioner, who had a Right, and by other undue Practices of Mr. Goring, and his Agents, he has procured an Indenture to be annexed to the Precept, as if he was elected, though the Constable refused to sign the Indenture for Mr. Goring, but signed the Petitioner’s, which ought only to be annexed to the said Precept: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Merits of the said Petition be heard upon Tuesday Seven-night, the Merits of the said Election,

and double Return, being appointed to be then heard, upon the Petition of Harry Goring, Esquire.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Borough importing of Tiverton, as also of the Merchants, Serge-makers, Irish Yam. Combers, Weavers, and others, employed in the Woollen Manufacture within the said Borough, and in the Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that great Quantities of Worsted, as well as Woollen Yarn, have been of late Years imported from Ireland into the Western Parts of England, and are sold at much lower Rates, than it is possible to make them for here; which Advantage is so great to the Importers, as to encourage them (though to the Prejudice of their Country) to enlarge their Commissions for those Commodities more and more yearly; by reason whereof the Labour of many thousand Hands in those Parts is loft, the Poor increased daily, the Value of Lands sinking apace, and all Trade miserably declining, and nothing but a feasonable Relief from the House, can prevent their Ruin, which, they humbly conceive, was their Intent last Session, though it had not its due Effect: And

graying, that this Grievance may be redrafted by proper Remedies.

Ordered, That the Confederation of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of Exon, is referred.

A Petition of several registered Seamen, in behalf of Seamen'* themselves, and other registered Seamen now living, Bounty* and the Widows and Children of such, as are dead, was monay' presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by an Act of Parliament, made in the 7th and 8th Year of the late King William (for Encouragement of Seamen) it is enacted, that every Seaman, who should register himself, and serve his said Majesty, his Heirs, and Successors, according to the Directions of the said Act, should have 40 s.per Annum Bounty, above such other Pay, as he should be entitled unto; That the Petitioners (in Obedience to the Rules of the said Act) duly registered themselves, and became intitled to the said Bounty- money, which amounted to £. 16,389. due to those registered in the First Year of his said Majesty’s Reign; and upon the 10th March 1697, the Commons passed the following Votes: Resolved, That the Sum of £.16,389,

Report, that Domingo Seraftno, Peter Montalta, and Ephraim Nafleta, Mariners, were also on board the said Brigantine, and said to the same Effect as delRofario, and swore it before the Court of Admiralty; which Affidavits, Speaker’s Chamber, ligned by Richard Crawley, Esquire, Register to the said Court, made it more fully appear.

Dr. Bramston attended, and said, that he made the Report, and had compared the Marks produced by Corfo, as in the Margent of his Report, and found the same exactly to agree with the Marks of the Goods found with Kidd.

Abr. De Almeda, Merchant, said, that he knew Mr.

Corfo ox Cadiz in 1684, and a considerable Merchant, trading in several Sorts of Merchandizes; afterwards had Correspondence with him in the Spanish West Indies, at which Time he had a very good Ship of his own, and was a man of Credit and Reputation: That about Six Years ago, or thereabouts, the said Corfo, coming to England, came to him, and told him, that he had been robbed by Kidd, the Pirate, and desired his Assistance, that he might get some Recompence for what he had loft (which was to a considerable Value) which the said Almeda did, ever since, to the utmost of his Power.

Mr. isaac Dyas and Mr. Abr. Nunes, Merchants, said, that they knew the said Corfo about 14 or 15 Years ago, in the West Indies', and at that Time commanded a good Ship of his own, and was always looked upon to be a very honest Man, and of Substance, before he was robbed by Kidd, as they have been credibly informed.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Art and Mistery of Masons, of the City of London, incorporated by royal Charter, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of their Fellow-subjects, employed in the said Trade, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that of late Years great Quantities of wrought Marblehave been imported into this Kingdom from Italy, and other foreign Parts, and exposed to Sale here, contrary to all former Usage, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and the Ruin of many hundreds of their poor Workmen, and their Families, who (now the publick Structures of the Nation are near finished) will want Bread, and become chargeableto their respective Parishes, unless such Importation be prohibited, their foie Livelihood being in the sawing, and otherwise preparing, the unwrought Marble for the Petitioners, the Workers therein, who make the same Sorts of Commodities much better in Workmanship, than those imported; and, if this growing Evil be not speedi/y prevented by Parliament, the Petitioners have no other Prolpect, but an utter Extirpation of the Art of working in Marble within this Kingdom: And praying, that the House will grant them all fitting Encouragement in their laid Trade, and give Leave to bring in a Bill to prevent the Importation of any wrought Marble, for Sale, into this Kingdom for the future.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir William Ashhurfi, Mr. Farrer, and Sir Wm. Whitlock, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A PETITION of the Merchants of Aberdeen was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that, by the 4th Article of Union, all the Subjects of the United Kingdom of Great Britain are to have free Intercourse of Trade to and from any Port or Place within the Dominions, or Plantations, of the United Kingdom: That in the last Session of Parliament there were Attempts of setting up of Companies, for particular Branches of Trade beyond Sea, exclusive of all others, which tended to restrain the Privileges, the Petitioners ought to enjoy by the Union; and, left there should be the like Addresses this Session, of which they, at so great Distance, could not have timely Notice of, and yet be excluded, they pray, that there may not be (and conceive there cannot be) any exclusive Articles, or Privileges, granted to any Society of Trade, to the Petitioners Prejudice.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Now, My Lords, permit your Pannel to lay, with the utmost Submission and Deference* that, whatever other End Mr. Chamillart might propose to himself to serve, by sacrificing so frankly a criminal Commis, some Part of his Design would leem to be so timed, as to lave the Marshal from any new Mortification by a Discovery (whenever it should happen) that would involve him equally in the Guilt. But, left your Lordships should think, that your Pannel. laid any manner of Strefe on a Present from the Marshal, upon his Return into France, which seemed, when he made that Promise* to be very remote, and uncertain, I do hereby declare, that I never looked upon it any otherwise, than as a men French Com* pliment, which Mr. Chamillart has very fealbnably marred, both for the Marshal, and himself, who, it would appear* was displeased at the Marshal’s engaging him too deep.

As to that villainous Expression " Prince Refugie," which his Grace my Lord Duke of Marlborough did so deservedly first tax your Lordships Pannel with j I declare solemnly, before God, and your Lordships, that my Heart did not go along with the Hand, that wrote it} for which, however, I acknowledge, the one ought to be struck off, the other pulled out alive, though but for mentioning it once in the whole course of my criminal Correspondence, nay (which is more) in all my Life before; and yet, that it escaped me that once, was rhore Matter of just Concern to me afterwards, in my lucid Intervals, than all I had wrote besides, though every Tittle of it was, in its own Nature, capital: For let me most humbly beseech your Lordships to believe, that, if I have foolilhly given a handle for so horrid a Tache, it is but of avery late Date, having never been reputed a Jacobite, nor frequented the Company of those inconsiderable few, whom the World branded with that Name, either here.

or at Edinburgh; on the contrary, my Lords, Murray, who was lately taken up there, intended me neither K.ind-ness, nor Honour (how proud soever I should have been of wearing that Character) when he called me, in a publick Company (as I heard afterwards) the flmover Resident $ which, considering the Ferment some of my Countrymen were then in, was not so very safe. I would not seem to make a Merit of this to her Majesty, or extenuate the Crime, for which I am impannelled before your Lordships; but, if I must die, according to my Demerit, let it be without the odious Name of a Jacobite; which I do hereby, and henceforth, utterly, disc claim, and abjure, as heartily and sincerely, as if I took that Oath in the most solemn Manner.

William Greg.

Signed by William Greg, being first read to him, at the,

January 3d, 1707, and owned to be all his own Hand-writing.

Turkey A Petition of the incorporated Company of Clothiers Trade. jn tjje City of Worcester was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioners employ many thousand Families in the said City, and Parts adjacent, for 15 or ao Miles about, in making fine Woollen Cloth for the Turkey Trade chiefly; but the Turkey Company (which consists but of a small Number of eminent trading Merchants) have of late shipped out but oncC in Two Years (and lay, they shall ship no more till 171b) and then lade but Eight or Ten ships, and so little fine Cloth of the Petitioners, that it’s probable, those Markets would take off more of them yearly, if lent thither; and this might readily be done by our British Merchants, but the most considerable Ports, for vending it, being within the Limits of the Turkey Company’s Charter, they are restrained, and the Turkey Trade in a great measure supplied by the Dutch and French, whilst the Petitioners are at a Rand, for want of Sales, and many of them broke thereby, though they have great Stocks lying dead upon their Hands, great Numbers of Poor reduced to great Extremity, for want of Work, and, if not timely provided for, will make many more of their Manufacturers leave their Country, for want of Employment, or force them to beg, starve, or Heal: And praying, that either the Turkey Company may be enlarged, by paying ealy Fines for Ad million, and obliging them to more frequent shipping, or by laying open the Turkey Trade, under such Regulations, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and of the Merchants and Traders, of the City of Exon, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousends, employed in the Woollen Manufacture within the said City, and Places adjacent, is referred; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House.

The said Address was twice read, and is as followeth; War. viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, considering the great Expence of Blood and Treasure, that your Majesty, and your Allies, have been at, in prosecuting this long War, for securing the Liberties of Europe, do most humbly beseech your Majesty, that, for the preserving the Repose and Quiet of Europe, and preventing the ambitious Designs of France for the future, your Majesty would be pleased to take care, at the Conclusion of the War, to continue and establish a good and firm Friend ship among all tho Allies; and that the French King may be obliged to own your Majesty’s Title, and the Protestant Succession, as it is established by the Laws of Great; and that your

Allies be engaged to become Guarantees of the fame:

And that your Majesty would take effectual Methods that the Pretender shall be removed out of the French Dominions, and not differed to return, to disturb your Majesty, your Heirs or Successors, in the Protestant Line.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled.

IN Obedience to her Majesty’s Commands, upon the Address of this honourable House, I do humbly certify, that out of the Sum of Fourteen thousand Eight hundred and Nineteen Pounds, Nine Shillings, issued to me, for her Majesty’s secret Services, from Michaelmas, 1707, to Michaelmas, 1708, or out of any such Money, to me issued since that Time, no Payment hath been made to any Member or Members of this honourable House, or to any in Trust for them, unless it be a yearly Sum of Five hundred Pounds to William Cotefvcurth, Esquire, which, by a Writing under her Majesty’s royal Sign manual, bearing Date the 8th Day of July, 1706 (for the Causes and Confederations therein mentioned) is to continue to be paid to him, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, during her Majesty’s Life; which God long preserve!
