A Petition of the Merchants, Weavers, and other Traders, concerned in the Woollen Manufacture, in relation to the Bill for the Encouragement of the Exportation of Tobacco, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the City of Norwich, and Parts adjacent, maintain a considerable Trade to Portugal, by exporting of Stuffs, and Corn; which will be obstructed by opening of a Trade to France, by reason an Opportunity will thereby be given of exporting Bullion, and Wool, to the Prejudice of the Kingdom in general; And praying the Premises may be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Cloth-dressers, and Drapers, within the Town and Parish of Wakefield, in the West Riding in the County of York, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, that most Families in those Parts are supported by the Cloth Trade, and chiefly by making of Cloth, called whole thick Kerseys, and whole thick Plains; and whereas the Traders and Dealers in those Sorts of Cloths have suffered very much, by the over-llretching and straining of those Commodities by the Makers, to the Loss and Disparagement of the said Trade in this Kingdom, and beyond Seas: And praying, a Clause may be inserted in the Bill for the regulating the Length and Breadths of Cloths, to inflict a Penalty on all Makers, who shall drain the said Cloths above half a Yard in Length.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be made from the Committee, to whom the Bill is committed.

A Petition of James Metcalfe, of London, Merchant, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Ship, called Francis and Samuel, Datoi-built, being every way fit for importing naval Stores for *her Majesty’s. has been, and is now, employed in that Service: And praying, a Bill may be brought in, for the making the said Ship a free Ship.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Mervin, Mr. Topham, and Mr. Swinfin, do prepare and bring in, the Bill.

The House being informed, that a Person attended from the Commissioners of the Customs, he was called in, and, at the Bar, presented to the House, A Return to an 22

Order, of the Sixteenth of February last, for an Account, what the Duties on Brass Wire, made from English Copper, have amounted to for Ten Years.

And being withdrawn;

The Title of the Account was read; and the said Return is as followeth; viz.

To the honourable the Commissioners, for managing, and causing to be levied and collected, her Majesty’s Customs, &c.

THERE being directed to me, from your Board, an Order of the honourable House of Commons, bearing Date the 16 Instant, That the Commissioners of the Cut toms do lay before this House, what the Duties on Brass Wire, made from English Copper, do amount to for the last Ten Years; I humbly certify, that Brals Wire, drawn from English Copper, and foreign Copper, manufactured here, and all Sorts of Brass Manufactures, pay a like Duty of Ten Pence perC. Weight; and therefore the Merchants, in their Warrants for Exportation, do not distinguish, which is which, but enter the same under the general Head of Brass Manufactures; so that no separate Account of the Duties arising from Brass Wire, drawn from English Copper, can be given.

Charles Davenant.

Custom-house, London,

Inspector General’s

Office, 25* Februarii,

Mr. Peyton reported from the Committee, to whom it. Expiring was referred to inspect the Laws expired, and near l-awi. expiring, and to report, what are fit to be revived, or continued 5 that they had inspected the Laws accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were read, and are as follow:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act of Parliament, made in the Eighth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign (intituled, An Act for the better preventing the counterfeiting the current Coin of this Kingdom) which was to continue for One Year, was, by a Clause in another Act, made in the Ninth Year of his said Majesty’s Reign, continued in force until the 25th'

Day of March, 1701; and which Act was further continued by an Act, made in the first Year of her present Majesty’s Reign, till the 25th of March, 1709, and from thence to the End of the First Session of Parliament then next ensuing; is fit to be made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the Third and Fourth Years of her Majesty’s Reign, (intituled, An Act for giving like Remedy upon Promissory Notes, as is now used upon Bills of Exchange, and for the better Payment of inland Bills of Exchange) which was to continue for the Space of Three Years, from the First Day of May, 1705, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament, is fit to be made perpetual.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the Time, that all the Principal and Interest, which by former Acts of Parliament are charged upon the said Impositions upon Wines, Vinegar, Tobacco, and East India Goods, and upon the said additional Impositions, and upon the said Duties upon Whale-fins, or upon them, or any of them, jointly with other Duties, shall be paid off, and satisfied, or that sufficient Money shall be reserved in the Exchequer for that Purpose, all the Monies, which shall from thenceforth arise by the said Impositions upon Wines, Vinegar, Tobacco, and East India Goods, and by the said additional Impositions, and Duties upon Whale-fins, shall be appropriated towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Tobacco, to be used or consumed on board any of her Majesty’s Ships of War, in any Part of Europe, be stamped.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty be laid upon the said Stamps.

8. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be One Penny for every Stamp, to be affixed to every Four Pound Weight of such Tobacco; the same to be paid by the Manufacturer thereof.

The First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth, Resolutions, hieing severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The sixth Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by inferring, after "Europe? these Words, "which shall " be sold by the Commander, or Purser."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, so amended. That all Tobacco, to be used or consumed on board any of her Majesty’s Ships of War, in any Part of Europe, which shall be sold by the Commander, or Purser, be stamped.

Privilege Mr. Compton reported from the Committee of Privileges, to whom it was referred to examine the Matter of the Complaint of a Breach of Privilege against George Duckett, Esquire, a Member of this House; that they had examined the same accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table;

.....were read.

The Report, and Resolutions, areas follow; viz. That the Counsel for Mr. Duckett infilled that Mr.

BenediB Browne had caused a Declaration in Ejectment to be delivered to one Henry who lived in a Cottage, built on the Wade of Mr. Ducket'% Manor of Caine, and wras Mr. Duckett'% Tenant.

That the Evidence on behalf of Mr. Ducket, was,

John Bohen-, who said he knew s Tene-

ment, which was built by Jof Hele, about 40 Years ago; and the Ground was granted to the said Hele, by Mr. Duckett's Grandfather, at the Request of the Parish: He said, the said Cottage, or Tenement, was not worth above vos. a Year, and was a Milevoff of Caine, and near the Highway; and that the Manor of Studley comes up to the said Highway, but the Tythingham of Studley is sworn. at Caine Court; and one Burges, that lives in the next Tenement to Bevin, and on the same Wide, did Suit and Service at Caine Court, which is Mr. Duckett's.

Then Mr. Duckett's Counsel produced a Paper, importing a Certificate of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Overseers, and others, of the Borough and Pariflx of Cain, of the Poverty of Joseph Hele; and praying, Mr. Ducket do grant him a Plat of Ground in same Part of his Lordship, to set up a Place of Harbour for himself, and his Wife, that he might work, and not be a Burthen to the Parish.

This Paper is subscribed Will. Ducket; and also by the said Minister, Churchwardens, Overseers, and others; and Mr. Blaake said, he believed it was old Mr. Ducket's Hand.

Mr. Henry Blaake, being further examined, said, that at the last Quarter Sessions Bevin and Burges appeared to an Indictmentupon the Statute against erectingCottages; and Mr. Brown a(ked Bevin, upon whose Land his Tenement waserested: To which Bevin anfivered, that it was always held to be Mr. Duckett's Land, and he owned Mr. Ducket for his Landlord; To which Mr. Brown replied, that he would make him know, that he would have it, in spite of him, and Mr. Ducket too. Mr. Blaake said, that the Land, on which s Cottage Hood, was always reputed Parcel of the Manor of Cahte, though, he believed, Mr. Brown's Land came very near it, and was divided only by a Ditch.

That, on the Part of Mr. Browne, same Court Rolls of the Manor of Studley were offered as Evidence; but the Committee did not think fit to read them, because the Question depended on the Possession, and not the Title.

Then, to prove Mr. Ducket out of Possession, Mr. Brown's Counsel produced a Copy of an Issue in the Common Pleas, in an Ejectment, joined Trin. 6° Anna Regina, brought for this Tenement, which is upon the Demise of George Duckett, Esquire; and Sir Geo. Hunger-ford, and Mr. Brown are the Defendants: And the Witness said. That Issue remained undetermined.

That, by way of Reply, Mr. Ducket's Counsel produced the Copy of the Declaration, for delivering which the Complaint was made, which Declaration is of Michaelmas Term last, and is mentioned to be of the Demise of BenediB Browne, Esquire: And Mr. Duckett's Counsel infilled, that, if the Ejectment, brought- by Mr. Duckett, was an Argument, that Mr. Ducket was then out of Possession, the Ejectment, brought by Mr. Browne and mentioned in the Complaint, was an Argument, that Mr. Brown was out of Possession at that Time.

And there being no Evidence, that Sir Geo. Hungerford was concerned in delivering the Declaration of Eje&ment;

The Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir George Hungerford is not guilty of a Breach of Privilege.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Mr. BenediB Brown, in causing a Declaration in Ejectment to be delivered to Henry Bevin, a Tenant of George Duckett, Esquire (a Member of the House') during the Time of Privilege of Parliament, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of the House.

The First Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A. Maynwaring.

March 10th, 1701

The Orders of the Day being read 1 Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday next, at. Twelve a Clock, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Report of the Lord High Treasurer (made upon an Address to her Majesty the Eighteenth Day of March, 1706) relating to the Losses of the People of Nevis and St.

The House proceeded to take into Confederation the Papers, which have been laid before this House, relating to the designed Invasion of Scotland, and the Proceedings thereupon, and against the Lord Griffin, and others, taken in Rebellion, and relating to the Persons, taken upon Suspicion, and also to the Garrisons in Scotland.

And a Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, that Orders were not issued, for the marching of the Troops in England, until the 14th Day of March, being Two Days after the Enemy had anchored in the Firth;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting, after the Word " March,* these Words, " it being necessary for the Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, that the Troops in this " Part of the Kingdom should not March into Scotland, till there was certain Intelligence, that the Enemy intended to land in that Part of the United Kingdom." And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out, at the End thereof, these Words, " being Two Days after the Enemy had anchored " in the Firth'*

And the feme was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that Orders were not issued for the marching of the Troops in England, until the Fourteenth Day of March, it being necessary for the Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, that the Troops in this Part of the Kingdom should not march into Scotland, till there was certain Intelligence, that the Enemy intended to land in that Part of the United Kingdom.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put. That it appears to this House, that timely and efteaual Care was taken by those, employed under her Majesty at the Time of the intended Invasion of Scotland, to disappoint the Deligns of Her Majesty’s Enemies both at home and abroad, by fitting out a sufficient Number of Men aa

of War, ordering a competent Number of Troops from Flanders, giving Directions for the Forces in Ireland to be ready for the Assistance of the Nation, and by making the necessary and proper Dispositions of the Forces in England j The House divided:

The Yeas go forth:

Tellers so, the Ye*, } '*<-

Tellers for the Noes,

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Seamens

Wages.

A Petition of many principal Inhabitants of the honourable City of London, as well in behalf of themselves, as the generality of Tradesmen within the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they have for many Years last past, found the Decay of Trade; one principal Reason whereof is the present Manner of paying her Majesty’s Ships of War, and recalling the fame, viz. the paying the Seamen, that are on board such Ships, when they are ready to fail, and often under Sail; and at the same time, Matters of Apprentices, Creditors of Seamen, and Seamens Wives, have often been denied Admittance into the Ships; whereby several Hundred thousand Pounds are carried out of the Nation, and expended in foreign Parts; and many of her Majesty’s Ships of War have been taken, with great Sums on board, and thereby enriched the Enemy; and notwithstanding the Wages of those Persons, who have died in the Service, or been discharged, have not been paid till several Months after the Payment of such Ships, but left to Recall, which have been at Porfmouth, Chathamand even at;

which have obliged many Hundreds to attend at those Places several Months, at great Expence, to the great Discouragement to Seamen, whole Families reside about the said City, and several Hundred thousand Pounds Annum have been carried down to those Places, for Payment of Recalls, which might at less Charge been paid at the Pay Office, as formerly: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, and Redress.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Ministers, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of the Parishes within the Hamlets of the Tower of London, as well in behalf of their respective Parishes, as of many thousand poor Families within the same, is referred.

A PETITION of the Matters, and Owners, of Foreign built Ships and Vdfels in Ipswich, in the County of Ships. Suffolk, on behalf of themselves, and other Inhabitants,' was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that several Bills being already brought, and others ordered to be brought into this honourable House, for making free divers Ships built abroad; that the Petitioners, upon the Faith of the Act of Navigation, and several other Acts of Parliament, have laid out the greatest Part of their Substance in building Ships at home, at much dearer Rates, than such Ships could be built abroad, find themselves obliged to pray the Consideration of the House, and of the Shipwrights, Smiths, Rope-makers, any many other Traders, depending upon the building of Ships at Home: And praying the Compassion of this House, and Relief against tins growing Evil.

Ordered, That: the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Reports from the Committees, to* whom the Bills for making foreign-built Ships free Ships, are committed.

A Petition of Edmund Dimmer, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that at the last Election for the Borough of Arundel/, in the County of Sussex, the 12th Instant, the Lord and the

Petitioner Hood Candidates; when George Moor, Mayor, John Deane, a Commissioner of the Taxes, Thomas

an Attorney, and several others, were Agents for the said Lord; and by Bribery, Threats, and other indirect and illegil Practices, procured several Votes for the said Lord, and deterred several Peffons from voting for the Petitioner; and other arbitrary Proceedings were made

A Petition of John Savage, Gentleman, in behalf of Duua several of the Inhabitants of the Counties of Wexford,'

Kilkenny, and other Counties, in Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in the Year 1690 the Government of Ireland ordered the Subjects of that Kingdom to subsist and maintain the Army, employed in the Reduction thereof, promising them Payment: That Brigadier Eppinger'% Dragoons, and other Dutch and Danish Troops, were quartered in and about the said Counties, and maintained by the Petitioners, two whole Winters, and hitherto have had no Satisfaction:

That the Officers, or their Agents, by Threats reduced the Demands of the Country to veiy inconsiderable Sums, and for which several of them gave Bills: That their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary appointed Commffioners in Ireland, to state the Accounts between the Army and the Country; which was done, and the Petitioners Agent delivered up to the Commissioners the Officers Bills, and the Commissioners signed printed Certificates of what remained due to the Petitioners:

That they are informed, this House intends to clear the Remains, due to the said foreign Troops without Regard to the Debts, due from them to the Subjects of Ireland:

And praying, this honourable House will use some Means for the Petitioners Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Saturday next, when the said Memorial is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

A Petition of Sir John Crisp, Baronet, and Charles African

Esquire, Grand Ions and Representatives of Sir Trade,

Crisp, Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that Sir Nicholas Crisp, the Petitioners Greatr grandfather, about 1632 had, with others, Letters Patents from King Charles the First, for the foie Trade of Guinea, Byn, and Angola, on the Coast of Africa, for 31 Years, and afterwards bought in the other Partners Shares:

That the said Sir Nicholas first opened the Trade to , and built the Castle of Cormanteen, and ere (fled Fadories in the Country, at the Expence (as he computes, by his Will in the Year 1^65) of £. 100,000. That in 1647 the King granted him 2o’r Years more, after the Expiration of the said 31 Years: That in 1660 King James (then Duke of York) obtained Letters Patents, for erecting a Company for the said Trade to Africa-, whereupon Petitioners Grandfather petitioned his Majesty in Council, and on 20th December, 1661, it was referred to a Committee, to endeavour to reconcile and adjust Matters betwixt said Sir Nicholas, and the then erected Company:

That afterwards the Lords Committees made an Order, that said Grandfather should receive of the said Company £. 20,000 to be paid by Two and an Half per Cent, upon all their Goods, outwardsand homeward bound; to which the Company leetii to acquiesce, and thereupon took possession of the said Castle of Cormanteen, but never paid a Peny to said Grandfather, or his Family: That ifi 1663 the Dutch took the Castle of Cormanand are dill in Possession thereof: That by a Bill now depending, the Royal African Company are to receive Satisfaction for their Forts and Callles upon the Coast of Guinea:

And praying, they may be admitted, by themselves, or Counsel, to make out their Claim and Right, and be relieved.

Ordered, That the Confederation of the said Petition bfc referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard before the Committee thereupon, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

Memorandum; The following Deductions are to be made in Abatement of the real Deficiency of the Funds,

In the Account for the Year 1704, the Sum of £. 218,161. 18 s.$±d is charged, as paid, pursuant to an Address of the House, to make good"} Alliances with the Duke of Savoy \ and in the Account for the Year 1705, the Sum of £. 40,000 was voted by the House, for Subsidy to the f Duke of Savoy from the 3d October, 1703,10 the 25th December, 1703; which £. 40,000 is taken to be voted Anno 1705, towards making good C

so much of the £.218,161. i8x. Sid. as was paid Anno 1704;' therefore (unless abated) makes a double Charge.....j

In the Account for the Year 1705, the Sum of £. 107,500 is charged, as paid, pursuant to an Address of the House, to make good Treaties^ with the King of Prussia; and in the Account for the Year 1706, the Sum of £. 48,630 appears to be voted by the House, for making goods Subsidies to the King of Prussia, which was not provided for Anno 1705 i which £. 48,630 is taken to be voted 1706, towards making good/ io much of the £. 107,500 as was paid Amo 1705, and (unless abated) makes also a double Charge - -y

Also, in the Account for the Year 1705, the Sum of £. 65,000 is charged, as paid, pursuant to an Address of the House, for Bounty Money to! Land Forces and Train; and in the Account for the Year 1706, the like Sum 65,000 was voted, to make good the said Bounty Money > Anno 1705 i which is likewise a double Charge; and therefore abate -

So that the real Deficiency of the Funds (after making the aforegoing Deductions for Sums doubly charged) to answer all the public Services') voted, addressed for, or enacted, pursuant to the particular Accounts referred to, is ----- -j

2d April, 1709.

Navy Debt Sir 'Thomas Littleton presented to the House, The humble Return of the principal Officers and Commissioners of her Majesty’s Navy, to the Order, of the 24th of March Iaft, for laying before the House, the Causes of the Increase of the Debt of the Navy.

And the Title thereof was read.

The said Return is as follows; viz.

Navy Office, 30th 7 The humble Return of the prin-March, 1709. 3 cipal Officers and Commissioners of

her Majesty’s Navy to the Order of the honourable House of Commons, of the 24th lnstant, for laying before the House, the Causes of the Increase of the Debt of the Navy; the like having been presented to the Committee, appointed to examine the Estimate of the Debts of the Navy, the 6th of December last, in pursuance of their Order, of the 3d of that Month.

THAT as for the two Heads, which relate to this Office; namely, that of the Wear and Tear, and Extra and Ordinary; and that of Seamen’s Wages; the Increase proceeds from the Charge of the said Services exceeding the Moneys received for them:

From keeping Ships at Sea for more than 40,000 Men:

From building, and buying of Ships, to make good the Losses, which have happened since the War, by the great Storm, Captures, and other Accidents:

.. From the addition of Buildings, and other Improvements, made at the several Yards since the War: Premiums for naval Stores, imported from the Plantations:

Rewards to the Officers, and Seamen, for taking Prizes, according to the late Acts of Parliament: Bounties to Seamen, who entered voluntarily on board the Fleet.

The like to Widows, and Orphans, of Men (lain at Sea:

The like to the Officers, and Seamen, for their good Service in the Battle of Malaga:

Half-pay to Captains and Lieutenants, whilst: out of Employment at Sea:

Payments made to the Office of Sick and Wounded:

The like, at the Beginning of the War, to the Transport Office, fsV.

We wrote to the Commissioners of the Victualling, to give us an Account of the Increase of the Debt on that Head; who have returned us the following Answer; viz.

The following extraordinary Services are humbly represented, as what have caused the Increase of the Debt of the Victualling, between the 8th of March, 1701 (the Time of her Majesty’s Accession to the Crown) and the 30th of September, 1708:

Costs and Charges for Provisions, furnished for Land Forces, sent to Sea, and the Garrison of Gibraltar, isle.

Freight and Demorages, paid on Account of Land Forces, sent to Sea, and the Garrison of Gibraltar:

Extraordinary Freights and Demorages to Merchant-ships, for carrying Provisions to her Majesty’s Ships in the Mediterranean, Portugal, West Indies, to Holland,

Ostend, £sV.

Hire of Ships and Vessels, for lodging the Men of War’s Provisions, while refitting at Portsmouth and Plymouth:

Vessels built for Transportation; Galleons, and Prize Ships, bought for the lodging Provisions, while the Men of War are refitting at Portsmouth, Plymouth, and Lisbon; also building Storchouses, and additional Works, at the several Ports:

Salaries and Wages to Clerks, Coopers, and Labourers, employed at Lisbon, Jamaica, Gibraltar, and other foreign Parts:

Provisions, bought in the West Indies, for supplying her Majesty’s Ships there, also at , and Genoa,

exceeding the Prices given in England t Interest on Bills in Course:

Losses at Sea, isic.

Note, There hath been issued out of the Proportion of the Victualling, in each Year, to the Service of the Sick and Wounded, and Prisoners of War, which is humbly conceived to be a Load upon the Victualling, more especially since the Proportion is reduced from ao s.to 19 s.a Man per Month.

E. Lee, Cha. Sergifon, D.

Ant. Hammond, B. TymewtU, Geo. Toilet.

The Lords, authorised by virtue of her Majesty’s Royal Assent Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this *» honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went to the House of Peers; where the Commission was read, for impowering the Lord Archbishop of , the Lord Chancellor, Lord Treasurer, the Lord Privy Seal, and several other Lords, to give the Royal Assent to several publick and private Bills, which had passed both Houses.

And they gave the Royal Assent accordingly.

And afterwards a Speech of the Lords Commissioners was delivered to both Houses by the Lord Chancellor.

After which the Lord Chancellor said, It was her Ma- parliament jesty’s royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued, prorogued to Thursday, the N ineteenth Day of May next; and this Parliament is prorogued accordingly to the Nineteenth of May next.

By the Queen:

Mr. Speaker,

The Queen commands this honourable House to -attend her immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend her Majesty:

And being returned;

Several Members present took the Oaths, and made Member* and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed take Oath*, the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes.

was read the First time.

Mr. Speaker reported, that her Majesty was pleased to The Queen'* make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parlia* Speech ment, confiding of many weighty Matters; and that report* he had desired, and obtained, the Favour of a Copy thereof, left, through the Defects of his Memory, he should either omit, or mif-recite, any Part: Which he reported to the House, and is as follows; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

IT is a great Satisfaction to me, that I am able to give you so good an Account of the Progress of the War since the last Session of Parliament.

In the Beginning of this Year our Enemies made use of all their Artifices, toamufe us with false Appearances, and: deceitful Insinuations, of their Desire of Peace, in hopes, that from thence Means might be found to create feme Pivifio'nS, Or Jealousics, among the Allies; but they were intirely disappointed in their Expectation, and such Meafores Were taken upon that Occasion, as made it N impossible for them long to disguise their Insincerity. The

3 G Operations

Address on the Queen’s Speech.

Operations of the War were not delayed; and the Campaign, which, notwithstanding the Backward nets of the Sealon, immediately followed, has been at lead as glorious for the Allies, as any of those, which have preceded it.

God Almighty has been pleased to bless us with a most remarkable Victory, and with such other great and important Successes, both before and after it, that France is thereby become much more exposed and open to the impression of our Arms, and consequently more in need of a Peace, than it was at the Beginning of this Campaign.

However, the War dill continuing, I find myself obliged again to desire you. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, to grant me such Supplies, as you shall judge necessary, for the assisting our Allies in all Parts, and the vigorous Prosecution of our Advantages; that we may put the lad Hand to this great Work of reducing that exorbitant and oppressive Power, which has so long threatened the Liberties of Europe.

I allure you, that all you give, shall be carefully applied to the Uses of the War, if it continues, or to the lessening of the Debts, it has necessarily occasioned, in case of a Peace; which though the many Wants and Dif-tresses of our Enemies may naturally lead us to expect, yet, our own late Experience may fully convince us, is not to be depended upon any other way, than by being in a Condition to compel them to such Terms, as may be safe and honourable for all the Allies.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

1 think it proper to take notice to you, that the great Dearth and Scarcity, under which our Neighbours abroad have differed this Year, begins to affect us, in some Measure, at home, by the Temptation of Profit in carrying out too much of our Corn, while it bears so high a Price in foreign Parts.

This occasions many Complaints from the Poor; for whose Sake I earnedly recommend to you to take this growing Evil into your Consideration, having not neglected any thing on my Part, towards the remedying of it, that the Law would allow.

I cannot conclude, without observing to you, of what great Advantage it will be at this Time to the End we all propose to ourfelve?, that the greatest Dispatch be given to the necessary Preparations for carrying on the War.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Ad-drels be presented to her Majesty, expressing the Thanks' of this House for her most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to congratulate her Majesty upon the continued Successes of the last Campaign, particularly the remarkable Victory, obtained over the near

Mons, by the Troops of her Majesty, and those of her Allies, under the Command of the Duke of Marlborough; and to assure her Majesty, that this House will enable her Majesty, by speedy and effectual Supplies, to carry on the War in such a Manner, as shall (by the Blelling of God) oblige the common Enemy no longer to depend upon Artifices to obtain a Peace, but to accept such Terms, as shall be a lading Security to her Majesty, and her Allies.

Addnf* on Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from the

the Queen’t Committee, appointed to draw up an Address, upon the p#<ch* Besolution of Yesterday, and upon the Debate of the House; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was twice read, and is as followeth;

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great , in Parliament alfem-

bied, beg Leave to return our most humble Thanks to your Majesty for your most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to congratulate your Majesty upon the continued Successes of the lad Campaign, particularly the Victory obtained near Moms by the Troops of your Majesty, and those of your Allies, under the Command of the Duke of Marlborough.

A Victory so remarkable in all its Circumstances, as mud convince your Enemies, that the Courage and Resolution of your Troops, conducted by so great a General, are superior to the greatest Difficulties.

And your Majesty may be allured, that, since the publick Credit has been so well supported, since your Councils have been so deady, and your Allies so firm, that no French Artifices could create Jealousies or Divisions amongd them; and, since your Arms have been so powerful, that no Entrenchments or Fortifications could withdand them; we, your faithful Commons, under such Encouragements, in Duty to your Majesty, and those we represent, will, by speedy and effectual Supplies, enable your Majesty to dispatch the necessary Preparations for carrying on the War in such a Manner, asthall, by the Blessing of God, oblige the common Enemy to accept a Peace upon such Terms, as shall be a Jading Security to your Majesty, and your Allies.

agree with the Committee, in the said Address, to be presented to her Majesty.

Mr. Farrer (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty thousand Men be employed in the Sea Service for the Year 1710, including Eight thousand Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds a Man per Menfem, be allowed for maintaining the said 40,000 Men, for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds, be allowed for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year 17x0.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Great Yarmouth, in the County of , concerned in the

manufacturing of Barley into Malt, in order for Exportation, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in pursuance of a Trade, which, for 20 Years pad, has been very beneficial to the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, the Petitioners have bought considerable Quantities of Barley at the Markets, and made the same into Malt for foreign Markets, the same not being fit for the English Markets, being under-dried, and so not proper to be kept, but will be all loft, if not exported in a very short time, to the utter Ruin of the Petitioners, who cannot now export the fame, by reason of an Embargo, lately laid thereon: And praying the House to make some Provision for the Petitioners Relief.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, Starch, low Wines, and Spirits, drawn from malted Corn, is committed;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of Thomas Bendish, Esquire, was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth, that at the late Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge, the Petitioner, and John Hind Colton, and Samuel Shepherd, junior, Esquires, were Candidates; and the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, though many were unduly hindered, and he ought to have been returned; but not only by Force, but also by Bribery, Treating after the Tejleof the Writ, and other undue Practices, used before the Election, by making an unprecedented Number of (most Strangers) Freemen, a Majority was gained on the Poll for the other Candidates: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Mr. Comptroller reported, that the Committee, appointed to wait on his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, did, at his Return to Town, wait upon him Yesterday, and delivered to him the Resolution of the House, of the 15th Instant; and that thereupon his Grace was pleased to make this Answer:

IT is a very great Honour, and Satisfaction, to me, that the House of Commons is pleased to take so much Notice of my Endeavours to serve the Queen, and iny Country.

I cannot be just to all (he Officers, and Soldiers, who have served with me, unless I take this Oc: ah on to alfure you, that their Zea! and Affection for the Service is equal to tire Courage and Bravery they have shewn, during this whole War.

Exporting Mr. Attorney General (according to Order) reported Cora. from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, Starch, low Wines, and Spirits, drawn from malted Corn, was committed, the Amendments, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: where the same were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to export Barley, Beer, or Bigg, and Malt, to any Place in Alliance with her Majesty, when the Price does not exceed per Quarter.

And the same was twice read, with a Blank; and which was filled up u’ith " Twenty Shillings."

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Clause lo amended, be made Part of the Bill;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, that all Persons, who expose any Corn or Grain to Sale* shall bring to, and fell the same at, the publick Market* and not by Samp.es, under a Penalty.

And the Clause was twice read, with Blanks; and, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

found just and plain, and the t)ebt has been allowed; so that nothing remains, but to find out, and assign, some Fund, out of which the Persons concerned may at laftbe paid, after having impatiently waited so long. Wherefore the under-wntten Envoy humbly prays your Majesty, in the Name of the States, that you would be pleased, according to the kind Assurances you have already given the States, to recommend this Matter so favourably, and so effectually, to your Parliament, that it may have a final Determination this Session, to the Satisfaction of the Persons concerned, who fuller extremely by these long Delays. Arrears of Mr. Secretary Boyle acquainted the Houset that he was

commanded by her Majesty to lay before them a Me-rgHDcnts. which hath been lately presented to her Majesty

by Monsieur Vryberg, in relation to the Pay of the 13 'Dutch Regiments, who served in the last War.

And he presented the same to the House, together with a Translation thereof.

And the Title thereof was read.

The Translation of the said Memorial is as followeth; viz.

Madam,

IT is not without great Concern, that the under-written Envoy Extraordinary from the States General of the United Provinces finds himselfobliged, byexprefs Orders from their High and Mightinesses, to trouble your Majesty again, to implore your Justice and Goodness, in Favour of the Thirteen Regiments of the States, which served the Crown of England the last War, that they may at last obtain the Payment of their Arrears. It is now the Twelfth Year, that they have solicited and expected it, not without great Loss, and the Ruin of some honest Families, which are interested in it. It would be very unnecessary for the said Envoy to lay again before your Majesty the great and faithful Services, performed by those Troops in your Realms: They are very well known, and the States have often represented them to your Majesty: Besides, the Validity of their Pretensions is such, as to be no more subject to any Doubt, or Contest, since their Accounts, after a long Examination, have been Yol. 16.

A Petition of several of the Proprietors of the Army Army, &r. and Transport Debentures, in behalf of themselves, and Debenture*, the rest of the Proprietors thereof, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there has not been any Principal paid on any of the said Debentures, but such, as have been funk by Putchafe of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, and the remaining unsatisfied Debentures amount to about £. 960,000, for which Provision has been made by Parliament only for the InterCll, at/. 3 per Cent, to Ckrifim as, 1707; but no Provision being made lor the Principal, or remaining Interest, has occasioned a Discount thereupon, of 30 per Cent, which is not only an unspeakable Prejudice to the Petitioners, but a very great Discredit to the publick Funds in general: And praying, that effectual Provision may be made for Payment of the Debt due to the Petitionets, according to the Act of Parliament, of the First Year of her Majesty’s Reign, for making good Deficiencies, and preserving the publick Credit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply granted to her Majesty.

-f*Dttdtt- Justices of the Peace, anti Gentlemen of the Grand Jury, assembled at the Assizes, held at Abingdon, for the County of Berks, the First Day of August, 1709, and also of several other Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of the same County, was presented to the House, and read; setting 15

forth, that the Lands in the said County are generally Freehold, which may be so secretly conveyed, that ill-disposed Persons have it in theif Power to commit Frauds* and frequently so do, to the utter Ruin of many Persons, who have pUrchafed, or lent Money upon, such Lands, by making prior and secret Conveyances, and Incumbrances, to the great Discouragement of Trade, and the Sale of Land: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the publick regillering of ail Deeds* Conveyances, Wills, and other Incumbrances, that shall be made of any Honours, Manors, Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, within the said County of Berks’, and also for the Inrolment of all Bargains and Sales of all such Honours, Manors, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments; and also, that the Officer, for keeping the said Registry, may be, from time to time, chosen by the Gentlemen of the said County.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace* and Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen, and Freeholders, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held at IVailing ford, for the County of Berks, the 4th Day of Anno

Domini 1709, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Lands in the said County are generally Freehold, and may be so secretly conveyed, or mortgaged, by ill-disposed Persons, that many times Persons, who have bought, or lent Money thereupon, have been defrauded by prior Conveyances, and Securities, to their utter Ruin; which Grievances may be remedied by erecting a Register, within the said County, of all Deeds, Conveyances, Wills, and other Incumbrances, and Instruments, that may affect any Honours, Manors, Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments; it being found by Experience, that in foreign Countries, as well as in those Parts of Great Britain, which have a Register, such Frauds are prevented, and the Value of Lands, and Trade, increased: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the publick registering of all Deeds, Conveyances, Wills, and other Incumbrances, that may affect any Honours, Manors, Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, within the said County of Berks.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, acr cording to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir John Stonehouse, and Mr. Nevill, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

African A Petition of the Planters, and Inhabitants, of the

Trade. Ill and of Barbadoes, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Commodities of the said Island are produced chiefly by the Labour of Negroes, and imported into European Markets cheaper, and dearer,

accordingly, which chiefly depends on the Number of Traders to Africa: That the laying open the Trade to Africa hath been of great Benefit to the Petitioners, whereby they have been admitted to fend thither for Negroes, who before were forced to buy only of the African Company, at such Prices, and Qualities, as they pleased to impose on the Buyer: That the Petitioners are of opinion, ’twill be the Interest of England in general, that the Trade to Africa be free and open, so that Negroes may be brought to the Plantations in the greatest Plenty, the rather, because the Number of Negroes in the said Island is very much diminished since the present War: And praying, that the Trade to Africa may remain free and open to all the Subjects of Great Britain, under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Tooke, Robert Knaplock, Timothy Childe, Richard Mount, Daniel Midwinter, and John Sprint, on behalf of themselves, and other Booksellers, and Printers, in and about the City of London, and elsewhere, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that it has been the constant Usage, for the Writers of Books, to fell their Copies to Booksellers, or Printers, to the end they might hold those Copies as their Property, and eqjoy the Profit of making, and vending, Impfeflions of them; yet divers Persons have of late invaded the Properties of others, by reprinting several Books, without the Consent, and to the great Injury, of the Proprietors, even to their utter Ruin, and the Discouragement of all Writers in any ul’eful Part of Learning: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for securing to them the Property of Books, bought and obtained by them.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Worthy, Mr. Compton, and Mr. Fey ton, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Catwater A Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Bo-

narbour. rougjj Qf Plymouth, in the County of Devon, and of the Merchants, and other Inhabitants, in or near the fame, waspresented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Town of Plymouth is of great Advantage, as well to her Majesty’s Service, and Revenue, as to the Trade of this Kingdom: That the Harbour of lying near

the fame, is a very commodious and safe Station for her Majesty’s Ships, and all others; but of late several Shoals,

and great Banks of Sand, have been caused there by hi Tides, and Violence of the Storms: That the Harbour is at present unsafe, and in danger of being ruined, if feme timely Care be not taken to prevent it; and so is also Sutton Pool, which lies in the Bosom of the Town, and whereby they convey Provisions to the Men of War, and Merchant Ships, almost choaked up with Oaze and Mud: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for cleansing, and prefenring, the said Harbour of Catwater, and Sutton Pool,

Upon the Petition of Sir Edward Leighton, Baronet, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of

was ordered to make Six Dozen, for his Share, by Mr. Mytten, and Mr. Phillips, Steward to Mr. Two

Years and a half ago.

That he was not solicited for his Vote, at the Time such Orders were given him, but was about a Month before.

That there was a general Meeting of the said Shoemakers at Neds Coffee-house; where k was proposed, that, in Considerat ion of their having made so many Shoes, upon the fitting Members Account, they should all vote for them.

That be (the said Gittens) upon the Day of EJeftioti John Kinaflon, and Richard Mitton, Esquires, to went to the Town-hall, designing to vote for the Peti-serve in Parliament for the Borough of Shrewsbury, tioner; but meeting with Mr. Phillips, an Agent for the

That Mr. Edward Tongue, of Bickton, an Agent for the fitting Members, offered to procure 25 to be lent h.im (the said Gittens) out of the Town Stock, without Interest, if he would vote for the fitting Members; who were present at such Offer.

Jacob Brown said, that Mr. Robert Phillips promised him a Horse, if he would "vote for the fitting Members; and that Mr. Kinafton, one of the fitting Members, told him, he would be kinder to him, than Sir Leighton

would be; and that he would help him to 25 out of the Town Stock, and £. 4 to put his Son out Apprentice: Upon which, he said, ne voted for the fitting Members, though he had before promised the Petitioner, to vote for him.

John Andrews said, that Mr. Cowper, a Clergyman, who has a Living in Mr. MGift, promised him $s. and a Guinea, to vote for the fitting Members; and paid him is. 6 d.in Earnest; and he had t s. more afterwards: That at the Time of the Election he was threatened, if he did not vote for the fitting Members, by one Beke, their Agent.

That he knows one Powell, who, as he was going to the Election, to vote for the Petitioner, was forced into a publick House, where several of the fitting Members Votes and Agents were; where being invited to eat and drink, he was told afterwards, that, if he did not vote for the fitting Members, he should pay ioj. for what he had eat and drank.

John Harris said, he, was going to poll, with Three Country Burgesses, who intended to vote for the Petitioner: They were met by Mr. and Mr.

Sons, whq he saw give Two Half-crowns to Two of the said Burgesses, bidding them vote for the fitting Members: And the said Harris asking them, if they made bribing People ? he was immediately knocked down by one Hulston: That he went to the Polling-place bloody, and saw there the Three Burgesses vote for the fitting Members.

Roger Chandler said, that he was a Constable and attended the Poll at a Back-door; and was solicited to let in one of the fitting Members Voters; which he refused, with put another was let in, who would vote for the Petitioner, the Door, he kept, not being the usual Way intp the Court;. and when they were let in, he observed, the Pferson, voting for the fitting Members, was admitted with Ease to poll, while the other was ill used, and pull’d about the Court, and, he believes, not admitted to poll.

That he went to enquire for one of the Petitioner’s Voters at a publick House; where he found him drinking with the fitting Members Voters, who would have kept him; but the Man declaring himself for the Petitioner, they let him go.-'

Benjamin Felton said, that he was in the Town-hall at the Election, and saw Mr. Kinafton and Mr.

Sons enquiring among the Burgesses for those, that would vote for the Petitioner; and few them use several of those Burgesses so ill, that, he believes, they went away without voting.

Then the fitting Members Counsel proceeded to give Evidence as to Bribery, and other indirect Practices, in the Petitioner; and, called

Tho. Crojje; who laid, he came out of the Country, to vote for the fitting Members; and calling upon some of his Friends at a publick House, he saw the Petitioner; who asked them for their Votes; and told the said Crojfe, that, if he would vote, and procure Votes, for him, he would make him Steward of an Estate, he had lately pur- ‘ chafed; and said, he could not treat them, but would pay a Shilling for. his Club.

That Robert Davis, an Agent for the Petitioner, offered him 3 qs.if he, and his two Brothers, would vote

for the Petitioner.

That he, and his Two Brothers, voted for the fitting Members.

John Gat hen said, that one Mr. Jones, a Gentleman, of a great Estate, solicited Votes for the Petitioner; and he was at Mr. Jones* House Two Days together, at the Time of the Election, and saw there about 40 or 50 People eating and drinking, who were led up to poll by Mr. Leighton, and voted for the Petitioner; but that he did not lee the Petitioner at Mr. s House.

Edmund Schofeild feid, that on the 8th of March was 12 Months, a Bonfire being made for the Queen’s coming to the Crown, the Petitioner asked him for his Vote, and gave him and another is. 6 to drink the Queen’s Health.

Andrew Griffith said, he was asked for his Vote by

both Sides; and the Petitioner promised to prefer his Son in the Excise, if he would vote for him; but owned, that he asked the Petitioner to prefer his Son, some Time after he had promised him his Vote.

Rowland Manfill said, that Sir Ed. Leighton gave him One Shilling, and the Lady Leighton gave him is. 6 for fetching his Son out of Cheshire.

Peter Machen said, that, about a Fortnight before tlje-Elettion, Mr. Harris, a Servant of the Petitioner’s,

brought certain Persons, by the Name 01 Pitts, to his House, and bid him treat them well, and he would pay the Reckoning.

John Griffith said, that Sir Edward Leighton gave him 2i. 6 d.and desired his Vote; which, he told him, he

had engaged for the fitting Members; but that he had some Relations, whom he would endeavour to prevail with; but does not know, whether any of them voted for the Petitioner.

That, as to the Money, said to be given to Andrews by Mr. Cowper, the Clergymen, the Counsel for the fitting Members examined

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for charging, and continuing, the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year 1710, without any Amendment.

Articles, exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of Great Britain, against Henry Sachever, Doctor in -Divinity, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against him for high Crimes and Misdemeanors.

WHEREAS his late Majesty King William the Third, then Prince of Orange, did, with an armed Force, undertake a glorious Enterprize, for delivering this Kingdom from Popery and arbitrary Power, and divers Subjects of this Realm, well affected to their Country, joined A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Aston. SachevereN’s Uses and the ACtings of the said well-affected Sub-bapeicbment. jests, in Aid and Pursuance of the said Enterprize, are also declared to have been necessary, and that the same ought to bejuftified: And whereas the happy and blessed Consequences of the said Resolution are, the Enjoyment of the Light of God’s true Religion, established among us, and of the Laws and Liberties of the Kingdom; the uniting her Majesty’s Protestant Subjects in Interest and Affection, by a legal Indulgence, or Toleration, granted to Dissenters; the Preservation of her Majesty’s sacred Person; the many and continual Benefits, arising from her Majesty’s wife and glorious Administration; and the Prospect of Happiness to future Ages, by the Settlement of the Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line; and the Union of the Two Kingdoms: And whereas the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled, did by their Address, of the Seventeenth of December, in the Year of our Lord 1705, lay before her Majesty the following Vote, or Resolution; viz. " That " the Church of England, as by Law established, which " was rescued from the extremest Danger by King fVilHam the Third, of glorious Memory, is now, by God’s " Blessing, under the happy Reign ot her Majesty, in a most late and flourishing Condition; and that whoever goes about to suggest, and insinuate, that the Church " is in danger, under her Majesty’s Administration, is an " Enemy to the Queen, the Church, and the Kingdom and by their laid Address did humbly beseech her Majesty to take effectual Measures, for making the said Vote, or Resolution, publick; and also for punishing the Authors and Spreaders of such seditious and scandalous Reports; and, on the aoth Day of the same December, her Majesty was pleased to issue her royal Proclamation accordingly: Yet nevertheless the said Henry preached a

Sermon at the Assizes, held at Derby, August the 15th, in the Year of our Lord 1709, and afterwards published the same in Print, with a Dedication thereof; and the said Henry Sacheverell also preached a Sermon at the Cathedral Church of Saint Paul, before the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens, of London, on the Fifth Day of November last, being the anniversary Thanksgiving to Almighty God, for the Deliverance from the Gunpowder Treason, and for beginning the late happy Resolution, by giving his late Majesty a safe Arrival here, and for corn-pleating the fame, by making all Opposition fall before him, till he became our King and Governor; which said Sermon, he, the said Henry Sacheverell, afterwards like-wife published in Print, with a Dedication thereof to Sir Samuel Garrard, Baronet, Lord Mayor of the City of London; and with a wicked, malicious, and seditious Intention to undermine and subvert her Majesty’s Government, and the Protestant Succession, as by Law established, to defame her Majesty’s Administration, to asperse the Memory of his late Majesty, to traduce and condemn the late happy Resolution, to contradict and arraign the Resolutions of both Houses of Parliament, to create Jealouliesand Divisions among her Majesty’s Subjects, and to incite them to Sedition and Rebellion.

First, He, the said Henry Sacheverell, in his said Sermon, preached at Saint Paul’s, doth suggest and maintain, than the necessary Means, used to bring about the said happy Resolution, were odious and unjustifiable; that his late Majesty, in his Declaration, disclaimed the lead Imputation of Resistance; and that, to impute Re-fiftance to the said Resolution, is to call black and odious Colours upon his late Majesty, and the said Resolution.

Secondly, He, the said Henry Sacheverell, in his said Sermon, preached at Saint Paul's, doth suggest and maintain, that the aforesaid Toleration granted by Law, is unreasonable, and the Allowance of it unwarrantable; and asserts, that he is a false Brother, with relation to God, Religion, or the Church, who defends Toleration and Liberty of Conscience; that Queen Elizabeth was deluded by Archbishop Grindall (whom he scurrilously calls a falle Son of the Church, and a perfidious Prelate) to the Toleration of the Genevian Discipline; and that it is the Duty ofl'uperior Pallors to thunder out their eccle-

fiastical Anathema’s against Persons, entitled to the Benefit of the said Toleration; and insolentiy dares, or defies, any Power on Earth to reverse such Sentences.

Thirdly, He, the said Henry Sacheverell, in his said Sermon, preached at Saint Paul's, doth falsely and seditiously suggest and assert, that the Church of England, is in a Condition of great Peril and Adversity under her Majesty’s Administration; and, in order to arraign and blacken the said Vote or Resolution, of both Houses of Parliament, approved by her Majesty, as aforesaid, he, in . Opposition thereto, doth suggest, the Church to be in danger; and, as a Parallel, mentions a Vote, that the Person of King Charles the First was voted to be out of danger at the same Time, that his Murderers were conspiring his Death; thereby wickedly and maliciously insinuating, that the Members of both Houses, who passed the said Voter were then conspiring the Ruin of the Church.

Fourthly, He, the said Henry Sacheverell, in his laid Sermons and Books, doth falsely and maliciously suggest, that her Majesty’s Administration, both in ecclesiastical and civil Affairs, tends to the Destruction of the Constitution; and that there are Men of Characters and Stations in Church and State, who are false Brethren, and do themselves weaken, undermine, and betray, and do encourage and put it in the Power of others who are pro-fefied Enemies, to overturn and destroy the Constitution and Establishment; and chargeth her Majesty, and those in Authority under her, both in Church and State, with a general Male-administrat ion; and, as a publick Incendiary, he peifuades her Majesty’s Subjects to keep up a Distinction of Factions and Parties, instils groundiefs Jealousies, foments destructive Divisions among them, and excites and stirs them up to Arms and Violence; and, that his laid malicious and seditious Suggcftions may make the stronger Impression upon the Minds of her Majesty’s Subjects, he, the said Henry Sacheverell, doth wickedly wrest and pervert divers Texts and Passages of holy Scripture.

All which Crimes and Misdemeanors the Commons are ready to prove, not only by the general Scope of the same Sermons, or Books, but likewise by several Clauses, Sentences, and Expressions, in the said Sermons, or Books, contained; and that he, the said Henry Sacheverell, by preaching the Sermons, and publishing the Books, aforesaid, did abuse his holy Function, and hath most grievously offended against the Peace of her Majesty, her Crown and Dignity, the Rights and Liberties of the Subject, the Laws and Statutes of this Kingdom, and the Prosperity and good Government of the fame. And the said Commons, by Protcftation, saving to themselves the Liberty of exhibiting, at any Time hereafter, any other Article or Impeachment against the said Hen. Sacheverell, and also of replying to hisAnswers, or any of them, and of offering Proofs of all the Premises, or any of them, or of any other Article or Impeachment, that shall be exhibited by them, as the Case, according to the course of Parliament, shall require, do pray. That he, the said Henry Sacheverell may be put to answer to all and every the Premises; and that such Proceeding, Examination, Trial, Judgment, and exemplary Punishment, may be thereupon had and executed, as is agreeable to Law and Justice.

Ordered, That the Report be read a Second time upon Wednesday Morning next.

The Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning Way* next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, anil Means, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Common Council, and other the principal Merchants, and trading Inhabitants of the Borough of Plymouth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that since the laying open the Trade to Africa, divers Ships have been fitted out from that Port for that Coast, to the great Benefit of the Lid Borough, and Parts adjacent, employed in the Woollen Manufactures: That, if the said Trade to Africa should be granted to the African Company, exclusive of all others, the Petitioners conceive, it will much prejudice them, and the Woollen Manufactures, and be a Discouragement to Navigation in general: And praying, that the said Trade may continue free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects, under such Regulations, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Royal African Company of England was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Trade to Africa has been ever held a Matter of high Importance to this Kingdom, and the Plantations, and that Forts and Settlements were absolutely necessary for its Defence and Improvement: That, considering the Methods of neighbouring Nations, ’tis hoped, the House will be of Opinion, that the said Trade cannot be securely and advantageously carried on, without a joint Stock, the Petitioners conceiving it the only way to serve the Plantations with a sufficient Number of Negroes, at moderate Prices, which the Petitioners did, while they enjoyed that Trade free from the Interruptions of the separate Traders: That upon the Encouragement of a Charter, granted by King Charles the 2d, in the 24th Year of his Reign, the Petitioners raised by Subscription a considerable Sum, for a joint Stock, and have since advanced several great Sums, Part of which has been expended in building, putrhafing, maintaining, and repairing. Forts and Settlements, and in improving that Trade, and encouraging divers new Manufactures to be made in this Kingdom, which were exported in great Quantities to Africa: That in the Wars the Petitioners have suffered unspeakable Losses, by frequent Captures, and injurious Practices by foreign Com-peiitars, thi ugh the Trade has been principally supported, and preterved from falling into the Hands of other Nations, at the Charge of the Petitioners, without any Advantage to themselves: That in 1697 the Parliament thought fit, as «i Means to p re serve and improve that Trade, to open the fame, by admitting all his late Majesty’s Subjects to trade to Africa for Thirteen Years,

paying 10 per Cent.on their Exports, towards the Charge

of Forts and Settlements; but that Expedient hath not anl wered the End proposed, the Natives of Africa only having reaped Advantage by it, and the Traders thither, as well as the Planters, have suffered greatly thereby: That . under all these Discouragements the Petitioners have, in order to preserve this Trade, paid in several additional Sums of Money upon their respective Shares of their joint Stock, and have, since the last Session of Parliament, so far convinced their Creditors of the present State of their Stock, that Four-fifths of them have already subscribed an Agreement, by which the Corporation will be intirely discharged from their whole Debts; and that they may not lose the reasonable Hopes of reaping some Benefit at last from the Foundation, they have laid, of securing so essential a Trade to the Nation, do pray, that they may have suitable Encouragement, to enable them effectually to carry on the Trade to Africa, with such additional Privileges, as may preserve, support, and improve it; and they are willing to submit to such Provisions, as the House shall judge reasonable, for the full Supply of the Plantations with Negroes at moderate Prices.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Afric.

A Petition of the Merchants, and Owners of Ships, in the Port of Whitehaven, was prefcnled to the House, and

read; setting forth, that the Petitioners wholly depend upon their Trade and Navigation, especially to the Plantations of Virginea and Maryland, where the Tobacco is principally produced by the Labour of Negroes, chiefly furnished by the separate Traders to Guinea; but should the African Company engross and monopolize the said Negro Trade, exclusive of all others, in consequence they will subject the Plantation Trade to their own arbitrary Will, and intirely discourage the Industry of the Petitioners, the People of the West Indies, and all others, and greatly prejudice the Revenue, and Navigation in general: And praying, that the Trade to Africa may be continued free and open, so that all her Majesty's Subjects may have the Benefit thereof.

Ordered, That-the Confederation of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgeflfes, with the Merchants, and principal Inhabitants, of the ancient Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that their Livelihood very much depends on Navigation to the Plantations, whose Products are raised by the Labour of Negroes, brought from the African Coast: That the

Vol. 16.

African Company are endeavouring *0 get that Trade Vi themselves, exclusive of all others, which, the Petitioner^ fear (if obtained) will very much le&n the Plantation Trade, for want of Negroes, and tend to the Decrease of Navigation, and confine most of the Plantation Trade to London only, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners t And praying, that the African.Trade may be continued open to her Majesty’s Subjects, under such Regulations, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Mr. Bacon reported from the Committee, to whom it Hackney was referred to inspeift the Laws, relating to Hackney Caaeh Coaches, and consider, how they may be better regulated; By*-"w* and to enquire into the Abuses, committed by Carmen, Draymen, and Chairmen, and consider, how they may be regulated j that they had come to several Resolutionsj which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read them in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where they were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Owners of Cars, and Carts, be prohibited from loading their Cars, and Carts, with excessive Burthens, by Means whereof the Pavements of the Streets are very much damaged, and the Inhabitants put to great Charges in repairing the fame.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That empty Carts, Brewers Drays, and Hackney Coaches,

Handing in narrow Streets, and Hopping up the Ways, by means whereof Gentlemen s Coaches are oftentimes flopped, is a great Annoyance, and tends very much ta the Hindrance of Trade, and therefore ought to be restrained.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Draymen, and Carmen, ought to be prohibited from fitting in their Drays, and Carts, while driving, which is a very pernicious Practice, to the endangering the Lives of Passengers going along the Streets.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Number of Hackney Coaches to ply on Sundays, be enlarged.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a certain Number of Chairs be licensed, and regulated in the same Manner, as the Hackney Coaches now arc.

The Four first Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The last Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out "a certain Number of," and, instead thereof, to insert " all."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by inserting after " be," the Word " numbered."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, so amended, That all Chairs be numbered, licensed, and regulated, in the same Manner, as the Hackney Coaches now are.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolutions; and that the Lord Wm. Powlett, Mr.

Mr. Farrer, Mr. Dolben, Mr. Medlicott, Mr. Denzill Onslow, and Mr. Mountague, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are to prepare the said Bill, that they do in the Bill provide for the regulating the Abuses, committed by Carts,

Cars and Drays.

A Petition of Robert Rolle, John Rolle, and Denys Rolle, Esquires, Grandsons of Sir John Rolle, deceased, and also of Denys Rolle, Esquire, the only surviving Son of the said Sir John Rolle, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by Articles, dated the 16th of March, 1704, made upon the Marriage of the Petitioner Robert with Eliz. Duke, the said Sir John and the Petitioner were to settle £. 1,500 per Annum, to the Use of the Petitioner Robert, for Life, Remainder to his First and other Sons, Remainder to the Petitioners John and Denys Rolle, the Petitioner’s Brothers, and also to Denys and Cha. Rolle (now dead without Issue) and then to the right Heirs of the said Sir John: That Eliz. the Petitioner Robert’s Wife, was to have a Jointure of £. 800 per Annum, and Sir John and the Petitioner were to settle all their Estates, other than the said £. 1,500 per Annum, to the Use of Sir John, for Life, with Remainders over? which last Effaces were to be charged with £. 10,000 for younger Children of that Marriage; and Sir John had also Power to charge the Premisses (the jointure Lands excepted) with £.15,000 for Debts, Legacies, younger Children and Grandchildren’s Portions; and by the Articles aforesaid they covenanted to suffer a Recovery, in order to make good the said Settlement; which was done in Sir John’s Life time; who by his Will directed his Debts,

Legacies, and younger Children’s Portions, to be paid out of the£. 15,000 aforesaid: That afterwards, \n October, 1706 (Sir John then being dead) the Petitioner settled all his Estate, pursuant to the said Articles, in Trustees, by leafing, or mortgaging, to raise 15,000 for Payment of Sir John’s Debts and Legacies, and Portions, the same amounting to more; and the Petitioner Robert has also contracted Debts, in repairing the old Mansion-house of the Family, and purchasing Lands lying near it, of about £.8,000. That the Trustees, finding, they could not raise Money, sufficient to pay the said Sums, by leafing, have endeavoured to mortgage sufficient Estates; but, because no Deed appears, to lead the Uses of the Recovery, they cannot borrow the same: That there arc fevc-ral small Parcels of Land, not liable to the said Jointure, lying at great Distance from the Bulk of the Estate, which cannot be managed, to pay even the Interest of Sir John's Devise; which he intended to fell, and which the Trustees have no Power to dispose of, though all the Petitioners are of Age, and the Trustees consenting to sell the same:

And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable Trustees to fell fbme Out-parts of the Estate of the Petitioner Robert (not in Jointure, as aforesaid) for Payment of the Debts and Legacies of the said Sir John Rolle, and his younger Childrens Portions.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir Walter Yonge, Sir Wm. Drake, Mr. Gwyn, Mr. Serjeant Hooper, and Mr. Mervin, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of the Gun-makers, inhabiting in and about Afriraa

London, was presented to the House, and read; setting Trad*, forth, that the Trade to Africa, when it was lolely carried on by the Royal African Company, occasioned the Exportation of very great Quantities of the Petitioners Manufactures, and was a great Help to their Support; but the late great Difficulties, the said Company have laboured under by the late Settlement, has Very much lessened that Exportation, to the Impoverishment of the Petitioners: And praying, that the said Company’s Trade may be secured to them, under such Methods, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Dyers, Packers, Setters, Drawers, Ditte» and Calenders, and others, inhabiting in and about London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Royal African Company, by their Trade to Guinea, were wont to give Employment to the Petitioners, and many Hundred others; but their Trades are very much lessened by the Misfortunes, the said Company labour under, by reason of the War, and the Irruptions of the separate Traders, whereby the Guinea Trade is in great Danger of being loft to the Nation; which tends to the Detriment of the Petitioners, and their Families:

And praying, that the House will grant the said Company such Privileges, as may encourage them to improve that Trade by more large Exportations, for the Good of the Publick, as well as the Petitioners Support.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Trade to Africa.
