The House being informed, that the Royal African Afntm Company, and separate Traders to Africa, attended, ’ftwA* they were called in, and, at the Bar, presented to the House their several Propositions, for securing the Trade to Africa.

Ajid then they withdrew.

And the said Propositions were read, and are as follow; viz.

in Obedience to the Order of the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled. delivered to the Royal African Company of England, they c'o humbly offer the following Scheme, or Propotal, for the better settling of the Trade to.

Africa, and securing the tame to this Kingdom, and the Plantations thereunto belonging: ift, THE said Company do most humbly conceive, since, in Concurrence with their Experience, Forta and Settlements are agreed to be absolutely necessarvy for preferring, and improving, that Trade, that the most effectual and certain Method for carrying on that Trade, for prelcrving the said Forts and Settlements, for receiving Grants, and making Agreements with the Native*, for furnishing the Plantations with sufficient Supplies-of Negroes, at moderate Prices, for giving a necessary Credit to the Planters, and contrafting for the Affienro, or with the Poriugucze, can only be effected by a Company, with a sufficient joint Stock.

2d, That the said Company be obliged to export annually for the Coast of Africa, in Manufactures, and other Merchandize, to the Amount of One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, or upwards; and if it IhaM at any tinrfo appear, by application to her Majesty in Council, that greater Number of Negroes are required to be sent to the Plantations, the said Company may be subject to the Direction of her Majesty in Council to export annually such further Value in Goods and Merchandize, as shall be judged necefikry. ~

3d, That the said Company be likewise subject to such further Orders and Directions of her Majesty in Council, as shall be found necessary to be given, in relation to the Price and Number of Negroes, to be delivered by the said Company in her Majesty’s Plantations and Colonies in America.

The said Royal African Company beg Leave further most humbly to represent, that, by Charter from King Charles the Second, they are incorporated, and have the Coast of Africa, and the Trade thereunto, granted to them; upon the Foot of which Charter, for many Years successiVely, whilst they had little or no Interruption, they were in as fioyrishing Circumstances, as any Company in Europe, in proportion to their original Stock; and, in pursuance of the said Grant, they have purchased, and erected, several Forts and Settlements on the said Coast, and ob tai ned Icvcral Privi leges and Immu n i t ies, by Grants, and Agreements, from, and with, the Princes of thqt Country.

And, at a Meins the better to enable them again to reap the Benefits, that may arise from the Premises, and to be in a Condition to answer the Ends, proposed by the forementioned joint Stock, they are, in Concert with by much the greater Part of their Creditors, endeavouring tp put themselves in such Circumstances, as, they apprehend, will effectually tiary on, and improve, that Trade, in every Branch theffcof, having the Assistance of this ho<-nourable House, in granting such further Privileges, as are necessary to that End; but, if it shall be agreeable to the Wisdom of this honourable House, that the Stock, for carrying on the said Trade, ought to be enlarged, the said Company are very willing to submit thereunto.

By Order of the Royal African Company of England.

John Pery, Secretary.

ift, THAT it may be free for all her Majesty’s Subjects to trade to Africa from any Part of Great or the Plantations.

A PETITION of several of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, in the several Counties of Stafford and Chejltf, on behalf of themselves, and several others in and near the said Counties, was presented to the House, and read; fefting forth, that the great Roads from the Northern Parts of this Kingdom, centering at Hulms Chappell, in Cheshire, towards London, being the accustomed

Poll Road, the Highways betweeen Chappell and Newcastle, in Staffordshire, being Eleven computed Miles, are frequently so out of Repair, that lor Nine Months in the year they are almost impassable, and are yearly a great Charge to the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Townships, who have not proper Materials of Stone and Gravel, within any reasonable Compass, to repair the fame; and, by reason of Fines, already levied, and more threatened, they are hot able to perform the Repairs, as they ought, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the said Highways between Hulms Chappell and the Liberties of Newcastle aforesaid.

And the said Henry Sacheverell doth further infill, and is advised, that the aforesaid Assertion is agreeable to, and warranted by, the common Law of England, and divers Acts of Parliament, now remaining in full Force.

The laid Henry Sacheverel doth, with all Humility, aver the Illegality of Resistance, on any Pretence whatever, to be the Doctrine of the Church of England, and to have been the general Opinion of our most orthodox and able Divines, from the Time of the Reformation to this Day. This Doctrine hath, in the most solemn Manner, been taught in that University, whereof he hath lpeen for more than.Twenty Years a Member: This hath been often, with publick Approbation of each House of Parliament, preached, and printed; and in Terms of greater Force, than any used by the said Henry Sacheverel, hath by the right reverend Fathers of our Church, dead 2nd living, been avowed and maintained.

And the said Henry Sacheverel was the rather induced to preach against the Doctrine of Residance of the supreme Power, upon the 5th Day of November, because on that Pay the Church commemorates our Deliverance from the traiterous Attempts of rebellious Papids; and because the Lawfulness of residing the supreme Power was originally a popish Doctrine; for which Reasons, as he humbly conceives, the Rubrick of the Office, appointed for that Day by her late Majesty Queen Mary, of blessed Memory, directs that, after the Creed, if there be no Sermon, shall be read one of the Six Homilies against Rebellion.

Whild, therefore, the Church of England, as by Law established, is in a safe and flourishing Condition, under her Majesty’s happy Adnainidration; whild popish Tenets are by all good Protedants condemned, and abhorred; whild the Laws of this Realm continue in their full Force and Vigour; the said Henry Sacheverel humbly hopes, that a dutiful Son of that Church, a sincere Protedant, and a faithful Subject of her Majesty, shall not suffer for asserting the Doctrine of Non-resistance of the supreme Powers: But if this Doctrine be declared erroneous, and it should please God, that he should suffer for asserting it; he truds, that God will enable him to shew his deady Belief of this Doctrine, by a meek and patient Resignation to whatever shall befall him on that Account.

To that Part of the 2d Article, which.charges, that he, the said Henry Sacheverell, doth lugged and maintain, that the Toleration, granted by Law, is unrealizable, and the Allowance of it unwarrantable} the said U

Henry Sacheverell faith, that upon the most diligent Enquiry, he has not been able to inform himself, that a Toleration hath been granted by Law; hut admits, that an Act did pass in the Fird Year of King and

Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act for exempting the ic " Majesties Protedant Subjects, dissenting from the " Church of England, from the Penalties of certain " Laws;" which Exemption the said Henry Sacheverell doth not any where maintain, or fugged to be unreasonable, or, that the Allowance of it is unwarrantable; but hoped, that he had prevented any such Milappre-hension, by declaring his sincere Meaning in these Words, contained in his Sermon, preached at St. Paul's: " I " would not be here misunderstood, as if I intended to " cad the lead invidious Reflection upon that ladulgence, which the Government hath condescended to " give them; which, I am sure, all those, who wish well " to our Church, are ready to grant to Consciences truly " scrupulous: Let them enjoy it in the full Limits, the " Law has prescribed."

If there be any other Expressions concerning Toleration, which may seem to carry a dubious Sense, in any other Parts of his Sermon, he hopes, that they will not be applied to the Exemption, granted by Law, but will be interpreted agreeably to his avowed Approbation of that Law.

And to such Part of the said 2d Article, as charges, that he, the said Henry Sacheverell, asserts, that he is a faife Brother, with relation to God, Religion, or the Church, who defends Toleration, and Liberty of Confidence; he, the said Henry Sacheverell, faith, that he, having so plainly declared himself in favour of the Exemption, granted by Law, when he blames those, who upon all Occasions defend Toleration, and Liberty of Conscience, cannot be thought to reflect on the Defender* of that legal Exemption, or Indulgence, which he him* self approves, and defends. He doth indeed fugged it to be one Part of the Character of a falle Brother, upon, all Occasions to defend Toleration, and Liberty of Conscience, and, to excuse the Separation, lay the Fault upon the true Sons of the Church, for carrying Matter* too high; which universal Defence of Toleration, and Excuse of Separation, attended with the laying the Fault of such Separation upon the true Sons of the Church, are by him jointly mentioned in one and the same Clause of the Sentence, and in one and the same Branch of the Character: So that his Reflection doth not extend to all* who defend Toleration and Liberty of Conscience, much less to those, who defend the Exemption, granted by Law to Protedant Difl’enters; but to such only, who at the same time they defend universal Toleration, and Liberty-of Conscience, do also excuse the Separation, and fey the Fault thereof upon the true Sons of the Church, for carrying Matters too high; and these he did then, and dill doth, with all Humility, conceive to be judly blameable, and, if Members of this Church, to be faife Brethren.

Answer to the 4th Article.

As to the 4th Article; it contains several Charges, of a very high and criminal nature, of which the said Henry Sacheverel knows his Heart to be intirely innocent , and be observes, with Comfort, that, whereas in the former Three Articles he is said to have maintained, or asserted, as well as to have suggested, tire Doctrines and Things, therein laid to his Charge, in this Fourth Article he is not aceufed of maintaining, or averting, but barely of suggesting, what is therein contained; and he humbly hopes, that bare Suggestions, or Insinuations, could they with any Colour, or Probability, be made out (as, he is fully satisfied, they cannot) will not, under the moll mild and gracious Government, at a time, when several new Laws have been made, for securing the Liberties of the Subject, by your Lordships, the great Guardians of our Laws and Liberties; be adjudged sufficient to involve an Eng/ish.Subject in the Guilt and Punishment of high Crimes and Misdemeanors.

To the several Parts of the said 4th Article, the said Henry Sacheverelldoth in all Humility answer: As to such Part thereof, whereby it is charged, that the said Henry Saeheverel, in his said Sermons, and Books, doth falsely and maliciously suggest, that her Majesty’s Administration, both in ecclesiastic and civil Affairs, tends to the Destruction of the Constitution; he, the said Heury Sacheverell, faith, that he hath not made any Mention in either of his Books, or Sermons, of her Majesty’s Administration in ecclesiastical or civil Affairs, or of tier Ministers: So far is he from suggest ing, that her Majesty’s Administration, both in ecclesiastical and civil Affairs, tends to the Destruction of the Constitution, that, amongst the incftimable Blessings, which arc owing to our Deliverance, annually commemorated on the 3th of November, he reckons this to be one, that her Majesty, the good and pious Relict of the Royal Family, fits now happily on the Throne of her Ancestors; and prays, that God may long preserve her, for the Comfort and Support of the Church; and profeffeth, that what he spoke proceeded from a tender Concern for her Majesty’s Person and Government; and in the Dedication also of his said Sermon, preached at St. Paul’s, solemnly declares (as he did before in his Discourse) that his only Aim and Intention was, earnestly to contend for the Safety, Rights, and Establishment, of her Majesty, together with those of the Church.

And as to such Part of the said 4th Article, whereby it is charged, that the said Henry doth fug-

ged, that there are Men of Characters and Stations in the Church, who are falle Brethren; the said Henry vercl laith, that the Life Brethren, as described by him in his Sermon, are either those, who propagate false poftrines; or, who give up the DiscipHneand Worship of the Church; or, who are fora Neutrality in Religion; or, who with well to the Church of England, and are ready to sacrifice their Persons and Effaces in her Vindication, but do not llievv their Zeal in the Communion of the Church, as well as for it, in obeying her Precepts, as well as defending her Rights: These being the several Sorts of false Brethren, enumerated by the said Henry Sacb.vere/l,if he should have suggested, that there are Men of Characters and Stations in Church and State Woids, by no means restrained to the bigheft Characters and Stations) to whom the Denomination of false Brethren, in some one or more Ssnfes of that Word, as by him interpreted, doth belong, he humbly hopes, that such Suggestion would not be deemed false, malicious, or highly criminal.

As to such other Part of the said 4th Article, whereby it is th uged, that the said Henry Sacheverell doth suggest, that there are Men of Characters and Stations in the Church and State, who do themselves weaken, undermine, and betray, and do encourage?and put it into the Power of, others, who are professed Enemies, to overturn and destroy, the Constitution, and Establishment; the said Henry Sachevereldenieth, that he suggesteth any such

things concerning Men of Characters and Stations in 18

Church, or State: Where he speaks of those, who weaken, undermine, and betray, and encourage, and put it in the Power of, our professed Enemies to overturn and destroy, the Constitution and Establishment, there Men of Characters and Stations are not mentioned by him; and where he mentions Men of Characters and Stations, Twelve Pages afterwards (the only Place, wherein he mentions them) there he speaks nothing of weakening, undermining, and betraying, or of encouraging, and putting it in the Power of, our professed Enemies to overturn and destroy, the Constitution and Establishment; and hopes therefore, that he shall be no ways answerable for a supposed Iiefleftion, which depends upon the Conjunction of Passages, so widely distant from, and lb little relating to, each other: The Weakeners, Underminers, and Betrayers, of our Constitution, and the Encouragers, to whom the said Henry Sacheverell doth in any Part of his Sermon refer, will, he presumes, upon a candid Examination of those Passages, appear to be one of these Three Sorts of Persons: Esther, First, such, as by their Writings endeavour to subvert the Foundations of our Church, and State: Or, Secondly, such, whether Writers, or others, who are for a latitudinarian, heterogeneous. Mixture of all Persons, of what different Faith loever, uniting only in Protestancy; which would let into her Bowels those, who neither believe her Faith, own her Million, submit to her Discipline, or comply with her Liturgy; which he afterwards stiles the Model of an universal Coalition: Or, Thirdly, those occasional Coiformifts, who have so far eluded the Corporation and Test Acts by their abominable Hypocrisy, as to have undermined the Foundations, and endangered the Government, by filling it (as far as they could) with its profefi'ed Enemies, that is, with themselves. Of all thele, and their Encouragers, the said Henry Sacheverellconfcffes himself to have luggefted, that they do, in his Opinion, weaken, undermine, and betray, the Constitution; but, that either these, or their Encou* ragers, are Men of Characters or Stations in the Church, or State, he hath not any where suggested.

And as to such other Part of the said 4th Article, which chatgeth the said Henry; Sacheverell with charging her Majesty, and those in Authority under her, both in Church and State, with a general Male-administration; the said Henry Saeheverel laith, that he abhors the Thoughts

of bringing any Charge against her sacred Majesty, whom he never mentions, but in Terms of the profoundest Duty and Respect; nor doth he tax those in Authority with a general, or with any, Male-administration, which is a Word he hath never used, nor, as far as he can find, any other Word or Words, by which the Thing is implied: So far is the said Henry Sacheverell from making any undutiful Reflections upon her Majesty, or her Administration, that in the several Writings, that he has published since her happy Accellion to the Throne, particularly in one, which is an avowed Defence of her Title to the Crown, and a Justification of her entering into a War with France and Spain, he hath expressed himself with, the most hearty and loyal Zeal for her Majesty’s Person, Government, and Administration.

And as to such other Part of the said Fourth Article, whereby it is charged, that the said Henry Sacheverell, as a publick Incendiary, persuades her Majesty’s Subjects, to keep up a Distinction of Fastions, and Parties; the said Henry Saeheverel laith, that he is so far from being guilty of this Charge, that in his said Sermon he invites the Separatists to renounce their Schism, and come fin-cerely into the Church; and complains of those, that have villainoully divided us with the knavilh Distinctions of High and Low Church Men; and willies we may be one Fold, under one Shepherd; and that all those invidious Distinctions, that now distract and confound us, were loft; so that we might be terrible, like an Army with Banners, to our Enemies, who could never break in upon such an uniform and well-compafted Body.

And to such other Part of the said 4th Article, as charges, that the said Henry Saeheverel infttls groundless Jealousies, and foments destructive Divisions, among

Saclieverell s which they had directed him to report to the House: tuipcachuiciit. And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read; and the Replication is as followeth:

THE Commons have considered the Answer of Henry Sacheverell, Doctor in Divinity, to the Articles of Impeachment, exhibited against him by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled; and observe, that there are many things in it, not warranted by the Course of Proceedings upon Impeachments, foreign to the Charge of the Commons, unbecoming a Person impeached, and plainly designed to reflect upon the Honour of the House of Commons in this Proceeding; for which they might demand your Lordships immediate Justice.

But the Commons being sensible, that the Nature of the Crimes, whereof he Bands impeached, and the Ne-eeffity of bringing him to a speedy and exemplary Puni foment, require, that all Occasions of Delay should be avoided; and not doubting, that your Lordships will, in due Time, vindicate the Honour of the Commons, and the Justice of their Proceedings;

The Commons do aver their Charge against the said Henry Sacheverell, for high Crimes and Misdemeanors, to be true; and that the said Henry Saebeverel is guilty in such Manner, as he Hands impeached; and that the Commons will be ready to prove their Charge against him at such convenient Time, as shall be appointed lor that Purpose.

The Replication being read a Second time;

A Petition of George Hickman, Gentleman, was pre- Cooper’s fented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there kftax*. being a Bill depending in the House for the Relief of Joseph Cooper, Gentleman, the Petitioner affirms, that Cooper doth not apply to the House for an Act, so much to enable him to discharge Incumbrances on the Estate, therein mentioned, as to strengthen his Title thereto; which being very well known in Ireland, is the Reason, that Cooper did not apply to the Parliament there for Relief; and, if this Bill should pass, it will greatly prejudice the Petitioner’s Interest: And praying, that it may not pass without the Concurrence of the Petitioner, before he hath Justice done him.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Upon the Petition of 'Thomas Bendish, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of John.

Hind Cotton, and Samuel Shepard, junior, Esquires, for the Town of Cambridge:

That the Numbers on the Poll were.

For John Hind Cotton, Esquire,7 Sitting C125,

That the Counsel for the Petitioner admitted that Mr.

Cotton was duly elected; but infilled, that the Petitioner had a Majority of Mr. Shepard, of such Persons, as were qualified to vote; and that Mr. Shepard's Election was procured by Bribery, and other illegal Practices.

In the first Place the Counsel for the Petitioner infilled, that the Right of Election is in such Freemen only, As had a Right to their Freedom by Birth, or Service, or who were admitted to their Freedom by Redemption, or Purchase, and who did not receive Alms, or any other Charity.

That the Counsel for the fitting Members infilled, that the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Bailiffe, Burgesses, of Freemen, at large.

That the Counsel for the Petitioner, to prove the Right of Election, called

And, to prove the Six Guineas, given to the said Lindsey, was neither by the Petitioner’s Order, or Know-lege, they called

Doctor Rutler; who said, that he meeting with the said Lindsey, he told him, if he would engage to procur 20 Votes for the Petitioner, and the fitting Member. Mr. Shepard, he would give him Six Guineas for that Purpose; which Lindsey undertaking to do, he gave him the Money, solemnly affirming, that it was without the Petitioner’s Privity, or Knowlege; and that he gave such Money for the Petitioner’s Interest, merely to the Regard and Friendship he had for the Petitioner’s Family, whose Grandfather had treated him with an extraordinary Kindness, when he was a Youth, and upon no other Account whatsoever.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee come to the following Resolutions; viz.

a. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Hind Cotton, Esquire is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Samuel Shepard, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge.

The First Resolution being read a Second time; Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That the Right of eleding Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge, is in the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Freemen, not receiving Alms.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

' Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That John Hind Cotton, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge.

The Third Resolution being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put. That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That Samuel Shepard, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Cambridge;

The House divided:

A PETITION of Margaret and Mary Molloy was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have several times applied to this House, to be relieved for an Estate in Ireland, which was their Grandfather’s, but sold by the Trusteees for Sale of Irish Forfeitures, upon Pretence of the Attainder of one Charles Geogehan, who claimed the said Estate under a Deed, made by the Petitioners Grandfather, when he was a Lunatick; which was fully made out to the Committee, of this House, to whom the now Petitionersformer Petition was referred; who thereupon came to this Resolution: " That the Petitioners had proved the Allegations of " their Petition; and that they are real Objects of Compassion, and justly deserve the Favour of this House That, notwithstanding their same has been also recommended to the House by her Majesty, yet the Petitioners have had no Relief; whereby they are very much indebted, and reduced to the lowed Misery: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as is consistent with the Justice of the House.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several of the Owners and Occupiers of Dittaf the Meadows, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, lying between Reading and Nezl'bery, in the County of Berks, and adjoining to the River Kennet, in the said County', was pitfented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners Meadows, adjoining to the said River, are of a peaty and spungy Nature; and, if the said River should be made navigable, the Banks will be raised, and, with penning up the Water with Locks and Wears, the Water will often be raised to a very great Height, and thereby the Meadows will be subject to be drowned, to the Petitioners Damage: And praying, that effectual Care may be taken in the Bill, now depending in the House, for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Ntzvbery, for making good to the Petitioners all Damages, that shall happen by reason of the said Navigation.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Mr. MtdJicott (according to Order) reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for ascertaining, and limiting, the Time of future publick Mournings, was committed; that they had made some Amendments to the Bill, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where they were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and another Amendment was made by the House to the Bill.

A Petition of Charles Pye, Esquire, was presented to Privilege — the House, and read; setting foith, that in the Year in a Suit 1691 the Petitioner’s late Grandfather, and Father, exhibited a Bill in Chancery against Henry Gorge, Esquire (a Member of this House) and Eliz. his Wife, the Daughter of Robert Pye, Esquire, deceased, to oblige the Performance of the latt Will of Sir Walter Pye, deceased, whereby divers Manors and Lands, ot£. 1,200 per num, ought to defeend to the Petitioner, but Mr. Gorge got into Possession, under Pretence of Incumbrances, which are long since satisfied; to which Bill the Defendants answered, but by their Delays, the Caule could not be brought to hearing till the 27th of Jan. 1695, when it was referred to a Matter, to state the Cafe; but before that could be done, by the Defendant’s Delays, the Petitioner’s Father died, and the Petitioner brought his Bill of Reviver; to which the Defendants demurred, and by the Privilege of Mr. Gorge the Petitioner has been so hindered, that he could not proceed in the said Cause till lately, and that only in the intervals of Parliament; but at length the Defendants have answered; yet the Petitioner cannot proceed, during the fitting of Parliament: And praying, that Mr. Gorge may wave his Privilege, and that the Petitioner may at least have Liberty to examine his Witnesses, in regard the most material of them are very old and infirm, and probably may die, before they are examined.

To the Matter of which Petition the said Mr. Gorge was heard in his Place.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Trade to Africa.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

The Lord Wm.Fowled took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

The Lord Wm, Powlett reported from the Committee, that they had made some further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to move, that the separate Traders to may lay before the

Committee, a Scheme, for carrying on the Trade to Africa in a free and open Trade, with such Regulations, and Provisions, as may be for the Preservation of the Trade and Settlements, according to the Resolutions of the House.

Ordered, That the separate Traders to Africa do lay before this House, a Scheme, for carrying on the Trade to Africa in a free and open Trade, with such Regulations, and Provisions, as may be necessary for the Preservation of the said Trade, and maintaining the Forts and Settlements, according to the Resolutions of this House.

The Lord William Powlett also reported from the said Committee, that they had directed him to move, that the Royal African Company may lay before the Committee, a distinct Valuation of each of their Forts and Settlements in Africa.

Ordered, That the Royal African Company do lay before this House, a distinct Valuation of each of their Forts and Settlements in Africa.

The Lord Wm. Powlett also acquainted the House, that the Committee had directed him to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morn-

ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Trade to Africa.

From all which Considerations the Company do humbly hope, upon Examination, it will appear, that the foregoing Valuation, made by them of their Forts and Settlements, is moderate, jud, equitable, and reasonable.

By Order of the Court of Assistants of the Royal African Company of England, the 16th of February,

Richard Beaumont, Accomptant to the said Company.

Then the separate Traders to Africa were called in> and, at the Bar, presented to the House their Scheme, for carrying on the Trade to Africa And being withdrawn;

The Title of the said Scheme was read.

And the said Scheme is as followeth; viz.

IN Obedience to an Order of this honourable House, of the 13th of February, 1709, the separate Traders to Africa do humbly lay before this House the under-written Scheme, for carrying on the Trade to Africa in a free and open Trade, with such Regulations and Provisions, as may be necessary for the Preservation of the said Trade, and maintaining the Forts and Settlements, according to the Resolutions of this honourable House.

1 ft, That in calc this honourable House shall judge it necessary, that the Traders to hould be incorporated, her Majesty may incorporate them accordingly, with such Powers, as shall be necessary, for enlarging the said Trade, and for the providing for incident Charges on extraordinary Occasions; so as every Subject of her Majesty may become a Member of such Corporation, upon paying such Fine, as this honourable House shall judge reasonable; and so as the Trade be preserved free and open, according to the Resolutions of this honourable House.

2d, That such Equivalent be given to the Royal African Company, for their Interest in the Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, now in their Possession, as to this honourable House shall seem meet.

3d, That the said Forts and Settlements be veiled in her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors.

4th, That her Majesty may appoint such Governors, and other Officers, and Soldiers, for the Defence of the said Forts and Settlements, from time to time, as to her Majesty shall fetm meet.

Vol. 16.

.479.555 ~ T-

th, That, for the enabling her Majesty to maintain such Forts and Settlements, as shall be necessary, for th^ carrying on and preserving the said Trade, and providing the Equivalent for the Royal African Company, the several Duties, appointed by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 9th and 10th Years of the Reign of the late King William the 3d, of glorious Memory, intituled, "An Act for settling the Trade to ," to be paid by the Traders to and from Africa, for the Use of the said Royal African Company, for enabling them to maintain their Forts and Castles on the Coast of Africa, be, from the time of veiling the said Forts and Settlements in her Majesty, made payable to her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors.

6th, That, in case the said Duties shall not be thought sufficient for the Purposes aforesaid, a further Duty be jgranted to her Majesty out of the said Trade, or a Duty of per Head be laid upon all Negroes, to be imported into any of her Majesty’s Plantations, to be paid by the Importers, to continue for such Term, as to this honourable House shall seem meet.

7th, That, for the better enabling her Majesty to maintain the said Forts and Settlements, every Master of any Ship or Vessel, of the Burthen of too Tons, bound for the Coast of Africa, shall be obliged, if required, to take on board Tons of Provisions, Ammunition, Stores, Materials for building, and other Necessaries, for the Garisons of the said Forts and Settlements, and deliver the same at such of the said Forts and Settlements, as shall be directed, Freight-free; and shall be obliged to transporc Soldiers to any of the said Forts and Settlements, at per Head; and so every Master of any other Ship, in greater or lesser Quantities, and Numbers, in proportion to the Burthen of his Ship or Vessel.

8th, That the several Clauses, Provisoes, Restrictions, and Regulations, relating to the Trade to , in the said Act of the 9th and 10th of King William the Third, be continued.

9th, That all Persons be prohibited from planting Sugar Canes, Indico, Ginger, Cotton, and Tobacco, and other Plantation Commodities, in Africa, under such Penalties, as to this hononrable House shall seem reasonable.

10th, That all Persons be prohibited, under a Penalty, from carrying off any free Negroes wrongfully from Africa.

11 th. That all the Forfeitures, appointed by the said Act, of the 9th and 10th of William the 3d, be granted to her Majesty, for and towards the maintaining the said Forts and Settlements: reserving the reout such Part of them for the Informers, as this House shall judge proper.

12th, That no Governor, nor any other Officer, belonging to the said Forts and Settlements, so appointed by her Majesty, shall have the Liberty of the said Trade; nor any Merchant, or other Person whatsoever, shall load Negroes on board of any Ships or Vessels, but such, as belong to Great Britain, or the Plantations.

13th, That her Majesty, if Ihe thinks fit, may grant Licences to the Traders to Africa, as aforesaid, to supply the Spanish or Portuguez Settlements in America with Negroes, to be carried thither directly from the Coast of Africa.

If this foregoing Scheme do meet with the Approbation of this honourable House, we humbly conceive, that the African Trade, being thus immediately under her Majesty’s most gracious Protection, and the separate Traders to Africa freed from die Oppressions of the Royal African Company, will be very mych improved, and extended over all the Coast of Africa: For We humbly

hope.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon the Petitions of John Forbett, and others, Creditors of the Earl of Kildare, deceased, and of George Rodney Bridget, and Richard Baggot, Esquires, Executors of the said Earl, and the Resolution of the Committee, which they had directed him to report to the the House; and he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered the Report, and Resolution, in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Counsel for the Petitioners, Mr. Bridges and Mr. Baggott, alleged, that the late Earl of Kildare by his last Will devised to them all his Lands in England and Ireland, in Trust, by Sale, or otherwise, to pay so much of his Debts and Legacies, as his executory Estate would not be sufficient to pay; and made the Petitioners his

1709.

Executors; and, after his Debts and Legacies paid, he devised the Surplus of the said Estate to the Duke of Richmond, for his Life, and, after his Death, to be divided amongst his the said Duke’s younger Children.

That, after the Earl’s Death, the said Petitioners proved the said Will in the Prerogative Court, though Mr. Francis Robarts(a Member of this House) and the

Lady Ann, his Wife (who was Sifter, and Heir, to the said Earl of Kildare) obstructed the Proof of the same; but being well satisfied, that it was the Will of the said Earl; they withdrew the Caveat they had entered against proving thereof.

That the said Duke of Rand his Children, preferred a Bill in Chancery against the said Petitioners, and the said Mr. Robarts, and his Lady, to prove the said Will, and to have an Account of the Estate; to which the Petitioners, and the said Mr. Robarts, and his Wife, having answered, the Cause was heard by the Lord Chancellor of Great Britain; who (amongst other things) decreed, that the Mailer should take an Account of the Debts of the said Earl, which, the Counsel for the Petitioners alleged, amounted to £. 13,000, and of the said Earl’s executory Estate, in order to appoint so much of the real Estate of the said Earl, to be sold, for Payment of the Debts, as the executory Estate would fall short of paying; and the Clerk in Court for the said Lady Ann Robarts was to have Notice from time to time, for attending the Account before the said Mailer; which was accordingly given; and the Clerk for the said Lady Ann Robarts did several times attend on the said Account; and the Mailer is now ready to make his Report.

That, during the said Tran last ions, the Petitioners have been sued by several of the Creditors of the said Earl, who have obtained Judgments agaii;ft the Petitioners; and to gain Time, till the Court of Chancery should make a Decree, for Satisfaction of the Debts, the Petitioners have been forced to give Judgments de bonis propriis, upon a Stay of Execution till the First Day of this present Hilary Term.

That the Petitioners endeavouring to take out the Report, that the same might be set down to be heard by the Lord Chancellor, for his final Decree, Mr. Robarts obstructs the lame, by infilling upon his Privilege,}though he is only intitled, in Right of his Wife, as Heir at Law, to the real Estate, in case there was no Will.

That the Counsel for the Petitioners, the Creditors of the said late Earl of Kildare, admitted the Fast, as to their Cafe, as was alleged by the Counsel for the Petitioners, the Executors of the said late Earl of Kildare.

And only further observed, that the late Earl of Kildare had taken all the Care, that was possible, for the Satisfaction of his Debts, by making his last Will in the Manner before set forth; which Will has been duly proved:

And that several of the Petitioners Debts, which were occasioned by Ample , Contraft, can carry no Interest; and consequently such Creditors must be ruined, if some Parr of the Testator’s real Estate be not speedily fold, for satisfying those Debts.

That the Counsel for Mr. Robarts admitted the Will of the late Earl, as set forth by the Counsel for the Petitioners; and that the Debts of the Testator were very considerable, but far short of what his personal Estate was sufficient to satisfy, which, they said, Mr. Robarts would be able to prove in Chancery, if he might have sufficient Time:

And that Mr. Robarts, being intitled to the Reversion of the real Estate, after the Limitations thereof by the Will directed, and at present to the Overplus of the executory Estate, they alleged, that Mr. Robarts was justly entitled to the Privilege of this House.

That the Counsel for the Creditors, by way of Replj?, said, that they conceive the Privilege of this House will not extend beyond the disturbing the Person, or Possession, of any Member of the House; which, in this Cafe, can no ways affect the fitting Member, Mr. Robarts, whose Expectancy to the Testator’s Estate can be

A Petition of divers Weavers, Flax-dressers, Whitfters, linen

Spinsters, Winders, and others, concerned in the Linen ^anu Manufacture within the several Towns of Manchester,

Wigan, Warrington, Eccleslon, Blackborne, Lay land, Walton, Preston, and elsewhere, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, on behalf of themselves and many Thousands more, concerned in the said Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that since the Duty, called the Two-third Subsidy, was taken off all foreign European Linen, such great Quantities of that Commodity have been imported into Great Britain, and sold at lower Prices, than can possibly be afforded at here, that many Thousands, Manufacturers therein, are reduced to great Extremities, for want of Employ; many

A Petition of several Creditors of the Royal African

Company of England, on behalf of themselves, and other Creditors of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Company owe the Petitioners, and others, about £. 300,000, and refule to pay them, and have stopt paying Interest on most of their Bonds, from Michaelmas, 1708; so that the Petitioners conceive, the Company are incapable to pay their Debts, which are Ten times more than the Value of their Stock, at the present Price: That the Charges of prosecuting at Law will be rnfopportable to the Petitioners, and, even if they should sue, it will be in the Power of the Managers of the Company to give Preference, as they please, to any of their Creditors, and leave the rest without Payment; and they may also make Dividends of their Effects amongst the Proprietors of Stock, and leave little or nothing for their Creditors, who (as advised) have no Remedy in Law or Equity, to compel the Company to apply theft Estate £nd Effects to an equal Proportion, for Payment of their Debts: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in Bill to enable the Creditors to name Managers of the said Company, instead of the Proprietors of Stock, and to pay the Produce of the Company’s Stock, proportion-abfy amongst: the Creditors, and the Surplus (if any) to the Owners of Stock, or that the Petitioners be otherwise relieved, as the House shall think fit:

A Petition of Sir Wm. Milman, and others, the Lessees of Rugby School, in the County of Warwick, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there are certain Lands belonging to the said School, lying in the Parish of St. Andrew's, Holboum, in Middlesex, the greatest Part whereof is built upon, and the other Part contrafted for: That, if the Bill to restrain the building upon new Foundations, within the Cities of London and Westminster, should pass, the Petitioners wiil be deprived of making the belt Advantage for the said Charity: And praying, that they may have a laving Clause in the Bill> or be otherwise relieved.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report shall be made from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of several of the Creditors by Bonds, Bills, and Specie Notes, of the Company of Mine Adventurers of England, on behalf of themselves, and other Creditors, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Company, to induce Persons to lend them Money, as a Bank, did publickly give out, that they had entered into a Deed of Subscription of f. 40,000 to circulate the said Bonds, Bills, and Specie Notes; and that the Deed was to be a Security for Repayment of the Money, deposited with them; and shewed a Deed, for that purpose, to some of the Petitioners: That, soon after the Petitioners had lodged their Money in the said Bank, the Deputy Governor and Directors postponed Payment of their Bonds, Bills, and Specie Notes, and stopt Payment thereof; and gave out, that they had can* celled the said Deed of Subscription, in order to prevent the Petitioners from having any Benefit thereon in Law or Equity: That, notwithstanding Payment was stopt, as aforesaid, yet they kept their Office open, by which Artifice many of the Petitioners (not knowing of a Stop of Payment) paid in their Money, and afterwards, going to demand it again, were told by the Officers, that, though they had Directions to receive Money, they had no Orders to pay any; by which deceitful Practices many of the Petitioners, who are Widows, and Orphans, are like to be ruined; and many Hundred Pounds, given to charitable Uses, and for erecting Schools, and educating poor Parish Children, is Part of the Money, the Petitioners are defrauded of: That the said Bills are generally made out in the Name of Tho. , Cashier of the said Company; and an Action being brought against the said Company on one of the said Bills, the Company pleaded a general Release from Dykes', whereby all the said Bonds, Bills, and Specie Notes, are at once made of no Effect: And praying, that the House will take

some effectual Means, whereby the Estates of the Persons, who have been concerned in setting up, and managing, the said Bank, as well as the said Company, may be made liable to satisfy the Petitioners, or that they may have such other Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Creditors, and Proprietors of principal Money, Annuities, and Shares, in the Mine Adventure of on behalf of themselves, and several Widows and Orphans, Members and Creditors of the Company of the said Mine Adventure, is referred.

P ET IT I ON of the Clothiers, Spinners, Weavers, Duty and others, at Dorchester, and in other Parts of the k^i

County of Dorset, employed in, and subsisting on, the Woollen Manufactory of Great Britain, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have observed, that, as often as any new Duties have been laid on any Commodities of the Growth of Spain, that Nation hath laden with fresh Duties all Manufactories exported thither, to the great Decay of Trade:

That a further Duty being intended to be laid upon Raisins, the Petitioners apprehend, it will have the illCon-sequences aforesaid, and so lessen their Employ, that their Families will want common Subsistence: And praying the 'Consideration of the House in the Premises, and Relief from the melancholy View, which seems to threaten them.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the WorRed Weavers of the City of Norwich, and County of Norfolk, in behalf of themselves, and of the Wool-growers, Combers, Spinsters, ThrowRers, Dyers, Hot-preffers, Grofiers, and others, concerned in the Woollen Manufactory, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, and other Woollen Manufacturers, have formerly laid before the Parliament the sinking Condition of the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom, by the excessive Use 0 fEaflIndia Silks, and printed and Rained

Calicoes; to prohibit which, an Act passed, which was then thought sufficient to protest the IntereR of our Woollen Manufactures; but since that Time some Persons here have found out Methods to print, and Rain, not only Paper, but also Calicoes, and other Linens, vaR Quantities whereof are daily fold, and used, for Gowns, Petticoats, Bedding, Curtains, Quilts, Hangings, and othe -wife; by which Means the Petitioners are in a worle Condition, than before, and their Manufactures at so low a Rate, that unless they have some speedy Relief, it threatens the utter Ruin of their Trade, and the Rarving ofimaoy thousand Families in the Kingdom, whole whole SubfiRcncc depends thereon: And praying, that the

House will take the Matter into Consideration, and prevent the using of printed Calicoes, and other Linen, and Paper Hangings in this Nation, which tend to the Ruin of the Trade of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Fishermen within the Manor and Hundred of Fever/ham, in the County of Kent, for and on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Fishermen within the said Manor, and Hundred, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they are entitled to several Waters and Fishings within the said Manor, and Hundred, and have enjoyed the same under the Lords of the said Manor for the Time being -, but the same being a Fishery for Oysters only, they go out to Sea, to dredge for Oysters, Mackrels, Herrings, and other Fith, and look upon themselves to be within the Jurisdiction of the Lord High Admiral, and are enrolled, and do appear, and owe Suit and Service, at all the Vice Admiral Courts: That there are several large Oyster 'Grounds, and Waters, called the Flatts and Cant, extending from Sheerness down to the North Foreland, about 20 Miles in Length, and Seven in Breadth, wherein they have fished and dredged Time out of mind, and are within the Admiralty Jurisdiction, and no Part of the River Thames: That in the Bill depending, for the better Preservation, and Improvement, of the Fishery within the River Thames, and for the Regulation and Government of the Company of the Fishermen of the said River; wherein ’tis pretended, they have Jurisdiction down to North Foreland, and from thence to Harwich, including the Flatts and Cants abovesaid: That the Petitioners will be put to very great Charge and Expence, if the said Bill pass: And praying, to be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard before the Committee, by their Counsel thereupon, if they think fit: And that Mr. Watson and Mr. Wentzvortk be added to the said Committee.

A Petition of Samuel Potts, Gentleman, Jane Hinds, Widow, George Ballard, Esquire, Alexander Akehurfi, Esquire, and Katherine his Wife, and Edward Nelthorpe, Esquire, Lessees of Conduit Mead, in the Parish of St. . Martins in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they are possessed, for a Term of 55 Years, in a Mead, called Conduit Mead, in St. Martin's Parish *, and a large commodious S.reet is intended to be made from marle Ground, through the said Mead, into a new Street, called Marlborough Street, in St. James's, Westminster; whereby those Persons of Quality, who live in said Marlborough Street, will have a convenient short Passage 20

through the said Mead to her Majesty’s Palace: AmL praying, that a Clause may be inserted in the Bill for preventing future Buildings on new Foundations, for excepting the said Conduit Mead.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report shall be made from the Committee, to whom the Bill was committed.

A Petition of several Mercers, and Grocers, inhabiting Mercer* and within the Borough of Leominster, in. the County of Hereford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they have followed their Trades several Years within the said Borough, and paid all Taxes, and at a considerable Expence served Apprenticeships to their Trades; and that divers Persons, who never served any Apprenticeships, do openly carry on the lame, to their great Prejudice: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Petitioners would then have proved, that the Directors, in making Bargains for the Value of £. 5,000, had exceeded the Power, given them by their said Settlement; but failed in Proof; it appearing, that though by the Deed printed for the Information of such Persons as are concerned, the Power of the Directors was confined to Bargains of £. 5,000 Value, yet, by the original Settlement, they could contrail for any Sum under 10,000.

Mr. Blechingdon laid before the Committee a sealed Bill of the Company of the Mine Adventurers, for to prove, the Company had ereiked a Bank: And then the Petitioners proceeded to make good the Allegation in their Petition, that deceitful Means were used, to procure Credit, and worse, for eluding Creditors, and preventing their recovering their just Debts.

To prove the First Part of the Allegation, Mr. , Agent for the Company at the Lead Mines, produced Three Letters, which, he said, he had received from Sir HumphryMackivonb, lettered C, D, and Ej which Letters being shewn to Mr. Sheeres and Mr. Wijhaiv, and being by them owned to be Sir Humphry Macktvorth's Hand-writing, the Committee have made such Extracts from them, as the Petitioners made use of, to prove their Assertions; viz. January the 23d, 1699, Sir Mackworth writes to Mr. Waller:

" You cannot imagine thcCry againstusin this Town. " All my best Friends begin to forsake us. If there be " no Prospect of Interest Money this June, neither " Blanks, nor Shares, will be worth picking up in the Streets; but, if we had a little Oar in the Banks, and " were raising Oar in Two or Three Places, I could get the Committee, perhaps, to buy the Company’s " Shares, and pay the Interest, at least to all the new " Adventurers. I believe, you had best tell us of that " Bargain in the North Vein, without distinguishing " whose Ground it is; which you may hereafter excuse, " alleging, you were informed, that I had granted the " Oar to the Company; for then we can still say, we are raising Oar in Two Places. In your next you had best " give us l'ome Account of your raising Oar, and tell us, " why you cannot raise much at first, the Water being " strong upon you, and you cannot suddenly drain it, " nor make room for many Men to work, but in time " you shall double your Men, and raise Quantities, but " much more, when the lower Level is brought home " to the Vein, and no Water trouble you: In the mean " time you have a full Trial of the Vein, as to its " Certainty of being a settled Vein, and bearing rich in " Oar; but that they must not expect, at first coming " up to any Vein, to raise Oar fast. 1 have demonstrated, that One thousand Ton of Oar, raised the First " Year after the Levels are brought home, and doubled " every Year, for Five Years, and then added together, " will raise 31,000 Ton of Oar; which, at £.6 per Ton, " fmeltiflgand refining, will amount to^.i86,000, which " will fully pay Principal and Interest, and £. 23,500 " Overplus: so this Notion must be kept up.

" I must beg of you to continue to raise Oar with " Pumps, or Engines, or any thing, either in the great " Shaft, or West Level, though it cost £. 40 per Ton. " See what you can bargain for: The Name of raising Oar in several Places will raise us Money, and keep " our Credit, till the great Vein is found, and our " Interest Money paid. Pray consider these things, and " fee what you can do."

Out of the Letter, marked D, dat. 160 Jamarii, 1706, the Petitioners read this Passage:

" I confess, we are now in great Hopes from both " Mines and Bank: The latter, in time, may alone " support us, had we but Quantity of Goods at any " Rate."

Mr. Sheeres, being examined, what he knew concerning Mr. Peck's buying Lead for the Company’s Use, said, *4

that Sit Humphry Mackworth had Orders from the Committee of Management to make a Contract with Mr. Peck 1 and accordingly Sir Hump. Mackworth had entered into Articles, and contrafted, in Consideration of£. 3,388, fot such Lead, and Workhouses, as were belonging to the said Peck; and that, as he*was a Man of Business and Reputation in the Country where the Mines were, and the Queen’s Receiver for several Counties, he was looked upon as one, might be useful in circulating the Company's Bills, and was promised by Sir Humphry Mackworth the annual Dividend of 200 Shares, which might be worth, about £.300 a Year,

He being aiked, whether Mr. Peck, besides the said Bargain, had not transacted other Business, and, whether he had not Orders from Sir Humphry Mackworth to buy Lead for the Company’s Use; he owned, that Mr. Peck had bought considerable Quantities of Lead, and Oar, in Flintshire, and thereabouts: That the Oar was fmeltal in the Company’s Work-houses; and that the Lead was shipt, or fold, as the Produce of the Company’s Mines.

Sheres, being aiked the Date of Mr. Peck's Articles with Sir Humphry Mackworth, owned, they were dated the 30th Day ot May, 1707, and prior to any Order of the Court of Directors; and that it was agreed by One of the Articles, that, if the Agreement was not confirmed, and the Conveyances executed in pursuance thereof, by the Company, in Two Months, those Articles were to be void; but that, he believes, by a subsequent Agreement, the Company was to have a longer time, for confirming the said Articles.

Mr. Peck said, that about the 30th of 1707, he did enter into Articles with Sir Humphry Mackworth, to fell such Lead, as was his own, with his Workhouses, to the Company of Mine Adventurers, with this Proviso,. that the Articles should be void, if not confirmed by the Company, and Deeds executed thereupon, in the Space of Two Months; which Condition was not perfo&ied, nor does he remember, he agreed afterwards, that the Company should have a further time allowed, for confirming their Agreement; but that, excepting the Bargain, mentioned in the said Articles, he had no other. Dealings with the Company; but that whatever he tr^nf-acted since, has been upon the Account of Sir Humphry. Mackworth, and by his and Mr. Sheres' Directions.

That the Letters, he received from Sir Humphry Mackworth and Mr. Sheeres, make no mention of Orders from the Company.

Mr. Jackson and Mr. Breton said, that they believed, the Proposal, that was made in the Discourse, that had passed amongst them, was for cancelling both the Deeds.

The Committee obstrved, that the cancelling these Two Circulation Deeds deprived the Creditors of a*Demand of £.33,200 that remained unpaid by the Subscribers.

The Petitioners laid before the Committee, an Extract of the Debts of the Company, contracted by banking, amounting to £. 88,049. 13,1. with this Observation, that when the Company had by Art raised their Credit, they thought convenient to put a Stop to their Payments, for which there was, at the time it was made, no immediate Necessity.

To prove the First Part of that Allegation, they produced the following Minute of the Court of Directors, held the 17th Day of March, 1707.

" Present,

" Sir Humphry Mackworth,

*( Sir Tho. Mackworth, Mr. Fenwick,

" Mr. Gardiner, Mr. Freeman Collins,

Mr. Edward Harrison, Sir James Hallet.

" Sir Humphry Mackworth acquainted the said Directors, that the Committee of Management had thought " it convenient, that the Payment upon Specie Bills " might be postponed for some time; and defirrd an " Order of that Court for that Purpose: W hich was " ordered accordingly."

The Petitioners also produced the Minute of the Committee of Management, of the 16th of , 1707; whereby it appeared, that such Order was made by the Committee of Management, as is referred to in the Minute of the Court of Directors; and that there was present Sir Humphry Mackworth, Sir Thomas,

and Mr. Fenwick.

The said Mr. Fenwick said, he was not present at the Committee of Management on the 16th of March, 1707, and never had been above Four times in his Life present at the said Committee; and complained to Sheres, who was Secretary to that Committee, for putting his Name present so often, in his Absence; and the said Sheres begg’d his Pardon for so doing: The which Mr. Fenwick proved by Mr. Gardiner-, who said, he was by, when Mr. Sheres begg’d Mr s Pardon, for

having entered him present, as aforesaid.

The Petitioners, to prove, that there was no immediate Necessity for the Company to make the aforesaid Orders, laid before the Committee the Company’s Calli Book j whereby it appeared, that the Day, the aforesaid Order was made, there was received by the Cashier the Sum of £. 500 more than paid j and that there was in Calli the Sum of £. 10,776. 5*. id.

Mr. Dykes, the Cashier, owned, there was charged to his Account the said Sum of £. 10,776, and that thereof £.6,140 was in Money, and the rest in the Company’s own Notes, Goldsmiths Notes, and other Notes, as good as Money.

The Directors present being asked, (everally, why they had agreed to an Order, for flopping the Payment of their Specie Bills, when they had so great a Calli;

Mr. Collins said, he knew nothing of any such Order, not being present, when the same was made; and that . the Directors never had any material Boliness before them.

but all such were transacted by Sir Humphry

or by his Directions to Sheres, the Secretary, whole

Orders, and Actions, be hopes will be detested

Mr. Harrison said, it was very plain, he could not be present when such Stop was ordered, for that he went, the next Day after such Order bears Date, to receive £. 600 upon the Company’s Bills, and was put off by Dykes till the Monday following, under the Pretence, that Sheeres was not present: when, and not till then, he was told of the Stop by Sir Humphry himself; and that it was necessitated, for want of Money to support their Credit.

Sir James Hallet said, he was not present, when any such Order, for postponing their Bills, was made; and if he had, he should have opposed the fame; and that he was drawn into the last Subscription by the Mifrepre-fentation of the Company’s Circumstances from Mr. Breton, a mighty Manager with Sir Humphry Mackworth.

Mr. Gardiner and Wm. Schaiter laid, they were present, when Sir Humphry Mackworth pr'posed the post-

’ poning the Payment of the Specie Bills: That they asked him, what induced the Company of Management to make that Order, since it appeared by their Calb Books, there had been no Run upon their Bank, and that the Company had a large Calli: And the Answer, that was made them by Sir Humphry Mackworth, was, that they were Fools.

Mr. Gardiner added, that Mr. Sheres, being present, laid, that the Bank of England had made an Order, which he had seen, not only for adding an Interest to their Bills, but for postponing their Payments; That this was an Opportunity of doing the same thing, and a good Example to follow.

The Committee observed, that, besides the Sum of £. 10,776 in Calli, which by the Company’s Books appeared at the Time the Court of Directors postponed their Specie Bills, they had a Power of calling in the Money in the Subscription Deeds, to the Value of £.32,200.

The Petitioners proceeded to prove, there had been undue Preferences i for that, notwithstanding the Order, of the 16th of March, of the Directors, to postpone Payments, that there had been since that time paid to several People, by Dykes, the Company’s Cashier, the Sum of £. 2,674. 10/. as appeared by an Account, given in by Dykes, lettered K.

Mr. Worfdale, one of the Clerks of the Company, said, that some Payments had been made to clamorous People, by verbal Orders from the Directors; and the Remainder was paid to Directors, their Favourites, and Relations.

Mr. Dykes, Cashier, said, that in pursuance of an Order, he had had from Sir Humphry Mackxvorth, to take Sheeres' Directions, he had consulted the said Sheres, and had had his Advice for all his Payments since the Order to postponed Specie Bills, except in paying £.800 to Mrs. Cotton, for which he had Directions from the Committee of Management on the 26th Day of March, 1708: That the Directors signed his Accounts, wherein there appeared such Preferences, as are complained of; and he thought, that such signing was an Instance of their Approbation.

Mr. Collins, Mr. Jackson, Mr. Fenwick, Directors, said, that they only cast up the Books: That they were told, some Payments had been made upon Clamour; and, as such, admitted them.

Mr. Sheres, being ask’d, by whose Orders £. 800 was . paid to Mrs. Cotton, produced Two Minutes otthe Court of Management; one made the 12th Day of March, 170J, by which it was directed, that the Bullion, belonging to the Company, should be deposited in Mrs. Cotton’% Hands, as Security for £. 800 with Interest at £. 6 per Cent, the other Minute made a Fortnight after, (Sir Humphry Mackworth and Sir Thomas Mackworth present,) whereby it is ordered, that Leave be alkt ot Mrs. Cotton, for to coin, at the Tower, the Bullion in her Possession; and that (he should be at liberty to deduct thereout the £. 800.

And it appeared to the Committee, by the Cash Books, that the Specie Bills for /.800 were paid; which Mr. Shares owned to be true.

It appearing to the Committee also, by the Account laid before them, that Sir Ja ,a Director, had been paid £. 700 for the Company’s postponed Bills;

The Committee, having observed, upon several Occasions, that Dykes and Shteres had grofly prevaricated, and given very indirect Answers, enquired, whether the Servants of the Company did not take an Oath of Secrecy.

Mr. Morifon said, that he was present at the Company’s House, at a Court held there, when Sir Humphry Mackworthy for his Justification upon a Point then in DHpute, ordered the Secretary and Cashier to be called up, and told the Court, that he hoped, they would believe them, for that they were upon their Oaths; Which Sheerer and Dykes did then own.

A Book was produced to the Committee, intituled,

That he therefore joined Issue, and went to Trial; but the due Execution of the Release being proved by the said Dykes, to the great Surprize of the Court, his Client was call, and the Court acquainted the Plaintiff, that there was no Relief to be had against such Release, but in Chancery.

As a further Proof of this Fast, the Record, and Verdict, was read to the Committee.

Dykes, being examined as to the executing such Release, said, that he did it with Reluctancy, upon Mr. Sheeres, the Secretary’s, Advice, and Directions; who brought him the Draught of the Release, to copy, and execute: That Sheeres told him, he should be indemnified; and that there was no other way, but that, to prevent the Company’s Stock, being all spent in Law, and the Mines being seized by the Creditors.

Mr. Wishaw, Attorney for the Company, being examined, said, that Mrs. Lucas having brought her Action in the Name of ‘Thomas Dykes against the Company, he acquainted Sir Humphry Mackworth at his own Chamber, Mr. Sheeres being present, that it was necessary to plead to Mrs. Lucas's Action the next Term, which was in the Year r 709: That thereupon there was iome Discourse of preventing Preference, if it could be avoided; and that Dykes executing a general Release was mentioned, as a proper Expedient: That he, the said Wyjhaw, objected, that it would raise Clamour; but, in pursuance of the Discourse at that time, he sent to Mr. a blank Release; and that soon after a general Release was returned him, executed by Thomas Dykes, and that he pleaded it in Bar of Mrs. Lucas's Action; but, disliking the manner of proceeding, within these few Days he cancelled the Release of his own Accord.

Mr. Sheres, after many gross Prevarications, and taking up much of the Committee’s Time, confessed, that he was present at the Discourse between Mr. Wishaw and Sir Humphry Mackworth about pleading to Mrs. Lucas’s Action: That the Discourse, that passed at that Time, he thought was sufficient Direction to him, to fill up the Blank in the Release, sent him by Mr. Wishaw, which he gave to Dykes, for to copy, and execute; and that, to lave Dykes, from Ruin, he obtained afterwards an Order from the Court of Directors, for indemnifying of him: Which Order of the 22d June, 1707, —

Present,

Sir Hum. Mackworth, Sir Tho. Mackworth, Mr. Freeman Collins, Mr. Wm. Gardiner, Mr. Hen. Buck, Mr. Bromjeild, Mr. Harrison

And being read;

It appeared to the Committee, that the said Order was subsequent to the Date of the Release, and was not for to indemnify Dykes, for having granted a general Release, but was only to make good the Damage he should fuffcr by Mrs. Lucas’s Action.

The Committee therefore examined the Directors, said to be present at the said Court, whether, at the Time of making the said Order, they had heard of a general Release.

Mr. Collins said, that he had never heard of any Order given by any Court of Directors, for Dykes giving any general Release to the Company: That a Release was once talked of, which he understood to concern only Mrs. Lucas's Suit; and that, since the Order, that was to be made, was to indemnify their Cashier against Mrs. Lucas only, he thought Dykes' Release extended no further, than her Action.

Mr. Buck, another Director, laid, that he had been a Director but for One Year; and, though he might be present the Day, when such Order of Indemnity appears to be entered in the Minutes, he knew nothing thereof; for it was a customary Usage for the Secretary to bring the Minutes ready prepared to the Court, and in the Hurry of Buiioels it often happened, that the Minutes were notread

over, by which means it Was in the Secretary’s Power to impose what Minutes he thought fit.upon the Court of Directors: He does remember, there was Come Discourse about a Release, that had been given upon Mrs. Lucas’s Action, but apprehended it to extend to her same only.

Sir James Hal/et, another Director, said, that he never

heard any thing of the Release, till Mrs. Lucas's Trial with the Company.

Mr. Edward Bromfield said that he knew nothing of the said Release; nor was present, when the Order of Indemnity was made, being at that Time out of Town; and observing, his Name to be made present at several Courts of Directors, when he was not there, he complained of that Usage to Sheres, the Secretary, who told him, it signified nothing.

The Petitioners observed, that, as there was indirect Practices used, to prevent the Creditors recovering their Debts at Common Law, Artifices had been also tried, to make it very difficult for them to have Relief in Equity.

To prove which,

Mr. Tho. Morrijon, Attorney at Law, said, that one Mr. Wilkins sent the Company £.300, and took their Specie Bills for the fame, which happened to be Two or Three Days before a Stop was made to the Payment of such Bills; and afterwards, going to demand his Money, and being refused Payment thereof, the said Wilkins, ordered Morrijon to fife a Bill in Chancery against the said Company, for Recovery of the fame, and obtained a Decree accordingly; but, pending the Cause, to his great Surprize, he found, that the Company bad filed in the said Court a Bill, in the Name of some of the Creditors, but without their Privity, wherein Mr. Wilkins, and the Company, were made Defendants, and wherein was fug-gefted a Combination and Confederacy between Mr. Wilkins (his Client) and the Company; and set forth a Deed, whereby the Company had conveyed all their Estate, Goods, and Effects, for the Benefit of the Creditors; and, to prevent any Preference, prayed, that Mr. Wilkins might not have Execution of the Decree. '

Part of the aforesaid Bill in Chancery was read: And it appeared, that Mr. Barker and Mr. Thomas Gray, Creditors, were Plaintiffs, together with several Persons, that were or had been Directors, but mentioned in the Bill as Creditors only.

Mr. Barker said, that his Name was made use of without his Consent or Knowlege.

Mr. Gray said, that Mr. Sheres asked him one Day, as he was passing by, whether the Company should make use of his Name ? That he did not refuse it, but did not esquire for what.

Mr. Wyjhaw, who had exhibited such Bill, being examined thereunto, said that the Draught of such Bill was brought to him by Mr. Sheres, the Secretary, with Orders to exhibit the same against the said Company, and Mr. Wilkins.

Mr. Sheres, being examined, owned, that he had received a Draught of the said Bill from Sir Humphrf Mackworth, which, by his Order, he, carried to Mr* Wyjhaw.

Mr. Wyjhaw laid before the Committee, by Order, the said Deed-poll, dated 15th February 1708, mentioned, and referred to, in the said Bill in Chancery, as also the Deed of Assignment and Confirmation to the Creditors, executed in pursuance of such Deed-poll, dated i° Febr, 1109; wherein it appeared, that the Company had granted the Mines and Stock of the Company in Trustees, fos 99 Years, for such Purposes, as should We declared by the major Part of the Creditors in Number and Value $ and in the mean time, till such Declaration shall be made, the said Trustees shall permit and suffer the chief Creditors, therein named, to manage, for the common Good.

A Petition of the Weavers, Dyers, and Combers, in the City of Coventry* in behalf of themselves, and many thousand other Persons, employed in the Woollen Manufacture in and about the said City, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the vast Importation, and excessive Use, of Callicoes, hath very much lowered the Rates of the Wool, and deprived the Poor of Business, being ready to starve: And praying the Consideration of their deplorable State, and Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

; Mr. Farrer (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for laying certain Duties upon Candles, and certain Rates upon Monies to be given with Clerks and Apprentices, towards railing her Majesty’s Supply for the Year 1710, was committed, the Amendments, they had made to the Bill, and had directed him to report to the House; and lie read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where they were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were (with some Amendments to some of them) agreed unto by the House.

And the same was twice read, with Blankswhich were filled up.

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir Richard Holford and Mr. Gery:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to a Bill, intituled, An Act to explain so much of the Act for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch, and low Wines, Spirits, Worts, and Walh, drawn from malted Corn, by which Act the said Commodities are admitted to be carried from the Isle of Wight to several Markets, and for giving Liberty to export certain Quantities of Oatmeal for the Uses of the Hospi-

tals beyond the Seas, without any Amendment:

Also, the Lords have agreed to a Bill, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Provision for the Poor of, the Town of Kingston upon Hull, without any Amendment:

Also, the Lords have palfed a Bill, intituled, An Act for the inclosing of Ropley Commons, in the County of Southampton, and for Improvement of the old disparked Park of Farnham, in the Counties of Surry and Southampton-, to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Memorandum: When Mr. Speaker came to the Door of the House of Lords, to demand Judgment against Doctor Henry Sacheverell, entering in with the Mace, the Deputy Gentleman Ullier of the Black Rod put his Rod cross the Door, to flop Mr. Speaker, and his Mace, from

foingjn; upon which Mr. Speaker bid him acquaint the ,ords, that he infilled upon it as his Right, to go to the Bar with the Mace: And the Door being shut, after fomq short time the Biack Rod returned, and opened the Door; and Mr. Speaker went, with the Mace on his right Hand towards the Bar; where the Black Rod attempting to interpose between Mr. Speaker and the Serjeant with the Mace; Mr. Speaker said,

" My Lords,

" If you do not immediately order your Black Rod " to go away, I will immediately return to the House " of Commons."

Upon which, the Black Rod was directed by the Lords to go from thence; which he accordingly did j and Mr. Speaker, with the Mace, went up to the Bar. After which, the Lord Chancellor directed the Black Rod ta bring the Prisoner to the Bar: And he bringing him accordingly, and going to place him on the right Hand of the Mace; Mr. Speaker said,

" My Lords,

" The Black Rod ought to be with the Prisoner on " the left Hand of me."

Whereupon the Lord Chancellor directed the Black Rod to go with the Prisoner on the left Hand of Mr, Speaker, at some Distance; and the Black Rod did it accordingly. And then Mr. Speaker demanded the Judgment, and it was pronounced accordingly.

Because ’tis a known pod principal Distinction in Law between Bills of p publick, and Bills of a private, Nature ,(of which later Sort the present Bill plainly is) -that the former are to be judicially taken Notice of by all Judges, and in all Courts; and that the later are pot so to be taken Notice of, but to be proved in Evidence by attested Copies or Exemplifications, or by the original Record: So that to insert such a Clause in a private < Bill is to confound, and take away an old approved Distinction in the Law, without any apparent Reason for doing it in this, rather than in any other, private Bill; and if such Clause should be admitted in one Bill, there would be the same Reason to admit the like jn all private Bills; which would abolish a Part of the common Law, without Rep-fqn plsigned for so doing: And there is the more Repfon agpinftaqing it in this Cafe, because the Clause in the Bill, to which the Commons have added this Amendment, has provided for the Iprqlp^ent of this Act in Ireland, where the Land lies; and.that Copies of such Inrolment there may be given in Evidence.

Mr. Compton reported from the Committee, appointed Copy Right to withdraw, and draw up Reasons, to be offered to the ^nt*d Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing to one of the Amendments, nude by the Lords to the Bill, intituled,

An Act for the Encouragement of Learning, by vesting > the Copies of printed Books in the Authors, or Purchasers, of such Copies, during the Times therein mentioned ( that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered . them in at the Clerk’s Table; where they were twice read, and agreed unto by the House; and ate as follow; viz,

The Commons disagree to your Lordships Amendment in Pr. 3. L. 41;

First, Because Authors, and Booksellers, having the lole Property ot Copies of printed Books vested in them by this Bill, the Commons think it reasonable, that some Provision should be made, that they do not set an extravagant Price on useful Books.

Secondly, Because the Provision, made for this Purpose by the Statute 25 H.VIII. Chap. 15. having been found to have been ineffectual, and not extending to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, it is neveflary to make such a Provision, as may be effectual, and which may extend to the whole united Kingdom.
