By the QUEEN:

A PROCLAMATION,

For dilfolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling of another.

ANNE, R.

Proclamation WfH EREAS we have thought fit, for divers weighty for diilolving V V Considerations, by and with the Advice of our Parliament. Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now Hands prorogued to , the Twenty-sixth Day

of this i»(buit September; we do, for that End, publUh this our royal Proclamation, and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spirituat and Temporal, a(nd the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the said

Parliament, are discharged from their meeting on the said Twenty-sixth Day of this instant September, And to the Intent our good Subjects may perceive the Confidence we have in the Assurances they have given us of their Duty and Affection, and how desirous we are to meet our People, and have their Advice, by their ftcpresentativev in Parliament; we do hereby make known to our said Sabjects, that we do intend, in some short time, to give Directions to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to cause Writs to be issued, in Form of Law, for the calling a new Parliament.

Given at our Court at the Twenty-full

Day of September, in the Ninth Year of our Reign.

ON which Day, being the First Day of the Meeting of this Parliament, pursuant to a Proclamation, hereunto annexed, and also to the Writ*, which had issued lor that Purpose, the most noble John Duke of Buc and Lord Steward of her Majesty’s Houshold, came, about Eleven of the Clock, into the Rooms belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons, called the Inner Court ot Wards, the usual Place to administer the Oaths, appointed to be taken by the Members, returned to serve in Parliament; and George Wright, Esquire, Clerk of the

Crown in Chancery, having delivered in a Book of the Names ot r! e Members, who had been returned; and Paul Jvdrel!, Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons, and Mr. Needier, Clerk Assistant, and the other Clerks, attending, according to their Duty; the Lord Steward did himfeil, in Person, administer the Oaths appointed to several ot tic Members, who appeared, and afterwards made a Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal (hereunto also annexed) impowering several of the Members, who had before been sworn, to administer the said Oaths to the rest of the Members returned; who administered the same accordingly to such other Members, as appeared: Which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons. After which,

A Message was delivered from the Queen by Sir William Older, Gentleman Uflierof the Black Rod: Gentlemen,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly the House went up, to attend her Majestyj who was plealed (by the Right honourable Sir Simon Harcourt, Lord Keeper of the great Seal of Great Britain) to command the Commons to return to their House, and chute their Speaker.

And the House being returned; the honourable Sir Thomas Hanmer, Baronet, Knight of the Shiie for the County of Suffolk, acquainted the House with the Queen’s Commands; and proposed, William , Esquire,

might be their Speaker; being a Gentleman of undoubted Loyalty and Affection to her Majesty’s Person and Government, and to all the just Rights and Prerogatives of the Crown; eminent for his true and unaffected Zeal for the Protestant Succession in the House of Hanover, and his firm Adherence to the Church of as by

Yoj.. 16.

Law established; and one, who, by a long Sendee in Parliament, had acquired great Experience in the Rules and Orders of the House, and had also given the World an equal Experience of himself, that nothing could ever draw him from the true Interests of his Country, and was sincerely and heartily affected to the common Cause in the present War.

Then George Pitt, Esquire, Knight of the Shire for the County of Southampton, said, that Mr. Bromley was lo well known to many Gentlemen present, and had in former Parliaments given so many Testimonies of his Zeal and Affection for the Service of the Queen, and Country, that it would be Vanity in him to pretend to say any thing of his Merits; and therefore he should only humbly beg Leave to second the Motion, made by the honourable Gentleman on the other Side, That Wm. Bromley, Esquire, might be their Speaker.

Whereupon Mr. Bromley stood up in his Place, and acknowleged the great Honour, that was done him, to be named for such a Station: That he had received many Instancesof the Friendshipof those Gentlemen, that had proposed him, and to that imputed their entertaining a better Opinion of him, than he deserved; but that he was onfeious of his own Inabilities to execute the fame, and lb sensible, there were many among them fitter for the Chair, that he hoped, they would consult the Interest of the Publick, and their own Honour, and chuse a more worthy Person.

But the House calling upon him to the Chair, he was conducted to it by Sir Thomas Hanmer and Mr.; and, being upon the lower Step, repeated his Request, that the House would please to excuse him, and chuse a fitter Person to be their Speaker: But the House crying,

" No! No!" he (hid, he hoped, they would then give him Leave to intercede with her Majesty to excuse him, and command them to m ice a better Choice. And thereupon he fat down in the Chair.

And M r. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainting the House, that her Majesty had directed, that they should prel’ent their Speaker to her in the House of Peers on Monday Morning, at Eleven a Clock;

The House adjourned till Monday Morning Ten a Clock.

THE House being met; and Mr. Speaker elect having . taken the Chair;

A Message was brought from her Majesty by Sir William OlJei, Gentleman UIher of the Black. Rod:

Gentlemen,

The Queen commands this honourable Houseto attend her in the House of Peers immediately.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went upf to atUnd -her Majesty; And they presented their Speaker, for her Majesty’s Royal Approbation; who spake to the Effect following; viz.

That the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, in Obedience to her Majesty’s Commands to them to chuse a Speaker, had tinanimously defied him to be their Speaker:

That they had many among them much fitter for this great Trust; and therefore, that the publick Service might not fufler through his want of Abilities todischarge it, he was an humble Suitor to her Majesty, that she would be pleased to excuse his undertaking it, and command the Commons to make a better Choice.

Whereupon the Lord Keeper laid, that her Majesty had commanded him to tell him, that (he well approved the Choice the Commons had made of him to be their Speaker; and that she did as little doubt of his Ability, as flie could of his Integrity; and that therefore her Majesty did not think fit to admit of his Excuse, but allowed and confirmed him to be their Speaker.

After which Mr. Bromley replied, that, since her Majesty had not been pleased to allow his Excul'e, but to approve of the Commons Choice, it was his Duty to submit; and he rendered her Majesty his most humble Thanks for the great and undeserved Favour:

That he was very sensible, the only Qualities he could pretend to, towards the Discharge thereof, were a sincere and steady Affection for our happy Establishment_ in Church and State, with an unfeigned Zeal and Devotion for her Majesty’s Person and Government; but, since her Majesty commanded him to this Service, he should humbly hope, her Majesty would pardon all his involuntary Failings, and accept his faithful Endeavours:

That he was persuaded, her Majesty would find, that Ihe is not disappointed, by confiding in the Assurances her good Subjects have given her Majesty of their Duty, and Afteftion: That they have chose such Persons to represent them in Parliament, as will effectually support her Majesty against all her Enemies; that will soon defeat all Artifices to destroy, or distress, the publick Credit; and enable her Majesty to bring that just and necessary War, in which Ihe is engaged, to a safe, honourable, and speedy, Conclusion:

That he did, in their Names, humbly present to her Majesty, their aecustomed Petitions for their ancient Rights and Privileges; particularly.

That, for their better Attendance on this Service, they, and their necessary Servants, might be free, in their Persons and Estates, from Arrests and Molestation;

That they might have Liberty and Freedom of Speech in their Debates;

That, as often as there should be Occasion, her Majesty would vouchsafe them Access to her royal Person;

And, that their Proceedings might at all times receive a favourable Interpretation, and be free from Miscon-itructions.

The House being returned; Mr. Speaker reported, that her Majesty had been pleased to give her Approbation of him for their Speaker: That he had humbly besought her Majesty to pardon his involuntary Failings, and to accept his faithful Endeavours to discharge the Duty of Speaker: And also, that he did, in their Names, 18

humbly present to her Majesty their aecustomed Petitions for their ancient Rights and Privileges; particularly,

I hat for their betrer Attendance on this Service, they, and their necessary Servants, might be free, in their Persons and Estates, from Arrests and Molestation;

That they might have Liberty and Freedom of Speech in their Debates;

That, as often as there should be Occasion, her Majesty would vouchsafe them Access to her royal Person

And, that their Proceedings might at all times receive a favourable Interpretation, and be free from Miscon-structions.

And that thereupon the Lord Keeper of the great Seal, by her Majesty’s Command, did signify, that her Majesty was so fully satisfied of his dutif ul Affection to her Service, that she was pleased to say, she would on all Occasions make the most favourable Construction of all his Words and Actions, in the Execution of his Duty; and that, as to the Suit, made in the Name of the House of Commons, her Majesty was so very well allured of the Temper and Wisdom of this House, as well as of their Loyalty, and Zeal for the present Establishment in Church and State, that she readily granted and allowed all their Privileges, as fully, as they have been at any time granted or allowed by any of her royal Predecessors.

After which, Mr. Speaker returned the House his humble Thanks, for the great Honour they had done him; which, he said, was the greatcfL Honour, they could confer, and, he thought, the greatest Honour a Commoner could leceive.

He promised an inflexible Integrity, an unbiafled Behaviour, and firm Refblution, to maintain the Honour and Dignity of the House: He said, these,-he hoped, were Qualities in his Power; that they might therefore expect them from him, and he would not fail to exert them on every proper Occasion.

In whatever else he was wanting, he begged the Assistance of Gentlemen, that had fat long in Parliament, and were well versed in the Methods of the House j whom he hoped would give good Example to others, by observing the Orders of the House: And earnestly desired, all Reflections might be avoided in their Debates.

He recommended their returning to the ancient Usage of Parliament, and meeting early in a Morning: He promised his Attendance: And then the Committees might fit, and prepare Business, as they used to do, in the Evening.

He concluded with entreating, that his Errors and Infirmities might be received with Candour, and forgiven.

And afterwards Mr. Speaker put the House in mind, that the first thing the y had to do, was to take the Oaths appointed, and to make and subscribe the Declaration, and take and subscribe the Oath of Abjuration, by Law required.

And Mr. Speaker first alone took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, accordingly.

And after him several other Members took the said Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member, to serve in Parliament.

Resolved', That, where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, in case it shall appear, any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, any Person hath been tampering with any Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdeameanour, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear any Person hath given tall'e Evidence in any same before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members, to serve for the Commons in Parliament, is a high Infringement of the Liberties nd Privileg es of the Commons of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do from time to time take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Cham, ber be locked up every Morning, at the fitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the

House: And that the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that from Nine of the Clock in the Morning, to Three in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and ,be

kept free and open j and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passageof the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care, there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or Passages leading to the House, during the fitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the high Bailiff of Westminster and that he do lee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Committees do fit in a Morning, without the special Leave of the House.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the printing thereof, and that no other Person do presume to print the lame.

Ordered, That the Committee, appointed to draw up the Address, to be presented to her Majesty, do fit Tomorrow Morning, if they think fit.

As we are Lovers of our excellent Constitution both in Church and State, and solicitous, that our Posterity may be as happy in all future Ages, as we hope long to continue under your Majesty’s moll auspicious Reign, we shall always Readily adhere to the Protestant Succession in the House of Hanover, and bemost watchful to prevent any Danger, which may threaten that Settlement, so necessary for the Preservation of our Religion, Laws, and Liberties.

These are Ends, truly worthy your Majesty’s Pursuit: And we do with all Humility represent to your Majesty, that the mosteflectual Way to give Spirit to your Friends, and defeat the restless Malice of your Enemies, will be, by difeountenancing all Persons of such Principles, and avoiding all Measures of such Tendency, as have lately threatened your royal Crown and Dignity, and which, whenever they prevail, will prove fatal to our whole Constitution both in Church and State.

Most grac:ous Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, do joyfully appear before your Majesty, to return our most humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne. We bring the Thanks of your whole People, whom your Majesty has made happy by that Confidence, you have been pleased to place in their Dhty and Affection; and we bring our own mostlolemn Assurances, that we will make all such Returns, as shall cotlvince your Majesty, that your Confidence has not been misplaced.

We are satisfied, we lie under all possible Obligations, both from our Duty to your Majesty, and the Care we owe to our Country, effectually and speedily togrant the necessary Supplies, for a vigorous Prosecution of the War in all its Parts, and especially in Spain. This we shall study to do in such a Manner, as may bell answer the publick Service, and be most easy to those we represent; and the same we shall continue to do, till such a Peace may be obtained, as your Majesty, in your royal Wisdom, shall judge to be safe and honourable for your Subjects, and all your Allies.

We have no Realbn to doubt of your Majesty’s Care in every thing, that concerns the Interest and Welfare of 1 your People; but we think ourselves obliged, in Justice to our Fellow-subjects, and in order to make them bear 'With greater Chearfulness the Burthens, we shall find necessary to lay upon them, most humbly to beseech your Majesty, that you will please to continue your powerful Influences with all your Allies, that they may exert themselves in the Common Cause with Resolutions equal, and Aids proportionable, to ours.

The Burthen of those heavy Debts, which prefles your People with so sensible a Weight, is in some measure alleviated by your princely Companion. We shall endeavour to trace the Source of this great Evil, and to apply a Remedy suitable to it. The Honour and Justice of Parliament shall by us be inviolably maintained, and all such other Measures pursered, by which the publick Credit may be preserved, and established.

Your faithful Commons are truly sensible of your Majesty’s Wifdotn and Goodftefs in those Resolutions, which you have declared; and do most heartily concur in all, which you have been pleased to recommend to them.

We return your Majesty our most humble Thanks for the firm Assurances you have given, both by your Words, and by your Actions, of supporting and encouraging the Church of England, as by Law established.

As we are true Sons of that Church, we cannot but be tenderly concerned for its Prosperity, and for its Honour; and are by Affection, and Principle, inclined to secure its Doctrine, Discipline, and Worship.

As we are Fellow-christians, and Fellow-subjects, With those Protestant Dissenters, who arefo unhappy to entertain Scruples against Conformity with our Church, we arc delirous, and determined, to let them quietly enjoy that Indulgence, which the Law hath allowed them.

As we are Britons, it is our common Interest, and shall be our joint Endeavour, to preserve that Union between the Parts of Great B, on which the Safety of the whole depends.

As we are Lovers of our excellent Constitution both in Church and State, and solicitous, that our Posterity may be as happy in all future Ages, as we hope long to continue under your Majesty’s most auspicious Reign, we shall always steadily adhere to the Protestant Succession in the House of Hanover, and be most watchful to prevent any Danger, which may threaten that Settlement, lb necessary for the Preservation of our Religion, Laws, and Liberties,

These are Ends, truly worthy your Majesty’s Pursuit: And we do with all Humility represent to your Majesty, that the most effectual Way to give Spirit to your Friends, and defeat the restless Malice of your Enemies, will be by difeountenancing ail Persons of such Principles, and avoiding all Measures of such Tendency, as may weaken your Majesty’s Title and Government, the Settlement of the Crown in the illustrious House of Hanover, and advance the Hopes of the Pretender, and all other Principles, and Measures, that have lately threatened your royal Crown and Dignity, and which, whenever they prevail, will prove fatal to our whole Constitution both in Church and State.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do hufttbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure, when Ihe will be attended by this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of the Justices of Peace, and Grand I)eV0B Jury, for the County of Devon, assembled at their General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, for the said County, u 1C the Third Day of October, in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her Majesty, and of divers other Gentlemen of the same County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by an Act of Parliament, made in the 19th Year of the Reign of King Charles the 2d, it was enacted, that the Sum of £. 2,000 should be laid out in the Purchase of Lands by the then Justices of Peace, for the publick Uses of the said County, in the said Act mentioned; £. 1,000 thereof certain Justices of the Peace for the said County had then provided, and the other £. 1,000 was added by some Charity-money, given to and agreed for with, the said*Gentlemen; and the said Purchase was accordingly made: That, since that Time, by the Produce thereof, and other Money, Two other Purchases have been made, of £. 2,500 Value; and the Petitioners have a further Sum to lay oyt, but are advised, they cannot safely do it, without an Act of Parliament: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to ratify the said Purchases, and to enable the Justices to lay out the Income thereof for the publick Good of the said County, as the Justices shall think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir Wm. Pole and Sir Nicholas Mortice do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Mr. Conyers (according to Order) reported from the Supply Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that Forty thousand Men be employed in the Sea Service, for the Year 17x1, including 8,000 Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding £. 4. per Man per ,be

allowed, for maintaining the said 40,000.Men, for 1 hir-teen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds, be allowed for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year 1711.

A Petition of Sir John Malcolm, Baronet, was read; fitting forth, that the Freeholders within the Shire of Kinroffe being assembled at Kinrojfe, to chuse a Commissioner to represent them in this Parliament, the Sheriff and his Deputy, and the now returned Member (neither of which had any Right to vote in the said Election) not only protected against all the good Votes there present, but illegally constituted themselves Three the only Meeting of Freeholders, to judge, that none else could be inrolled, to elect at that Meeting, but themselves; all which appears by the Minutes of the Election,

24

annexed to the Petition: That the Petitioner, with Four more, being the only Five unquedionable Votes at the Election, did protest, and infill upon their Right of voting; but the Sheriff, being Precefs, having Authority over his Clerk, did most scandalously admit Three miserable notorious Bankrupts to vote, which the Sheriff himself well knew, he having then Possession of all the Lands they ever had in that Shire; and that the Majority in any case might be secured, a Presbyterian Minister waa likewise admitted, whose Freehold did not consist of the Tenth Part required by Law; and even by these Four same Votes do they justify the Return, against the Petitioner’s Five unquestionable Votes; all which Practices do not only discourage the Attempts of honed Men to serve their Country, but endanger the very Conditution of Parliaments: And praying the House to take into their Consideration this unprecedented Election, and relieve the Petitioner from the Injudice of the said Return, and discourage the like evil Practices for the future.

Ordered, That the Merits of the Election for the Shire of Kinrojfe be heard at the Bar of this House upon Thursday, the 25th Day of January next.

A Petition of the Mayor, and divers Burgesses, of the Pembrok. ancient Borough of Wifton, in the County of Pembroke, Ele^oa-on the behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Burgesses of the said Borough, was read: setting forth, that the said Borough is an ancient Borough by Prescription, and their Mayor and Burgesses, and also the Mayor and Burgesses of Tenby, together with the Mayor and Burgesses of Pembroke, have a Right to Vote at the Election of a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Pembroke, and have frequently exercised that Right, and the Mayor of Pembroke has given Notice of such Election; but Sir Arthur Owen, Baronet (to gain the Government of Pembroke wholly into his own Hands) in 1704 procured himself to be elected Mayor (although by the Charters he was not qualified so to be) and so continued illegally for Two Years; during which time, he admitted great Numbers of his Dependants, Tenants, and Servants; who did not live within the Liberties of Pembroke, to be Common Council Men, and Burgesses, thereby intending (contrary to the Charters and By-laws of the said Borough) to deprive the Petitioners of their Right of Election: That Sir Arthur hath procured divers of his Dependants, of mean Fortunes, who were not House-holders in the Town, to be elected Mayors, who have also admitted great Numbers of unqualified Persons, as Burgesses of Pembroke; and the present Mayor, Joseph Rickfov, solicited in the last Election for Sir Arthur, and proceeded to Election, without giving the Petitioners such Notice, as the Law requires; yet they, and others,

A Petition of Francis Godolphin, Esquire, commonly called Lord Ryalton, was read; setting forth, that at the lad Election of Burgesses, to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, Alexander Pendarvis, Samuel Trefufis, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates: That Tho. Herle was then Portreeve of the said Borough, and the Precept for Election ought to have been delivered to him by the Sheriff of the said County; but he, to influence the Election, delivered it to Penhallow, who had no Pretence to the said Office, nor had been in Possession thereof for many Years before; yet he took it upon him, and refused several good Votes for the Petitioner, and took great Numbers of bad Votes for the said Mr. Trefufis; who by illegal Practices procured several Votes; and the said Penhalloio hath returned Mr. Pendarvis and Mr. Talthough the Petitioner had more good Votes, than either of them, and ought to have been returned with Mr. Pendarvis: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Henry Gorges, Esquire, was read; setting forth, that at the last Election of Knights of the Shire, to serve in this Parliament for the County of Hereford, the Right honourable James L-ord Viscount John Price, Esquire, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates:

That Mr. Price, and his Agents, with Samuel Clark, the Receiver General, and other Receivers General, by Bribery, and other illegal Practices, did procure and influence great Number of Votes for Mr. Price, several Hundreds whereof were Copyholders, and Cottagers, not having 40 s.a Year; and further to influence Votes for Mr.

Price, scandalous Libels were printed, and dispersed, reflecting upon the Privileges of the House of Commons; notwithstanding all which Proceedings, the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes of Mr. Price, and ought

to have been returned....

Ordered That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

That there are several ancient Entries of Stewards Names in the same Book: Some are,‘that they were chosen Stewards; others, that they were chosen and elected; and one in the Year 1699, that they were nominated and chosen Stewards for the Year ensuing, according to the Custom of the said Borough.

That it does not appear, any of the said Persons were chosen or elected out of Turn.

That Hajkins's Evidence, upon the last controverted Election for Caine, was, that he had known Caine Forty Years, and Four or Five Elections; and that the Returns were always made by the senior Steward.

That Two Polls were taken at this Election; one by Direction of S eager, and the other by Direction of Simpkins and Brook.

Upon Seager's Poll the Numbers were thus:

44 for Mr. Hedges:

18 for Mr. Bayntun:

17 for Mr. Duckett:

Upon Simpkins and Brook's Poll they were thus:

17 for Mr. Duckett:

18 for Mr. Bayntun:

13 for Mr. Hedges:

2 for Mr. Johnston:

That the Counsel for Mr. Johnston and Mr. Hedges infilled, that the Borough is an ancient Demesne of the Crown: That the Inhabitants of the Demesne Houses had Right of Common, and owe Suit and Service at

burn-, and that the Right of Ekdtion is in those Inhabitants, Commoners, who are sworn at Ogburn Court.

That the Counsel for Mr. Bayntun and Mr. Duckett infilled, that the Right of Election is in those Inhabitants, who are first clewed Burgesses, presented by Caine Stewards, and afterwards sworn at Ogburn Court.

And it was admitted by the Counsel on both Sides, that, if the Right of Election was in the Commoners, sworn at Ogburn Court, without a previous Election at Cain by the Burgesses, Mr. Johnston and Mr. Hedges were duly elected; and, if the Right was only in those, who were first elected Burgesses at , and presented by the Stewards, and sworn at Ogbur, Mr. Bayntun and Mr. Duckett were duly elected.

That the Voters on both Sides in this Election were sworn at Ogburn.

That the Counsel for Mr. Johnston and Mr. Hedges produced a Copy out of Doomfdav Book, where it is entered, that this Borough was Terra Regis-, and that there were Fi ve-and-Forty Burgenfes, and Five-and-twenty genjes.

r And they examined Witnesses; viz.

Sir George Hungerford-,who said, he had known the Borough Sixty Years; and always took the Right to be in the Inhabitants, having Demesne, and being sworn at Ogburn: That they are usually nominated by the Bur--gestes in Cain Hall, and are presented by Stewards to the Steward of Ogburn Court, to be sworn: That in 1685 Four were so nominated, and presented by the Stew- aids, and sworn: That Mr. Bayntun and Mr. Blaake then brought Twenty more to Ogburne, who were not elected in Caine Hall, or presented by the Stewards of Caine: That Ogburn Steward fworc them, and said, when -sworn there, they had good Votes; and they have ever since been taken as such: That he has served for the Borough Three times, and in 1685 he submitted to the Votes of those Twenty against him; and that he apprehends, every Inhabitant, having Right of Common, has

a Right to be sworn at Ogburn, and, when sworn, they are called Burgesses; and that the Presentment of them

byCaine Steward is only to justify their being Inhabitants, having Right of Common.

John Landrick said, he has been a Burgess 28 Years: That Caine Steward sent to him to go to Ogburn, to be sworn; and if he did not, he told him, he should lose his Right of Common: That there is about Six or Seven Score Common Houses, that have Right of Common in the said Borough; and that those, that were sworn in 1685, have always been taken to be good Votes.

John Norman and John Ladd said, they were Two of the Twenty carried by Mr. Bayntun and Mr. Blaake to Ogburn, and there sworn in 1685: That they were not objected to by Ogburne Steward, nor were they elected Burgesses, nor did they go with the Stewards; and that they have voted ever since, and never been objected to.

That the Counsel for Mr. Bayntun and Mr. Ducket produced the Town Book of Caine, and the Minutes of several Courts Leet at Ogburn, wherein are Entries of le-veral Persons Names, there said to be elected, and sworn Burgesses.

And they examined Witnesses; viz.

Henry Stevenson, Esquire, the Steward of Ogburn

Court; who produced a Copy of the Oath, taken at bttrn 101705; where the Word "Burgesses" (which Word is in the Burgesses Oath) is left out.

Francis Richens said, that IVm. Jeffery and Anthony Pearje were elected Burgesses about 40 or 50 Years ago; and the usual manner is, for the Stewards and Burgesses in Caine Hall first to elect Burgesses, and then fend them to Ogburn, to be sworn: That he never knew it otherwise; and that the Hayward (by Order of the Stewards) summons the Burgesses to meet, to elect Burgesses.

That there are about Forty or 60 Commoners, and near 3 or 400 Houses in Caine; and that he never knew the Burgesses exceed Thirty: That Mr. Blaake's 20, who were sworn in 1685, were first chose at the White Bear at Caine.

Walter Dcleman said, he had known Caine 30 Years; and that he never knew of any Election, but in the Hall: That the Burgesses are summoned to elect: That in 1705 some were refused to be sworn at Ogburn, because they were not returned by Caine Stewards: That different Oaths were then taken; some were sworn only as Commoners, others as Burgesses; and none were sworn Burgesses, unless presented by the Stewards of Caine.

John Minfon said, he was elected, and sworn at Ogburn; the Word " Burgess" was not in the Oath: That he has voted for Members of Parliament twice; and was both times objected to by all the Burgesses.

Henry Blaake, Esquire, said, that he had been acquainted with Caine above 35 Years; has served in Parliament Three Times for the Borough; and that in all his time the way to make Burgesses has been, to meet in Caine Hall, and there to chuse, and to give Notice to thore, who are chosen; and at the next Court they go to Ogburn, to be sworn: That he never heard (till the late Dispute) any pretend to be Burgesses, that were not elected: That, notwithstanding the Two new Charters in 1685, the Ogburn courters elected Members to Parliament, for those Charters were never accepted.

That he, and Sir Geo. Hungerford, went to John Ladd, and several others, and prevailed on them to act, though they were threatened, there being a new Corporation: That in 1685 all the Four-and-twenty went, and were sworn at Ogburn: That they were all elected by Majority of Burgesses: That Sir Geo. Hungerford went with them, was consenting to their being sworn, and would have prevailed on John Ladd to go to Ogburn, to be iworn; and that Part of the Certificate, produced to the Committee, of those Four-and-twenty being sworn at Ogburn, dated the 9th of May, 1685, is of Sir George Hungerford's Hand-writing.

Sir Geo. Hungerford, being called, and confronting Mr. Blaake, said, that only Four of those 24 were nominated by the Burgesses in the Hall: And, being shewed the aforesaid Certificate, he denied, any Part of it to be his Hand.

Mine Adventure of England, on the behalf of them- Adventure lelves, and several Widows, and Orphans, Creditors and ComP®n7* Members of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that on the 13th of February, 1709, the Petitioners presented their Petition to this House, setting forth, that they were Creditors of the said Company for a great Sum of Money, which they had been artfully drawn in to advance; and that, without the Assistance of the legislative Power, they could not recover their just Debts; and thereby charged the then Deputy Governor, Sir Humphry Mackworth, and the Directors, with very indirect Practices; the Consideration of which Petition was referred to a Committee; who, upon Examination, came to several Resolutions, and made their Report to the House, now extant upon their Journal; and the Petitioners had Leave to bring in a Bill for their Relief, but had not Time to pass it, by reason of the Conclusion of the then Session of Parliament; and still labour under the same unfortunate Circumstances, and cannot expect any just Relief, without the Assistance of Parliament: They therefore pray, that they may, in their Circumstances and Difficulties, be relieved by the Assistance of the legislative Power, in such manner, as shall be thought meet.

Upon the Petition of J Walter, Esquire, and William Forbes, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of the Lord Wm. Powlett, and Paul Burrard, Esquire, for the Borough of Lymington, in the County of Southampton:

That the Question was whether the Right of Election is in the flavor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, or in the Mayor and Burgesses, of Lymington:

If in the latter, it was admitted, the fitting Members were duly elected.

That the Poll of the Burgesses, taken in the Town-hall, was thus:

For the Petitioners, each - 7

That the Populace polled themselves out of the Hall, and 87 voted for the Petitioners only.

And the following Resolution, in the same of Boston, in Lincclnshire, was insisted on for the Petitioners;

8® Matt, 40 Car.I. " Agreed by the Committee, that " the Election of Burgesses, in all Boroughs, did, of " common Right, belong to the Commoners; and that nothing could take it from them, but a Prescription, " and constant Usage beyond all Memory."

And John Edwards said, he has been a Burgess Fifteen Years, and has known the Borough above 35 Years: That about the time of the Convention he was a Scotland Lot Man; and then several of the Burgesses sent to him, and told him, he had a Right to vote for Members of Parliament; and asked him, why he did not try that Right: That at Two Elections the Votes of the Populace have been asked; viz, by Mr. JervoiJe and Mr. Cromwell, and by Mr. Pitt and Mr. Clark, the then Candidates, who flood by the Populace; and in both those Elections Mr. John Burrard flood a Candidate by the Mayor, and Burgesses: That those Elections were contested; the Votes of the Populace were then lejedted by 11

this House, and the Persons, chose by the leledt Number, fat in Parliament; and since that the Populace have not voted.

Sir Robert Smith said, when he was Mayor of Lymington (above 20 Years ago) he refused to make honorary Burgesses, and his Deputy, David Edwards (who was above Fourscore Years old) commended him for it j for he said, it never had been well with the Town, since the Inhabitants had lost their Right of voting: That Edwards meant, it would never be well with the Town, till that" Right was restored; but did not say, he eyer knew, they had such Right: That the Inhabitants thought, they had Right of voting; and that they were injured by the honorary Burgesses, who took it from them.

Charles Hackman said, there are about 70 Burgesses, of which 15 or 16 are Inhabitants; and there are near 100 other Housekeepers, Inhabitants, who are not Burgesses, but are generally in as good Condition, as the Burgesses; and all pay to Church and Poor, except about Four of them: That at the last Election the Constables refused the Petitioners Admittance into the Town-hall; and ’tis usual to fluit out all Candidates, and others, who are not Burgesses.

Petition*, now in Prison in her Majesty’s Gaol within the City and County of Bristol, was predated to the House, and read; letting forth, that they have been long confined for Debt, and are in a miserable Condition, and Tome of them almost starved, having no other Subsistence, but the Charity of well-disposed Persons: And praying, that an Act may pass, for the Petitioners Discharge from their Confinement.

A Petition of a great Number of both Sexes, poor Prisoners, and insolvent Debtors, in the Prison of Freemen, and Free-women, of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more in this Kingdom of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioners are reduced to a miserable Necessity, by great Lolfes, unforeleen Accidents, and Decay of Trade, and mult inevitably perish, unless relieved by the Goodoeli of the House: And praying such Relief, as the House shall think proper, in their deplorable Condition.

A Petition, and Cafe, of the numerous distressed, and pe,.rt"* long confined, Prisoners for Debt in the Qiecn’s Bench uc*’ Prison, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners(with others)have made repeated Applications to this House for their Liberty: That in the last Session of Parliament a Bill passed this House, for the Relief of all insolvent Debtos, but it did not pass the House of Lords: And praying, that a Bill may now pals into a Law, for the like Purposes, the able Petitioners being willing to go into her Majesty’s Service.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to oblige the Creditors of poor insolvent Debtors to accept the utmost Satisfaction they are capable to make, and to restore them to their Liberty, shall be read a Second time.

A Petition of several Hundreds’of Gentlemen, Merchants, and such, as have been considerable Traders, with a far greater Number of Handicraft Tradesmen, &c.

Prisoners in the Queen's Bench Prison, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that Multitudes of Persons lie languishing in the several Prisons of this Kingdom, under greater Miseries, than can be comprehended, but by those that feel them: That the Weight of these Miseries falls on such only, as would pay their Debts, were they able, and are ready to come to any Composition for their Liberty; who are now shut up, as it were, in their Graves by the mcreiless Cruelty of their Creditors, who otherwise might yearly diminish their Debts, and be advantageously employed against the common Enemy: That there is Room to suppose, her Majesty, in her Speech at opening of this Session, had the poor Prisoners in View, when ihe expresses herself l'enfibly touched with what her People futfered by so long and expensive a War: That, might the Petitioners be permitted, they would enlarge upon the Difference between Persons, who have lived in Plenty, and dealt for Thoul'ands, and such, whose Dealings and Debts, are under an Hundred Pounds to one Man: And praying, that some Remedy may be applied for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, and that the Petitioners may have a Share of the Companion of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to oblige the Creditors of poor insolvent Debtors to accept the utmost Satisfaction they are capable to make, and to restore to them their Liberty, shall be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of St. Olav in Southwark, in the County of Surry, together with the principal Inhabitants of the adjacent Parishes, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that about 18 Months ago above 500 Palatines were brought into the said Parish, and continued together in one Place" several Months, dangerous Distem-pers being amongst them: That in October last: about 200 of them are come again (supposed from Ireland) into the said Parish, inhabiting in one House: That the Petitioners are extremely fearful, some contagious Distempers may happen thereby; and that they, having not wherewithal to subsist, are likely to become chargeable, to the utter Ruin of the said Parish: And praying such Relief, as shall be thought fit, for the said Parish.

Ordered, That the Lid Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the

A Petition of the several Maltsters of die Town of dover, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners receive daily great Abuses from the Gaugers, in tumbling their Corn, and treading it, in meaforing with theBufhel in the Couch after wetting, so that, by bruising, it never Can come to work into Malt; and that, notwithstanding the last Clause in the late Act of Parliament, to prevent fraudulent wetting of Corn, yet those, that live at Dif- . tance from a Town, may run Wettings, if so minded*

That, to prevent these Abuses, the Petitioners all agree to wet Corn but twice a Week, and to give in their Entries what Days they will wet, and be obliged to let it lie iivthe Ciftem, under Water, 48 Hours, and 24. Hours.after the Water runs from it, desired, it m-y be deemed Couch, for the Gauger to take his Gauge at any time within the said Hours, for that there is no true Gauge, as they now gauge it* in the Couch; which Course, if taken, will not only bring the full Duty to her Majesty, but Two-thirds of the Excise Officers will be sufficient to culleft it: And praying, that the House will take the Premises into Confederation, and relieve the Petitioners therein.

A Petition of the poor Debtors in the Gaol at IVin-chester, for the County of Swas presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they have been so long languishing in Prison, that they are wiHing to yield up all they have to their Creditors, to obtain their Liberty, in order to get a future Livelihood for their ne-cefiitous Families: And praying the House to take the miserable same of poor Prisoners in general into Consideration, and that feme Relief may be found out for them.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Prison of Newgate, London, was presented to the House, and read.; setting forth, that by many Misfortunes the Petitioners are reduced to the utmost Want and Poverty, and are like to continue intombed alive, through the merciless Rigour of their Creditors, to whom they have offered (and are Hill willing; their All, for their Liberty, that they might thereby get a Livelihood; but they refuse to accept the fame; so that the Petitioners have no Hopes of being released from their Bondage, but by the charitable Companion of the House: And praying the House to consider of some Methods for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to oblige the Creditors of poor insolvent Debtors to accept the utmost Satisfaction they are capable to make, and to rellorc to them their Liberty, shall be read a Second time.

Upon the Petition of William Esquire, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Sir Thomas Webfier, Baronet, for the Borough of Col-chef er, in the County of Essex:

That the Poll was thus:

693 for the fitting Member:

685 for the Petitioner.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and Burgesses.

That the Question was, whether the Mayor, of his own Authority, without Consent of the Common Council, can make Foreigners free.

Against such Authority, in the Mayor, (everaiEntries in the Town Books were producedviz.

In 1654 an Order, that no Foreigner should be made free, without Consent of the Majority of the Common . Council. x

And several instances were produced of Persons, admitted by the Mayor and Common Council in the Years

*656> 57* 58> and 93-In 1694 a Disfranchisement, in the Town Book, of Alderman Mott, for Misdemeanors.

And William Boyfe, and Sam. Hayward', said, one of those Misdemeanors was, for making a Person free in the Year of his Mayoralty (which was the precedent Year) without Consent of the Common Council.

In July, 1697, an Order in the Town Book, that no Foreigner should be admitted, without Consent of the Majority of the tree Burgesses, assembled in the Common Hall.

John Potter, Esquire, said that John Raynham, when he was Mayor in i7o-|-, Two Days before the Election to Parliament, without Consent of the Common Council made 100 Foreigners free, and swore them in the Nighttime, in Alehouses, and Taverns, without the Town Clerk, who ought to swear them publickly in the Town Hall. That the Counsel for the fitting Member called Oliver Birkin, Tho. Grigson, and Tho. who said, that

all the Mayors since 1697, but ^ne or Two, have of themselves admitted Foreigners; and that there are some instances of Admittances of the same Nature before that Time, but they are very few.

And that the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Mayor of the Borough of in the County of Essex, cannot make Foreigners free of the said Borough, without Consent of the Majority of the Aldermen, and Common Council.

And upon this the fitting Member’s Council admitted, the Petitioner had a Majority.

And the Committee came to the following Resolutions: Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Thomas Webber, Baronet, is not duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Colehejier, in the County of Essex.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That William Gore, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Colehejier.

Sir William Windham reported from the Committee,

to whom the Petiti n of the Wire-drawers, Card-makers, and Clothiers, ot Fuout, and Parts adjacent of in behalf ut themselves, and others of the same Trades, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Kef lution of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where it was twice read, and the Report and Retolutioa are as follow; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the Matters contained in the said Petition,

It appeared to them, that the using of good Wool Cards, in the making ol Cloth, is of great Concernment to the Trade of this Kingdom in the Woollen Manufacture, the Iron Wire of old Cards being too weak, and inlulficient, for the well carding of Wool.

Ti'.at by an Act, made in the 13th and 14th Years of the Reign of the late King Charles the id (intituled, An Act against importing of foreign Wool Cards, Card W ire, or Iron Wire) it is enacted, that no foreign Wool Cards, or foreign Card Wire, or Iron Wire, for making of Wool Cards, be imported into this Kingdom* nor any Card Wire, taken out of old Cards, be put into new Leather, and new Card Boards, nor any such Wool Cards, made thereof, be put to Sale, under the Penalty of the Forfeiture thereof, or the Value.

It appeared also to the Committee, that, notwithstand-ir.g the said Act, it is now become a common Practice to put old Iron Wire into new Leather, and on new Boards, and expose the same to Sale; by which Means great Part of the Woollen Cloth of the Kingdom is ill made, and the feverr.l Traders, in the Petition mentioned, very much damnified in their Trades; the Consumption of Iron Wire is very much lessened; and many Persons abul'ed, and defrauded j and great Numbers of poor Persons, and Families, employed in the Woollen Manu-iafture, are become great Charges to their respective Parishes.

Whereupon the Committee came to this Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more effectual preventing the Importation of foreign white Wire, and felling of old Wool Cards, and supplying the Defects of an Act, made in the 13th and 14th Years of the Reign of the late King Charles the ad, intituled, An Act against importing of foreign Wool Cards, Card Wire, or Iron Wire.

Ordered, That Lcsve be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual preventing the Importation of foreign Vo 1.. l(j.

white Wire, and the felling of old Cards, and supplying the Defects of the Act, made in the 13 and 14 Years of the Reign of the late King Charles the 2d, intituled, An Act against importing of foreign Wool Cards, Card Wire, or Iron Wire; and that Sir Wm. Windham, Sir The. Wroth, and Mr. Phelips, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Counsel called

Bucknall, who said, they had known the Borough 30, 40, and 50, Years: That at an Election, 40 Years ago, the Potwallers were refused, and none but Scotland Lot Men voted then: That at all Elections since the Potwallers have claimed a Right to vote; and at an Election in 1679, upon a Report being spread, that they would be refused, they pulled down the Place, built tp take the Poll in, and the Balcony of the House, the Poll was adjourned to:

That, since that Tjtjie, they have been admitted to poll, for Peace-fake, but the Returns were made by the Scotland Lot Men: That they have been told by several ancient Men of the Borough, who are now dead, that the Right ol Election was in the Scotland Lot Men only, and they take it to be so: That there are Three or Four Potwallers in an House.

John Walter and Tho. Hughes laid, they have heard Sir Walter Yonge say, he thought, the Right of Election was in the Scotland Lot Men; and that, in case of Opposition, he should think himself safe, if he had the Majority of them: That at this Election the Votes of the Potwallers were solicited on both Sides; and they polled on both Sides, without Objection; but Mr. Sheppard objected to them, upon the Scrutiny: That in all Elections, since 1660, all, that did not receive Alms, have been polled; and the Majority of the Scotland Lot Men, and Potwallers, have been of the same Side, as for as any Polls can be found,

Upon the Petition of Sir fames Wijhart, Knight, and Sir Wm. Gifford, Knight, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Sir Charles Wager, Knight, and Sir John Knight, to serve

for the Borough of Portsmouth, in the County of Southampton:

That the Poll was thus:

66 for Sir Charles Wager:

64 for Sir John Jennings:

51 for-each Petitioner.

That it was agreed, the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses.

That the Question was, whether Joseph Esquire, who was elected Mayor of the Borough upon the 10th Day of December, 1709, was a legal Mayor; and whether the Aldermen, and Burgesses, elected during his Mayoralty, are good and legal Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the said Borough.

That it was admitted, that all Elections of Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough, must be made by the Mayor. Aldermen, and Burgesses, for the Time being, or the major Part of them.

That it appeared to the Committee, that Mr. -horn xsz Presbyterian, and goes to their Meeting-houses; and that he had not, within One Year next before his Election into the said Office of Mayor, taken the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper according to the Rites of the Church of England-, and that several of the Aldermen protested against hisadingas Mayor; and several Aldermen, and Burgesses, were elected, during the Time he acted in the Mayoralty.

That, on the fitting Members behahy the Resolution of this House, 18° Car. "ldi, in the same of Mr. Austin, who was elected for the Port of Winchelsea, was infilled on: In that same it appears by the Journal, Mr. Austin was returned by a Mayor, who had not, within a Year before his Election, taken the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper according to the Rites of the Church of;

and the House resolved, That Mr. A 11ftin was duly elected, and ought to fit.

That, upon Perusal of the Clause in the Act of Parliament, for the well governing and regulating of Corporations, which enjoins the taking of the Sacrament, the Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Joseph Whitehorne, Esquire, who was elected Mayor of the Borough of Portsmouth on the Tenth Day of December, 1709, and had not duly qualified himself for that Office, according to Law, by taking the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper according to the Rites of the Church of England, within One Year next before his Election, was not legal Mayor of the said Borough.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Aldermen, elected during the said pretended Mayoralty of the said Mr. Whitehorne, are not legal Aldermen, and the Burgesses, elected during his pretended Mayoralty, have not a Right to vote in Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Portsmouth.

After which the Counsel for the fitting Members admitted a Majority for the Petitioners, without those Burgesses.

And thereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Charles Wager, Knight, is not duly elected 3 Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Portsmouth, in the County of Southampton.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir John Jennings, Knight, is not duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Portsmouth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir James Wijhart, Knight, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Portsmouth,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Wm.Gifford, Knight, is duly elected a Burgess,

to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Portsmouth.

Mr. Foley also reported from the said Committee, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon the Petition of Adam Brown, Edward Ward, and John on be-

half of themselves, and others, the poor Creditors of the old Debt of the Office of Ordnance, which the Committee had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee heard several of the Petitioners, and I'ome of the Officers of the Ordnance, thereupon.

The Petitioners alleged, that the Sum 97,722. 19J.

%id. mentioned in the Petition, is due to them; and that they have Debentures for the greatest Part of it:

That, for want of Payment, they, and their Families, have suffered much.

That the Officers of Ordnance acquainted the Committee, that none of the present Officers w'ere in the Office, when this Debt is said to be contracted: They own, that they found in the Office an old Book, wherein this Debt is mentioned; which begins in 1673, and ends in 1679.

That in 1682 this Debt was laid before King Charles the 2d, in Council, and referred to the then Commissioners of the Treasury; but that no Provision was ever made for satisfying the fame, or any Part of it paid, either in that Reign, or since.

That, upon a Reference from her present Majesty, the Board of Ordnance did, the 2ft Ja, 170^, make the following Report:

May it pleafo your Majesty,

IN Obedience to your Majesty’s Commands, signified by Mr. Secretary. Harley'% Letter, of the aiftof December last, we have examined into the Allegations of the annexed Petition of Adam Brown, and others; and find by the Books in this Office, that there was-a Debt contracted in King Charles the- ad’s Time, for Stores delivered, and Services performed, to the last of 1679,

amounting to ,£.97,722. 19J. 8 We believe the Debt to be very just, and that a great many Families have suffered, for wane of its being paid; but, though several Applications (as we are informed) have been made in King Charles's Time, and in the succeeding Reigns, yet no

Consideration has hitherto been had of it; and how realisable it may be, when this Office lies under a Debt of near £. 200,000 contracted in this present War, we humbly l’ubmit to your Majesty s better Judgment.,

That the Committee cannot find, that any Notice hath been taken by the Parliament of this Debt.

A Petition of John Henry Scheidman, Michael Remy, Arrears of Henry Miller, arid William Miller, in behalf of themselves. Regiment*, and several Commission 'and Non-commission Officers, with hundreds of private Troopers, Dragoons, and Soldiers, of the Thirteen Dutch Regiments, that served in the late War, upon the English Establishment, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the , Petitioners are now settled here, and have spent much Time and Money, in their Applications to the House of Commons, to recover the Arrears due to them: That Mr. Vander Efch refusing to settle his Accounts, and the superior Officers absenting themselves beyond the Seas, have occasioned those Arrears: That Mr. John Hallun-gius, in his printed Papers, delivered the last Session of Parliament, endeavoured (as still he doth) to deprive the Petitioners of their just Arrears, by getting the same into his Hands, by villifying the Petitioners, untruly suggesting, that most of the Money, allotted for the Petitioners, was due to the Officers for Money, by them borrowed at high Interest; which when the Petitioners had falsified, they were promised to be paid out of the Money received, but by whom, or in what manner, does not appear; and now at last, to wipe them of all Relief, claims the

whole in behalf of the States General, by alleging those 1

Troops to be Auxiliaries; but does not make it appear, how, or to whom, they were Auxiliaries, they being under the English Establishment, subject to the late Kin?

William, to whom, they took the Oaths of Fidelity, ana were no ways subject to be recalled by the States: And praying, that the said HaHungius may receive no Money, until the whole Acedunts, relating to the said Dutch Regiments, be dated, which the Petitioners are ready to state and settle, not doubting to prove, that all his Pre* tendons are unjust, and groundless.

That the Committee find, there have been Deductions made from the Garison, at Newfoundland, to the Year 1709; but, upon the the Examination of Mr. Sloper, some of the Officers belonging to the English Regiments in Gibraltar, and of several Agents, cannot find, that any

Deductions have yet been made from any of the Forces sent to or Portugal, for Provisions supplied them by the Commissioners for Victualing; but, in cate it shall be thought reasonable to make any Deductions from the Regiments, sent to Spain and Portugal, for those Provisions, or that the Dutch repay what has been furniflaed their Troops, or that an Allowance be made for what hath been supplied the Spanish Soldiers, and Inhabitants, at Gibraltar, or that any of the Money, given by Parliament for the Extraordinaries of the War in Spain and Portugal, be applied to this Service, whatever those Sums shall be, will lessen the Debt on this Head; and when the Deductions are made from the Garison at Newfoundland, for the Two last Years, those will a!so so much lessen this Debt.

Mr. Sloper also acquainted the Committee, that, over and above the Provisions, the Garison of Gibraltar have had from ibe Commissioners of Victualing, above £.30,000 hath been paid for soft Bread, and other Extraordinaries, for that Garison; and that there is a Demand of £. 50,000 more on that Account.

Drake, and Mr. Kent, West India Merchants; who acquainted them, that they never knew the Exchange at Jadtaich, sita'ce i 701, to be under £. to per Cent. That they generally received there 130, and sometimes£. 135 for £. 100 to be paid at 30 Days Sight here.

The Committee find, that from February, 1704, the Commissioners of Victualing employed other Merchants, and from that time have had £.18 Cent, allowed from Jamaica, till lately; and that now they have £. 20 allowed; and that the Debt of the Office was much greater, when they hud £. 18 and £.20 per Cent, allowed, than when they had but£. 8 per Cent.

Mr. Conyers (according to Order) reported from the Ways Committtee of the whole House, who were to consider ^eans* farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table j where they were read, and arc as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, her Majesty’s Revenues, both inland and foreign, to arise in the general Letter Office, or Pod Office, or the Office of Postmaster General, be increased.

RcfAved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Increase be made, by adding One Peny to the present Rate of Two-pence for every single Letter, carried within Eighty English Miles Distance from London, and by adding proportionable Rates for double and treble Letters and Packets, carried the same Distance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Increase be also made, by adding One Peny, to the present Rate of Threc-pence for every single Letter carried in England above Eighty such Miles from London, or to the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and by adding proportionable Rates for double and treble Litters and Packets, so carried.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Increase be likewise made, by adding One Peny to the present Rates of Three Pence, and Two Pence, payable for Letters passing between London and Edenburgh, or between London and or Cock-

burn-speth, and by adding proportionable Rates for double and treble Letters and Packets, so carried.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Increase be made, by establishing a Rate of 4 d.(\nlieu of the present Rates) for every single Letter, carried any Length in Scotland, being above 80 Miles Distance from Edinburgh, and by settling proportionable Rates for double and treble Letters and Packets, so carried; and that the present Rates for carrying Letters in Scotland to and from Edinburgh, within 80 Miles Distance thereof, be continued, as they are now.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Rates for carrying of Letters and Packets, in respect to Ireland, be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Revenue be increased, by settling a Rate of One Peny for every Letter, or Packet, directed on board, or brought from, any Ship or Vessel, riding, or Hopping, in any of her Majesty’s Harbours, or Ports.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Letters and Packets passing or repassing by the Carriage jfually called the Peny Post, within Eight

English

Ways and Means.

496 14 Februurii.& 17 tx>.

Ifaae Howard, a Waterman; who said, that he was employed by Mr. Cheney 2nd Mr. Two Surveyors

of the Excise, some Days in lad, to observe,

whether any Beer from the Hartjkorne Brewhouse was put on board Colliers, or Merchant Ships, or landed fraudulently in other Places:

That, during the Time he was thus employed, he saw 153 Barrels carried in several Parcels from the Hartjhorn Brewhouse to Colliers, Merchant Ships, and other Places, some of which were carried by , a Waterman bc-Jonging to the Victualing Office, the rest by other Watermen.

Samuel Hill, a Waterman, said, he was employed in the same manner, as Mr. Howard; and saw 42 Barrels carried at several Times from the Queen’s Brewhouse to Merchant Ships, and Colliers.

It was pretended, that the Beer, thus disposed of, was only prtly Warrant Beer; but upon comparing the Information with the Acount of the Issues from the horn Brewhouse, it appeared to the Committee to be Sea Beer, anti not petty Warrant Beer.

Mr. John Smith, Brewer, said, that he has often had Beer from the Queen’s Brewhouse, by the means of one Moxley, a Servant there, at the Rate of a Ton.

That he always agreed for the best Calks, and has had the Liberty to chuse them himself, as they have lain upon the Key:

That heneverpaid for bringing any Beer from the Brewhouse; and knows, a great many Colliers were supplied with Beer from thence; and they have told him, they could have it much cheaper there, than of other Brewers.

He farther said, that heufed to return old Calks, good for little, which he bought for for. per Ton, in lieu of the Queen’s Calks:

That he fold the Queen’s Calks, without Beer, for 28 s.and sometimes for 40/. Ton; so that he had in one same a Ton of Beer for which cost the Queen £.3. for. and in the other same he had a Ton of Beer clear, and 8 s. Profit besides.

Mr. Nutt, a Brewer, said, that he has had several Quantities of Beer from the Hartfhorne Brewhouse, for 22 s.per Ton; and that he has fold it again to the Queen, for Store Beer, for 48 j. per Ton, he being a contracting Brewer: That several Tons of Calks have been offered to be sold at the Queen’s Brewhouse; and that telling Mr, Horfmgton(Clerk of the Brrwhouse) that he had bought 14 T ons of Beer of a Purler, he said, that it was a very common thing for Pursers to fell the Queen’s Beer. He said farther, that Mr. Gregory Page was his Partner, and had his proportionable Share, in Profit and Loss, of all Beer, that was bought in, or fold out.

Mr. Curtis, a Brewer, said, that he has lent Merchant Ships Calks to the Heartjhorn Brewhouse, to be filled with the Queen’s Beer, and then sent the same on board his Customer’s Ships; for which Beer he paid 24.1. per Ton, and fold it again for 48a. per Ton.

IVm. Hcrjington, Under Clerk to the Heartjhorn Brewhouse, being asked, when the Accounts of the Brewhouse were made up, said, that they were never made up in his Time; and that he had belonged to that Brewhouse, about Six Years.

He having further informed the Committee, that great Quantities of Beer, brewed at the Heartjhorn Brewhouse, had been Rung into the Thames, being not fit to be drank; and the Committee finding, by the 3d Article of the Instructions to the Commissioners for Victualing, that they were to take care (among other Things) that every Guile of 20 Tons of Iron-bound Beer should be brewed with 20 Quarters of very good Malt, as good, as generally is to be had at the Place, where the said Beer is brewed, and a sufficient Quantity of very good Hops, to keep for the Time of its Warranty, and 18 Quarters of the like Malt, with the like Quantity of the like Sort of Hops, to every Guile of Wood-bound Beer;

The Committee examined into the Quality of the Malt and Hops, that had been used at the Hartjhorn Brewhouse.

Vol, 16.

Wm. Warren, the Mailer Miller, said, that some time ago he acquainted the Commissioners of Victualing, that great Quantities of Malt were delivered by the Contractors, and taken into the Stores, not fit for her Ma-jeRy’s Service; and shewed them Samples of the said Malt: And it appeared to the Committee, from the Minutes, produced by the Commissioners, that nothing more was done upon this Complaint, than only cautioning Mr. James, Mr. Horjington, and Mr. Overing (who are the Surveyors of the Malt, and the Persons complained against) to take care, that the Malt received be in all respects good, and fit for the Service, and answerable to the Sample.

Jones, the Miller’s Mate, laid, there had been great Quantities of Malt used, not fit for her Majesty’s

Service.

Mr. Overing, the Matter Brewer, laid that no Contractor, for Malt, or Hops, could have their Bills of Payment, without Certificates from the Matter Brewer, Clerk of the Cheque, and Clerk of the Brewhouse, of the Quality, as well as Quantity, of such Malt, and Hops: That he had often refused to sign the Certificates, and complained to the Commissioners, that the Malt, and Hops, were neither answerable to the Sample, nor fit for Ufc; but, upon the C intractors applying to the Commissioners, the Commissioners have been willing, such Malt, and Hops, should be made use of; and then he has signed the Certificates:

That he persisted, for Three Months together, in refusing to sign a Certificate for 14 Bags of Hops, delivered lait Summer from one John of; but atlaft

was sent for by the Commissioners, and ordered by them to sign the Certificate in their Presence, notwithstanding he then told them, as he had before, that the Hops were the worst, that he ever law in his Life, and not fit for any Use.

Mr. Colehy (one of the Commissioners) denied, that the Commissioners ordered Overing to sign the Certificate; but owned all the other Parts of the Information to be true, and acknowleged, that he did sign that Certificate in their Presence.

Mr. Reynolds (another Commissioner) owned, that Overing had often made Complaint to the Board, of the Malt and Hops not being good; but thac the Clerks of the Cheque and Brewhouse never had made any Complaint.

Mr. Overing said further, that some Years ago he was a contracting Brewer; and that, by the Commissioners Order, he one Year brewed 300 Tons of Beer in the hot Months of July and August, but refilled to warrant it, because Beer, brewed in those Months, will seldom keep:

A great Part of this Beer (as he feared it would) did prove bad; upon which the Commissioners llopt near £.400 of his Money; which" he thought a very great Injustice, and often represented the Hardship of his same to them, but Hill without Relief: He then petitioned the Lord High Treasurer, who ordered the Commissioners to certify to him a true State of the Petitioner’s Cafe; but when he could not obtain that from them, after Two Years Solicitation, he resolved to petition the House of Commons, and put a Petition into a Member’s Hand, complaining of this hard Usage, and offered to discover several Abuses, committed in the Victualing Office; upon which a Letter was sent to him, signed by every one of the Commissioners (which Letter he produced to the Committee) desiring him to come to them the next Morning; and he accordingly went, and they immediately paid him the Money; and Mr. Croger, the Matter Brewer, being soon after turned out for Misdemeanors, he was put into his Place.

Mr. Colehy owned, Overing was paid the Money, without making any Report to the Lord Treasurer.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That it appears to this House, that in the Management of her Majesty’s Bi*ew-house, as well as in the Contrafts for furnishing the Navy with Beer, there have been many notorious Imbezzle-tnents, and scandalous Abuses, to the defrauding the Publick of great Sums of Money, and to the Injury and Discouragement of the Seamen.

Ordered, That the Commissioners of Victualing have a Copy of the said Report.

After which Mr. Ridge was heard in his Place, to the Matter of the Report, relating to him: And then he Withdrew.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that Thomas Ridge, Esquire, a Member of this House, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, by having contracted tofurnish Five thousand Five hundred and Thirteen Ton of Beer upon his own Account, and Two thousand Seven hundred and Four Ton of Beer in Partnership with Mr. Dixon, and having received Bills for the Whole, although he delivered but Three thousand Two hundred and Thirteen Ton on the first, and but One thousand Two hundred Sixty-nine upon the latter, Contract.

Resolved, That the said Thomas Ridge, Esquire, be, for the said Frauds and Abuses, expelled this House.

Resolved, That an humble Addrefe be presented to her Majesty, that (he will please to give Directions to her Attorney General, to prosecute the said Mr. Ridge for the said Frauds and Abuses.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That the farther Consideration of the said Report be adjourned until Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That Mr. Joseph Nutt do attend this House upon Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That the Commissioners of the Victualing, and their Secretary, do attend this House upon Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That the farther Consideration of the Merits of the Election for the Shire of Dumfreize be adjourned until Saturday Morning next.

Ordered, That the hearing the Merits of the Election for the Borough of Oakbampton be farther adjourned until Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That all Committees be revived.

Thomas Morphy, in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms A Person attending this House, was (according to Order) brought reprimanded to the Bar; where he, upon his Knees, received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker; and was discharged, pay- ar* ing his Fees.

An ingrossed Bill for securing the Freedom of Parlia- Members hients, by the farther qualifying the Members to fit in Qualification, the House of Commons, was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered, as a Ryder, to be added to the Bill, To oblige the Candidates to take an Oath of the Value of their Estates.

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; and the Clause was amended, and the Blanks were filled up.

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Press 1. L. 11. After " England" to insert " Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed?'

Line 31. After "Lands" to insert " Tenements, or Hereditaments."

And the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and the Bill amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass; and that the Title be. An Act for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by the farther qualifying the Members to fit in the House of Commons.

Ordered, That Mr.. Freman do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.
