Henry Humfry, Abr. Mathew, said, that Brotvn receives a Charity of Six Pence a Quarter: That Clap owned, he did not pay Scotland Lot at the Time of the Election, nor for a Year and a half before:

That Thomas Blackaller is only a Boarder;

That John Ravenhill fold his Goods at Mich, and was not an Housekeeper in the Borough at the Time of the Election.

That, to disqualify Mr. Shep Voters aforesaid. Sir Walter Yong's Counsel examined Witnessesr

Samuel Ash, Francis AJb,said, that the Witness, Samuel Ash, has collected the Poor Rate Eight Years to-

gether, was Overseer last Yearj and they never knew Collins pay the Poor Rate:

That Henry Toofe is not in the Rate, and they never knew him pay:

That John Smith, William Richards, Samuel Clap, and Samuel Whitmore, pay Scotland Lot for Estates, which are in the Parish, but out of the Borough.

That Henry Hue, Wm. Viney, Geo. Ash, Edward Saunders, junior, and Bickerftaff Williams, are not in the Rate:

That Joseph Toofe never paid to the Highways:

That Thomas Serle'% Taxes are paid by his Landlord: That Wm. Bovet is not an Inhabitant; That he lives out of the Town, and went about begging at the Time of the Election.

That, to justify the Four Votes, objected to by Mr. Sheppards Counsel,

Samuel Ash said, that the 6 da Quarter, paid to Brown, is not a Charity, but it is paid him as a Door-keeper: That John Clap, John Blackaller, and John Ravenhill, always paid Scotland Lot, and they are in the Rate.

That, to add Six to Sir Walter Yong's Poll, viz. John Skinner, Samuel Stocker, Wm. Newton, Wm. Abbott, John Farr, and Wm. Pippett;

Francis Ash said, those Six tendered their Votes for Sir Walter Yonge-, and are all rated, and pay Scotland Lot;

and Three of them pay for Lands lying in the Parish, out of the Borough.

Against these Six Mr. Sheppards Counsel called Samuel Clap; who said, he never heard, they paid Scotland Lot: That Skinner and Newton's Estates are under 50 Sli. a Year, and so not rateable:

That the Mortgagee of Farr's ... is in Possession: That Peppit lives a Mile out of Town, is rated in the Parish, but not in the Borough.

Henry Humfryssaid, that Three of those Six are put

down in the Rate Book, not to pay: That he took a Copy of the Poor Rate for this Year, and examined it, as it was signed by the JuRices:

That Samuel Stocker Rood then excused, and was marked in the Book, not to pay the Rate; but that Excuse is since struck out, and he Rands charged in the Rate.

Francis Ash laid, that Alteration was made with the Privity of the JuRices, who signed the Rate.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That James Sheppard, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon.

The said Resolution being read a Second time) Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That James Sheppard, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon.

A Petition of Edward Dennefton Was prfcfented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in 1700 the Petitioner was general Surveyor of Excite, and having Reason to suspect, some clandestine Practices were used at the Queen’s Brew house at St. Katharine's (in 14 Months time, by keeping Men upon the River, and a strict Survey on the Brewhouse)did discover notorious Frauds, amounting (by a modest Computation) to the yearly Loss of £. 50,000, which Frauds were fully proved before a Committee of the House of Commons in 1701; for which Services the House voted, that the Petitioner should be rewarded: That, notwithstanding his great Fatigue, and Expence of several hundred Pounds, he has not received any Reward, but cteated to himself a great many Enemies: And praying, that, in Confederation of the Matters aforesaid, the House will order him such Reward, as they shall think fit.

St. Maiy a Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and In' Church0*1 habitants, of St. Mary Le Strand, in the County o* Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that formerly the said Parish had a good Stone Church, with a Church-yard, and other Appurtenances, which in 1549, or thereabouts, were quite demolished by Edward Seymour, then Duke of Somerset, to make way for his building the House now called house, the Materials of the Church being used in building that Palace; by which Means the Inhabitants of that Parish have never since had any Church, or Chapel, for Divine Service, and are not only destitute of a Church, but also of Ground, fit for a Church, and Church-yard: And praying, that their same may be considered, and effectually provided for.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con-

lideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and several other Inhabitants, of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, is referred.

A Petition of several Parishioners, in behalf of them- Deptford selves, and many Thousands, poor Inhabitants, of the Church. Parish of Deptford, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in 1697 the Petitioners were obliged to pull down their Parish Church, it being irreparable, and build a new Church by a voluntary Contribution, as well as a Pound Rate, which very much added to the yearly Charge of the Poor (who are very numerous) which proved a great Burthen to moll of the Inhabitants; and yet the old Steeple was untouched, though it is so weak, that ’tis in danger of falling and thereby may destroy great Part of the Church; yet the Petitioners have done all they are able, to support it: That this Parish, as near as they can judge, conlifts of Eleven or 12,000 Souls, who cannot polfibly be accommodated in one Church, to hear Divine Service; for want of which, they fear, many have wholly neglected all publick Worship on the Lord’s Day, and others, who would gladly join with the established Church, re-lort to the Assemblies of Separatists, Three whereof are constantly held in the said Parish: That the Inhabitants are unable to make a better Provision, the much greater Part of them being subsisted by the Sea Service, and the Town of late Years has been sensibly impoverished by great Numbers of their destitute Widows, and Orphans, and by the Calamities of an expensive War: And praying, that they may be allowed £. 6,000, or what the House shall think fit, for rebuilding their old Steeple, and building another convenient Church.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and several other Inhabitants, of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, is referred.

APetition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and others, st. Botolph the Inhabitants of St. Botolph without London, without

was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that Alder^ate in the late dreadful Fire of London, in 1666, the said C urc ' Parish Church took Fire, but by the Industry of the Inhabitants was saved, though very much damnified thereby; and by the Negligence of the then principal Inhabitants, who before had lived in the principal Streets of the City, and intended to return thither again, so soon as Houses could be built for them, the said Church was not inserted in the Act for rebuilding the City of London, and the Churches, burnt and damnified by the said Fire: That, the said Church is now become so weak, and ruinous, that, though the Parishioners have been at great Charges to prop up the Walls, the Inhabitants are in Danger it will fall on their Heads, when they go to Church, and there is a Necessity of rebuilding the same; which they are unable to do, without some publick Assistance: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

The House resumed the farther Consideration of the Report from the Committee, appointed to enquire into the Abuses of the Victualing.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. # Dixon, Brewer at Portsmouth, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contiacted to furnish 2,704 Tuns of Beer for the last Year’s Service, in Partnership with Mr. Ridge, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when he had delivered but 1,269 Tuns.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. Player, another Brewer at Portis guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contracted to furnish 7,724 Tuns of Beer for the last Year’s Service, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when he had delivered but 4,164 Tuns.

Resolved', That it appears to this House, That Mr. Bolfe, a Brewer at Harwich, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contracted to furnish 2,782 Tuns of Beer for the last Year’s Service, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when He had delivered but 1,102 Tuns.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. Best, a Brewer at Chatham, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contracted to furnish 455 Tuns of Beer for the last Year’s Service, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when he had delivered but 331 Tuns.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. Tyhurst, a Brewer of Rochester, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contracted to furnish 883 Tuns of Beer for the last Year’s Service, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when he had delivered but 126 Tuns.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. Kelly, a Brewer of Deal, is guilty of great Frauds and Abuses, in having contracted to furnish 1,424 Tuns of Beer, for the last Year’s Service, and receiving Bills for the Whole, when he had delivered but 202 Tuns.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, that Ihe will please to give Directions to her Attorney General, to prosecute the said Mr. Dixon, Mr. Player, Mr. Rolf, Mr. Best, Mr. Thurst, and Mr. Kelly, for the said Frauds and Abuses.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Captaia Whitehall, Agent Victualer at Dover, is guilty of a great Misdemeanor, in dispensing with Mr. Kelly's {wearing to the Affidavits for Delivery of Beer, and in being privy to the Frauds and Abuses, committed by the said Mr. Kelly.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr. Wilkins, Agent Victualler at Portsmouth, is guilty of a great Misdemeanor, in certifying the Delivery of much greater Quantities of Beer, than were delivered.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Stephen Moxley, Servant at the Hartjhornt Brewhouse, is guilty ot a great Crime, in being privy to the embezzling great Quantities of Beer, and Calks.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Mr< Horfington, Under Clerk at the Hartfhorne Brewhouse, is guilty of a great Misdemeanor, in giving Mr. a Certificate, to defraud the Queen of 25 Tuns of Beer.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Noah Overing, Mailer Brewer, Bernard Goddard, deceased, late Clerk of the Brewhouse, and Thomas James, Clerk of the Check at the Hartfhorne Brewhouse, have been guilty of very great Misdemeanors, in Agoing Certificates for great Quantities of Malt, and Hops, which were neither answerable to the Sample, nor fit for Use.

As to the Contract Brewers, at London, giving the Purlers Money instead of Beer, and disposing of the Calk:

That the said Commissioners are wholly ignorant of an such Practice, as that of giving the Pursers Money instead of Beer, their Injunctions to their Officers being, to deliver all in Kind; which they had reason to think had been always complied with, having received no Intimation, or Complaint, to the contrary, at any time, from any of the Commanders of her Majesty’s Ships, who, by their Handing Instructions, are to take care to fee, that all the Provisions, ordered for their Ships, are brought on board in Kind: And as to the Brewers difi poling ofhei Majesty’s Calk, the following Rules will shew the Care, that hath been taken, to prevent that likewise:

Then the House proceeded to the hearing of the Merits of the Election for the Shire of

And the Counsel were called in.

And the Petition, complaining of the said Election, was read.

And the Petitioner’s Counsel infilling, that the fitting Member had not a Right to vote at the Election of a Commissioner for the said Shire; and the Sitting Member’s Counsel infilling, that they ought not now to be permitted to make the said Objection, the Petitioner (who was the Prafes) having signed the Freeholders Roll; Touching which Matter the Counsel were heard, and then they withdrew.

Resolved, That the Petitioner, having signed the Freeholders Roll, in which the fitting Member was inserted with a Protestation, was at Liberty at any time to renew his Objection against the fitting Member’s Vote, before the Election was proceeded on.

And the Counsel were called in, and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the Resolution.

And then they proceeded, and were heard, whether the fitting Member had a Right to give his Vote at the said Election.

And then they withdrew.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the fitting Member was duly qualified to give his Vote for a Commissioner for the Shire of Wigtown j It passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel were called in again, and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And then the fitting Member’s Counsel infilled against the Qualification of the Petitioner, for that neither the Petitioner, nor any of the Electors, did, before the Election, take the Oaths, and Assurance, required by Law.

The Certificate of the Clerk of the Meeting thereof was also read: And then the Counsel were heard:

And being withdrawn;

And the Question being put. That Patrick Fans,

Esquire, is duly elected a Commissioner, to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Wigtown;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of several of the Owners, and Occupiers, of the Meadows, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, lying between Reading and Nin the County of Berks, and adjoining to the River Kennett in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the making the River Kennett navigable from Reading to Newberry, in the County of Berks, as intended by a Bill for that Purpose, now depending in this honourable House, will be rather detrimental, than advantageous, to the Publick, and in no fort commodious, or profitable, for the Inhabitants, or Proprietors of Lands, in the said County, but, on the contrary, likewise prejudicial to them, as the Petitioners humbly hope to make evident: And praying, that they may have Leave to lay their Reasons before this honourable House, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, before the same do pals.

A Petition of divers Merchants of London, Traders to Africa, and thence to the Plantations, in behalf of themselves, and many others, concerned in the said Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that since the laying open the Trade to Africa, in the Year 1698, the Petitioners became large Adventurers in the said Trade, which they have very much increased, improved, and carried on to a much greater Degree, even in the time of War than formerly, when the African Company had that Trade, exclusive of all others, in time of Peace, whereby the Petitioners humbly conceive, they have preserved this Trade, which otherwise must have been loft to the Nation by means of the Royal African Company; and the Petitioners understand, that the said Royal Company have petitioned this honourable House, that their Charter may be confirmed to them by Act of Parliament} and which, if granted, will tend to the Ruin of the Plantations, and the Out-ports of Britain, and be a Detriment to the Balance of Trade abroad, and destructive to our Trade in general: And praying, that they may be heard touching the Premises; and that the said Trade may remain free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Royal African Company is referred.

A Petition of the Planters, and Merchants, inhabiting the Island of Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that since the laying open the Trade to Africa, in the Year 1698, the Island of Jamaica hath been better supplied with Negroes by the separate Traders to Africa, than at any time before by the Afican Company, when exclusive: That the continual Supplies of Negroes, which the separate Traders have afforded us, at moderate Prices, has produced infinite Advantage to this Island, in respect to its Productions, which have greatly added to the Improvement of Navigation, the increale of the Revenue of the Crown, and advancing the Balance of the Trade of Great Britain', and that, if the African Company should obtain this Trade in a joint Stock Company, exclusive, and if granted, will occasion the Ruin of this Island, the Loss of the Spanish Trade, and the Decrease of the Navigation: And praying, that the Trade to Africa may be open and free, for all the Subjects of Great Britain to trade thither on equal Terms, as shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, tQ whom the Petition of the African Company is referred.

Answer to Mr. Speaker reported, that both Houses did Yesterday Address. attend her Majt-fty with their Address; and that her Majesty was pleased to give a most gracious Answer thereunto, as so.loweth:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I take this Addrds very kindly from you, on the Occasion of that barbarous Attempt on Mr. Harley, whole Zeal and Fidelity in my Service mud appear yet more eminently by that horrid Endeavour to take away his Life, for no other Reason, that appears, but his known Oppofttion to Popery and Faction. Your warm Concern for the Safety of my Person, and the Defence of those, employed in my Service, is very grateful to me; and I shall always continue my Care for the Welfare and Happiness of my People, by using all Means, that may most efYChially conduce to those Ends, and particularly, by giving the proper Directions for removing Papilts from the Cities of London and according to

your Desire.

I think, it would be reasonable to make a Law, to punish with Death such villainous Attempts on the Lives of Magistrates in the lawful Execution of their Office, though, by God’s Providence, the Mischiefs designed do not take Effect.

Mr. Rolle reported from the Committee, to whom the Importing Petition of the Town of Tiverton, and other Petitions, re- Irish Yarn, lating to Irish Yarn imported, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which thpy had directed him to report to the House: And be read the (amt in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, that great Quantities of Worthed Yarn, and also of Bay or Woollen Yarn, have lately been imported into divers Ports of England.

That Irish Bay or Woollen Yarn may legally be imported, paying but a small Duty, and yet great Quantities of Worded Yarn are imported under the Denomination of Bay Yarn, paying the like Duty only, though it is easy to distinguish the one from the other. . '

That Worded Yarn, imported from Ireland can be afforded 5 \d.per Pound cheaper, than what is made i,n the West of England, which amounts to about 36 per Cent. Difference, though of equal Goodnels; by which Means the Weavers make up their Worded Stuffs, and Serges, with Irish Worsted Yarn, without employing the

poor Combers, Spinners, and other Labourers in the Woollen Manufactures, as formerly, who are thereby reduced to great Necessitics for want of Work.

That combed Wool, imported (torn- Ireland, is fold cheaper than English Wool, by a Pcny in the Pound.

That the Labour of Worsted Yearn is at least Pound cheaper in Ireland, than in England, for the middle Sort, which is most used, and 8 d. and 10 and more for the finer Sort; and Woollen Yam id. per Pound.

That the Importation of Irish Worsted Yarn is a great growing Evil, and yearly increases, and, if not speedily remedied, will utterly impoverish the Labourers in the Woollen Manufactures in the Western Parts of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Ordered, That the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Tavistock (which was ordered to lie upon the

Table, until the said Report was made) be referred to the Corisideration of the said Committee.

Tho. Gerrard, Robert Hallett, Edward Bayfy, Cha. Langrish, Tho. Whatley, Jo. Jo. Jo.

Parker, Tho. Bayly, James Hunt, Wm.; who laid,

that, about a Month or Two before the Election, Mr. Betts' Agents caused Four* Bullocks to be bought, and distributed in Fourteen Pound Pieces, with a Twelve-penny Loaf, and One Shilling a-piece in Money, to those Voters, and their Votes were asked for Mr. Betts; and that he would not allow of a Six-peny Loaf, that was given to a poor Widow, who had no Vote.

Cha. Langrish, Jo. Thrup, said, that on behalf of the fitting Member, Mr. Littleton, a Bond was given for Payment of £. 200 to the Mayor, and one Mr. and they gave a Counter-bond, to deliver up that£.200 Bond, if Mr. Littleton was not elected, and to pay the Money to the Use of the Town, if he was: That the Mayor declared, he was for the present Tense, and, before the Election, the £. aoo was paid, and the Bond cancelled: That, after that Bond was given, Mr. Littleton was complimented with the Freedom of the Corporation, and gave the Mayor 10 Guineas for the Poor; and that some of the Voters had One Shilling, and others Five Shillings, a-piece, of that Money, to vote for Mr. Littleton.

Robert Coul/on, Jo. Thrup, Cha. said, that

in July last Admiral Aylmer and Sir John Jennings came from Spithead into Portland Road, with a Squadron of Eight Men of War, Two of which were First Rates, viz, the Royal Soveraigne, and the Royal ;and several Merchant Ships with them:

That they were bound Westward, and jay there 10 Days. The Witnesses said, the Weather was fair, when they came in, and sometimes ftermy, while they were 24

there; and in that Time several other Ships from Plymouth came into, and went out of, the Harbour, again i and they never knew a First Rate Man of War there before:

That the Corporation was invited, and treated, on board Admiral Aylmer-, and Mr. Betts' and Captain Littleton's Healths were often drank there: Some People lay, the Fleet came thither by contrary Winds, and others say, they came at Captain Littleton's Instance, and to make Interest for him: That the Fleet was a fine Sight, and the Country People, for 20 Miles Distance, came to fee it.

That, To prove ill P raft ices in the Mayor, several Witnesses were called; viz.

Wm.Humfryes, Jo. Thrup, Jo. Parker, James Hunt, Wm. Lindsey, Tho. Whatley, said, that the Mayor, solicited Votes for the Four fitting Members, and declared, he would shew a new Game at All Fours: That divers old Voters, who lived remote, and had always polled before, were now refused their Poll by the Mayor, when they offered it for the Petitioners, because they had not brought the Deeds of their Freeholds, though they were known to be good Voters: That Deeds were not required from the Voters of the fitting Members; and the Mayor admitted several for them, who were only Lease-holders, and had no Title; and caused several, who came to vote for the Petitioners, to be beat and abused by the Constables, and thrust out of the Hall, without taking their Poll; and threatened some, and refused others, who shewed their Deeds, and offered to poll for the Petition's, alleging, they were not for his Interest; and he declared, that if Mr. Ward had Forty Majority, he should not be returned.

That the fitting Members Counsel examined Witnesses; viz.

Tho. Cooper, junior, Taylo, Edward Mitchell, Richard Ptarfywho said, that other Gentlemen, besides Mr. Littleton, have given Ten Guineas for their Freedom; That the Mayor admitted several Persons to vote for the Petitioners, who did not produce their Titles, and some, whose Titles were doubtful: That Mr. Ward desired a Scrutiny, and, when it was granted, he desisted, and sent word to the Mayor, that he would give him no further Trouble: That Matters were transacted fairly at the Election, in the usual Manner; and none were turned out of the Hall, but to make room for such, as had not voted: That the Mob came from Portland to the Poll with Clubs, and swore, they would have Mr. Ward, right or wrong.

F.dward Tucker, Ph. Ungby, Taylor, said, that several Persons who had no Votes, had Mr. Betts's Benevolence of Bread, Beef, and Money; and some, who had it, voted for Mr. Ward.

And Edward Tucker said, that it was very stormy Weather, and the Wind blew hard at South and South-weft, when the Fleet came in: That he was sent by the Mayor and Aldermen with a Compliment to the Admiral, to invite him athore: That the Admiral said, he could not tell, how soon the Wind might come fair, and that he could not leave his Ship; but, if the Corporation would come aboard, he should be glad of their Company: That the Wind blew so violent then, that the Corporation did not think fit to venture in open Boats, but they went afterwards in a Hoy: That the Wind was then commonly South, and South-weft, and South-weft and by South, and contrary to the Fleet; and the Two-and-twentieth of July they failed, and it was said, they went back again to Spithead: That they had an Account Six Weeks before, that the Fleet was riding at Spithead: They had this Account by a Yatch, that came from thence to Weymouth, to buy Provisions; but they had no Account by that Yatch that the Fleet w’ould touch there: That the Road is large enough for the Navy Royal, and there is no Danger in the Harbour, but in an easterly Wind.

Kingston upon Thame* Church.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Parishioners, of the Parish of Kingston upon Thames, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in the Year 1703 the Steeple and Tower of the said Church was very much damnified by the violent Wind: That they were necessitated to take down the said Spire, and a great Part of the Tower, to prevent the Ruin of the whole Body of the Church, which otherwise mud soon have happened by the Fall of the said Spire, and Tower; and that they have, at a very great Charge, rebuilt the said Tower in a very strong and decent Manner, but are not able (by reason of the Poverty of1 most Part of the Inhabitants) to go on with the rebuilding the said Spire, nor to finish the other necessary Reparation of the Church, both within and without, which, by a moderate Computation, will cod more than Fifteen hundred Pounds: And praying, that they may be enabled to perfect so pious a Work.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the

[St. George Southwark Church.]

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Overseers of the Poor, and others, Inhabitants of the Parish of St. George the Martyr, in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, on behalf of themselves, and divers other poor Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that their Parish Church is very ruinous, and much out of Repair; and the Roof thereof is decayed and rotten, so that the same is in Danger of falling in: That to repair and adorn the said Church, upon a moderate Computation, will cost the Sum of Two thousand Four hundred and Eighteen Pounds, Three Shillings, and Seven Pence: That the Prisons of the Queen's Bench, County Gaol, Palace Court, and Bridewell, and also the Mint, being within the said Parish, so loads the same with Poor, that the Petitioners are wholly unable to repair and adorn the said Church: And praying, that the said Sum of Two thousand Four hundred and Eighteen Pounds, Three Shillings, and Seven Pence, may be assigned, for repairing and adorning the said Church.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and several other Inhabitants, of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, in behalf of themselves, and others, poor Parishioners there, is referred, shall be made.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Vestrymefl, St. Buttolph and others, Inhabitants, of the Parish of St. Buttolph Bishopsgate, London, on behalf of themselves, and the Church, rest of their Parishioners, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Parish Church is so old, and ruinous, that, although it has all along been carefully-repaired at the great Charge of the Parishioners, and for many Years part supported by Props, and held together by strong Iron Work, yet so weak and decayed is its present Condition, that it cannot possibly (land long; and by reason of these dangerous Circumstances many of the Inhabitants are deterred from coming to Church, it having more than once given terrible Signs of falling, even ' in Time of Divine Service: That the Petitioners have chearfully borne their Shares of the Duty on Coals, for the rebuilding of St. Paul’s, and the parochial Churches of the City, and, that blessed Design being now happily accomplished, they hope, that in this the Time of their own like Necdlity they shall not want the like Assistance of the lcgiflative Authority in so pious a Work: And praying, that out of the Duties on Coals, or any other Duties, such a Sum of Money may be granted, as may be sufficient for rebuilding their said Church.

ders, and other Countries, where they received Encouragement, and at this Day carry on the Trade, to the great Detriment of her Majesty’s Dominions: That all the Employment, that remained to the People of this Voi. 1(J.

Country, was the spinning and combing the irWocd, which was and is imported into Great Britain, under such Restrictions, and such a Duty laid thereon, as barely to afford the Manufacturers a poor Subsistence; but if a further Duty be imposed, ’tis unavoidable, that the Per-.

Tons, who are now employed in combing and spinning, will remove themselves into France and other foreign Countries, where they may be employed; and that the Protestants of this County, which are generally,

and the moll in Number of any other County in Ireland, will be very much discouraged and weakened, in regard there is no other Manufacture, or Employment, where to to turn the useful Hands of that People; and that such Proceedings will also, in the End, bring great Disadvantage to the English Manufacture, in railing the Price at

home, and lelfcning the Exportation Cloth to

other Countries: And praying, that they may be heard by their Counsel against laying an additional Duty on Irish Yarn, imported into Great Britain.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of the Importing County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and Infll Y,rB' re. d; setting forth, that the Petitioners being informed, that there are several Petitions before this honourable House, for bringing in a Bill for laying a greater Duty on hrish Yarn,-which may prevent the Importation; the Petitioners are apprehensive, if a Discouragement of such an Importation, by a farthet Duty, should proceed, it may occasion Quantities of Irish Wool unwrought to be sent into this Kingdom, or elsewhere; which would be of dangerous Consequence, and, as we humbly conceive, c-iufe a very great Fall in the Price of Wool, to

A Petition of the Worsted Weavers, and Combers, of Ditto, the City of Norwich, and Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the importing of Irish Yarn into Great Britain, at such cheap Rates and Prices, lor several Years part, haS been very detrimental to the Weavers, Combers, and Spinners, of Yarn in this Kingdom of Great Britain, especially in the City and Counties aforesaid, and has so far lessened the Prices of Yarn in this City, and the said Counties, that the Combers, and many Thousands of their Journeymen, and Spinners, are in a miserable Condition; and that, unless a Stop be put unto the Importation of Iriflo Yarns, or a Duty be laid upon them, to make their Prices equal with English Yarns, the Petitioners will be wholly ruined, and the Combers and Spinners must inevitably perish: And praying, that these, or some other proper. Methods, to redress these their Grievances....

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

A Petition of the Merchants of Edinburgh was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners understanding, the present Royal African Company in England are still endeavouring to obtain an exclusive Trade, pretending, the same cannot be managed but with a Company Stock, exclusive of all others; whereby the said Trade would be confined to some few Merchants in and about the City of London, and the Petitioners thereby excluded; which is directly contrary to the Articles 01 the Treaty of Union, particularly to the Fourth and Twenty-first Articles, whereby, from and after the First Day of May, 1707, it is stipulated, and agreed, that all the Subjects of the united Kingdom of Croat Britain Shall have full Freedom and Intercourse of 'trade and Navigation, and that there be Communication of all other Rights, Privileges, and Advantages, which do or may belong to the Subjects of either Kingdom, except where it is otherways expressed and agreed in these Articles; and by the said Twenty-first Article the Privileges of the Royal Boroughs are expressly referred; And praying, that the Trade to Africa may not be confined to a Monopoly under a joint Stock, but remain open and free to all the Subjects of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Adventurers and Creditors of the Royal African Company, and others, Subscribers for the Support and carrying on that Trade, is referred.

Mr. Amtfley reported frotn the Committee, who were Address on appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to her Menage re. Majesty, for returning her the Thanks of this House for her Majesty’s most gracious Message, in recommending. urc the building of Churches in and about the Cities of don and dVejflmitffter; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was twice read, and, upon the Question put there-, upon, agreed unto by the House; and is as followeth;-viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, have, with the utmost Satisfaction, received your Majesty’s gracious Message, recommending to us the great and necessary Work of building new Churches in and about the Cities of London and iVeJ

We are sensible, how much the Want of them hath contributed to the Encrease of Schifin and Irreligion, and shall not fail therefore to do our Parts towards, supplying that Defect, being entirely disposed to pro-, mote every thing, that is for the Interest of the efta*, bl ished Church, and the Honour of your Majesty’s Reign.

Neither the long expensive War, in which we are engaged, nor the Pressure of heavy Debts, under which, we labour, shall hinder us from granting to your Majesty whatever is necessary, to accomplish so excellent a Design, which, we hope, may be a means of drawing down Blessings from Heaven on all your Majesty’s other Undertakings, as it adds to the Number of those Places, where the Prayers of your devout and faithful Subjects will be daily offered up to God, for the Prosperity of your Majesty’s Government at home, and the Succels of your Arms Abroad.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, da humbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure, when die will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That Sir John TreviUian have Leave to go Lear* of into the Country for a Fortnight, upon extraordinary Abfeace. Occasions.

presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the extreme Poverty of the Petitioners, and the ruinous Condition of their Church, makes them incapable either of rebuilding, or repairing, the lame, being at least Six Foot under-ground $ and many separating, and absenting from publick Worship, for want of a Place in the said Church; all which may be remedied by the rebuilding the old Parish Church, and building a new Chapel, according to the Scheme, now lying before your Honours: And praying, that out of the Money, granted towards building of Churches, such a Sum of Money may be granted them, as shall be thought fit to rebuild the said Church.

A Petition of the Bailiffs, High Steward, Aldermen, Malden capital Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the ancient Bo- Church, rough Town of Malden, in the County of Essex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Borough Town had formerly Three Churches, One of which, viz. Saint Peter's, having many Years since fallen down, and the Parish being united to that of All Saints, the Number of Parishroners, though poor, are very great: That the said Church of All Saints is a very large old Church, consisting of Three I lies, and Three Chancels, on which is a very heavy Roof, which, by its vast Weight, and the failing of the Pillars on the North Side, hath so drawn the whole Fabrick after it, that it is every Day in Danger of falling, and not fit to have Divine Service performed in it: That some time in the Month of October last past, a Commission issued from the Lord Bishop of London, directed to the Reverend William Bramftm, Doctor of Divinity, the Reverend Daniel Uorjemanden, Rector of Purleigh, Thomas Barrington, William Fy/che, Esquires, and others; who caused able Workmen to view and inspect the said Church, which by them was found so dilapidated, by reason of the breaking of the said Pillars of the North Ille, that it is not possible by any means to uphold it, but that it mult necesstrily fall down; and that the Charge of the pulling down, and rebuilding, thereof, will amount to the Sum of One thousand Pounds, or upwards, besides the Benefit of all the old Materials: And praying, that their same may be taken into your Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table; until the Report shall be made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, and Churchwardens, and several other Inhabitants, of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, was referred.

New Mr. Annejley reported from the Committee, to whom Churches, the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and several other Inhabitants, of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, in behalf of themselves, and other poor Parishioners, and several other Petitions, were referred; and who were also to esquire, what Moneys remain in the Hands of the Commissioners for rebuilding the Cathedral Church of St. Paul's, and consider, what the Produce of the Duties in being, appropriated for that Purpose, may amount to for the time to come, and make an Estimate, what will be necessary for finishing and adorning the said Church, and other the Purposes in the Acts mentioned, for building the Cathedral Church of St.; and also to consider what Churches are wanting within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, and report the feme to the House; that the Committee had considered the several Matters to them referred, and had directed him to report, how the same appeared in relation thereunto; and had come to a Resolution, which they had also directed him to report to the House: And he read the said Report, and Resolution, in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where the feme were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee (pursuant to the Order of the House) have considered and examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and find the same to be as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Greenwich.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the Roof of the Parish Church of Greenwich fell down in the Night of the 28th of November last, without the least Apprehension 6f any Danger, there being Prayers twice a Day, and several hundred Pounds laid out in the Repairs and Decoration of the said Church within Three Years last part.

That in the judgment of ikilful Workmen, who have viewed the said Church, the same is incapable of Repair, and must inevitably be rebuilt, the old Foundation not being Three Foot in the Ground, and therefore not capable of bearing new Walls.

That the Petitioners produced Plans of the intended new Church, signed by proper Workmen, with an Estimate of the Charge thereof, amounting to the Sum of £.6,260. 4 s.id.

Jfiat the said Parish ye unable to raise such a Sum,

for rebuilding their Church: Mod of the great Houses upon the East Side of the Park, and down the Hill, to the Town (being left by the Gentry, and richer Sort of People) now Hand empty.

That Nine Parts in Ten of the Inhabitants are Seafaring-men, and Watermen, who subsist only on their Labour and Pay, and have no Manufacture there, whereby to oblige them to a rebuilding of the Church.

That the Petitioners pay 15 din the Pound to the Poor’s Rate, though formerly but Twelve Pence.

That by the late and present War, and Storms at Sea, the Widows and Orphans of the deceased, to the Number of about 3,000, have become a Charge to the rest of the Parish for their Subsistence.

That Thirty Years ago the Parish Books, for the Poor’s Rate, were under £. 40 per , and now they are

above £..500 per Annum.

And that there is notone DiflentingMeeting-house in Greenwich Parish, nor ever was.

Upon the Petition of the Parish of St. Mary Woolnoth, London.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the Church of St. Mary Woolnoth was entirely burnt down by the great Fire of London, in the Year 1666.

That by an Act, made in the 22d Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for rebuilding the City of London, the said Church was included in the Number, of the One-and-fifty Churches, to be rebuilt out of the Duties arising by Coals.

That by another Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of King James the Second, for adorning the Cathedral Church of St. Paul's, a Clause was therein inserted, to perfect, and rebuild, the said One-and-fifty Churches.

That, for the more expeditious assembling of the Inhabitants to Divine Service, only the North Side, fronting Lombard-street, and about Two Yards of the Corner at the East End, was rebuilt out of Moneys arising by the said Duties; but the rest of the East End, adjoining to the Poll Office, with the South Side, W eft End, and Tower, were not rebuilt, and are now become so ruinous, and weak, that the Inhabitants dare not go to Church, for fear it should fell upon them; and that to rebuild the said Church, and Tower, it will cost above^.6,50o, as appeared by an Estimate thereof, produced to the Committee.

That St. Mary Woolnoth is one of the united Parishes of London after the said Fire: and that Part, which lies about Stocks Market, consists of many poor Families, in Alleys, who receive Relief from the Parish, to the Amount of 100 per Annum; and that the Petitioners are unable to build the said Church at their own Charge.

That in the Year 1707 a Bill passed the House of Commons, for the more effectual finishing and adorning the Cathedral Church of St. Poufs, London-, wherein there is a Clause, to impower the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, Lord Bishop of London, and Lord Mayor of London, to appropriate so much of the Coal Duties, as should be sufficient for the rebuilding such Parts of the said Parish Church of St. Mary Woolnoth, and the Tower thereof, as should be necessary; but this Bill did not pass the House of Lords.

Upon the Petition of the Inhabitants of St. Mary le Stroud.

That the Petitioners proved (by Extracts taken out of divers ancient Histories) that formerly there was a Church, called St. Mary le Strand Cross, then Handing where Somerset House is now built; and that the same was long since demolished.

That the Petitioners have never since had a Church, though they have alyvays chose their own Officers, and yearly go the Bounds of their Parish, and pay their own Poor; and by Permission of the Mailer of the Savoy (where there is a Chapel for the Royal Hospital) they now go to Divine Service there; but they have heretofore been turned out from thence, for a Year together; and the said Chapel is abundantly too little for the Petitioners, and the Inhabitants of the Savoy.

;o Ann. 6* Aprilis. 581

That there is in the Parish of St. Strand 217

Houses, and 1,154 Souls, as appeared by an Account thereof.

That the Petitioners have but Annum towards

defraying the Charges of their Parish.

That the Poor’s Kate for this Year is ^.329. 141. which will not be sufficient for that Purpose by near too, so that their Poor yearly increase upon them.

That the building a Church (according to a Draught, produced to the Committee) sufficient to hold about 1,500 Souls, will cost about £-7,500, as the Workmen compute it.

That, if the Petitioners be supplied with Money, for building a Church, they will purchase Ground to build it upon, they having none at present for that Service.

Upon the Petition of the Town of Deptford.

That it appeared to the Committee, upon the Evidence of Dr. Stanhope, Dean of Canterbury, and Vicar of the

£iid Parish, that in the Year 1697 the Church of Deptford was so ruinous, that the Petitioners were obliged to pull it down, and build a new Church upon the same Foundation, which coll them near 5,000.

That above £. 1,800 of that Sum was raised by voluntary Contributions (Mr. Loader himself giving above £900) the rest by Assessment of a Pound Rate; and, though the Contributors did bear their equal Proportion in the Assessment, yet all the Money raised extended only to build the Church and Chancel; io that the old Steeple was left Handing, and is so weak and decayed, that if it should fall (as, *tis feared, it toon will, though no Care has been wanting to support it) it may endanger a great Part of the Church. And

Thomas Lucas, Bricklayer, laid, the Steeple is so weak, that the Bells have not rar.g for some time, for fear they should throw down the Steeple; and that it will cost above f.i,oooo to new build the Steeple with Brick.

Dr. Star.hcpe further laid, that Deptford i: a great Parish, confiding (as near as he can judge) of 2,400 Families, and Eleven or Twelve thousand Souls, who cannot polTibiy be accommodated in the said Church, or any other tingle Church, for Divine Worship; for want of which (he doubts) many have wholly neglected I heir Duty on the Sabbath Day, who would other wise have come to Church, and many others go to Meeting-houses, of which there arc Three in the Parish; One of Quakers, One of Presbytcrians, and the Other of Anabaptists; and many of the Inhabitants ferupling to pay their Parish Duties, for want of Conveniency at Church.

That the Inhabitants oiDeptfrd are utterly unable to build another Church, by reason the greater Number of them conftfts of Seamen, or Workmen and Labourers in her Majesty’s Dock-yard, and Two other Yards there, for building of Ships (many of which live in One House, and so are rated only as One Family) and of Butchers, Viclualers, and others, who give them Credit, and con-lequently are great Losers by such their Customers; so that the greatest Part of the Town do subsist and depend upon the Business of the Sea, and the Poor’s Rate is risen,

since 170a, from £. 40 to £.72 per Month, amounting to near £. 900 per Annum.

That to build a new Church, and rebuild the old Steeple, will (as it is conceived) cost about £.6,0001 but the Parish have no Ground of their own, to build the Church upon: And the Dr. said, that he has no View of any Profit to himself by this new Church, and proposes to keep a Curate for that Service.

LTpon the Petition of AlderJlgat Parish.

That Mr. Carpenter and Mr. Bird said, they law the

Church of St. Butto/pb's, Aldersgate, on Fire in thedread-ful Fire of London, in 1666; and that the Fire was put out by the Industry of the Inhabitants, but the Church was very much damnified thereby.

That this Church is nor mentioned in the Act for rebuilding of Churches, burnt by the said Fire; the Reason whereof was (as they believe) because many of the then chief Inhabitants (who before lived in the principal Streets of London, and intended to return thither again, as soon as they could be accommodated with Houses) took no Care to have it inserted therein.

Mr. Blijjhrt, and Mr. Smith, Workmen, said, that they, with others, had viewed the said Church, and Steeple, and find the same so decayed, that it cannot be repaired, but mull of Necessity be pulled down: That the Walls are propped up with great Timber, and the main Pillars give way so, that the Roof is in Danger to fall in, and the Inhabitants afraid to go to Church: The Steeple is also cracked Six or Seven Inches wide, and is split and crushed: And produced a Draught of the ill State of the Church.

That the said Church is 57 square and an Half of Building; and that to rebuild the same it will cost about £. 5,760, and the Steeple £. 2,750, together £. 8,510.

Mr. Foxall and Mr. Keys said, that the Parish consists of about 700 Families, computed at Four or 5,000 Souls, many whereof receive Alms of the Parish, inso much that their Poor increases, that, for 12 Months Assessment, they are forced to make 30 Months Assessment in the Year, amounting to about £. 600 per; and that the

Parish is unable to build their Church, without publick Assistance.

That within the Parishes, mentioned in the said Scheme, there are but 28 Churches j and Chapels, or Tabernacles, if:

That There are within these fttrilhes, Meeting-houses ft)t Presbyteriatw *6, Anabaptists 23, for Quakers 14,

for Independents 12; in all 75; and also 13 French Congregations.

That there are, by Computation, within the said Parishes 80,159 Families, and in those Families about 513,000 Souls.

That allowing the Eighteen Chapels, or Tabernacles, to be capable of receiving as many Persons, as Eight Churches do, and supposing the present Number of Churches, upon that Allowance, to be 36, and 4,750 Souls to belong to each of those 36 Churches, they will, in the Whole, contain but 171,000 Souls, which is only a Third Part of the said 513,000 Souls; so that there will be about 342,000 (being Two-thirds of the whole Number of Souls) for whom no Churches are as yet provided.

That, upon the Foot of this Computation, 72 new Churches would be requisite for the Reception- of those Two-thirds, if ^11 of them were of the Communion of the Church of England.

A Petition of several Creditors by Bonds, Bills, and fj'ecie Notes, of the Company of the Mine Adventurers of England, on behalf of themselves, great Numbers of Parish Children, Widows, and Orphans, and other Creditors of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Company borrowed of the Petitioners, and others, several great Sums of Money, in order, as they pretended, to carry on their Works V01. 16.

with’ greater Effect: That the Proprietors of principal Money, and Annuities, being also Proprietors of Shares in the said Company, and thereby qualified to vote in general Courts, did, contrary to the Constitution of the said Company, divide amongst themselves upwards of Seventy thousand Pounds of the Money borrowed, as aforesaid, as by Receipts, under their several Hands, may appear; whereby the said Company became utterly uncapable to pay their just Debts: That the Petitioners, and other Creditors, having no Hopes of any other Remedy, were contented to accept of the Alignment of the Mines and Effects of the said Company, as a full Satisfaction: Which’

Mines, and Effects, were accordingly assigned by Order of, and by the Trustees, Appointed by the said Company; and the Petitioners, for raising a new Stock, to work the said Mines, did agree to admit the said Proprietors to be Partners with them, upon Payment of no more than Five Pounds per Cent, though the said Proprietors had so divided, as aforesaid, upwards of Seventy Pounds per Cent, amongst themselves: That, notwithstanding this great Condescension of the Petitioners and other Creditors, and that the Petitioners were, and are, legally entitled to, and actually in Possession of, the said Mines, with Power to prosecute, and call all Persons to Account, for Misappii-cation ot Money, or any other Wrong done, some of the said Proprietors, apprehensive of being prosecuted for Misapplication of the said Money, so divided amongst themselves, as aforesaid, have obtained Leave to bring in a Bill to this honourable House, which (as the Petitioners are advised) tends to divest the Petitioners, and the other Creditors, of the Possessionof the said Mines, and of the Powers to sue and prosecute all Offenders, as aforesaid:

And praying, that they may be heard by their Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard before the Committee thereupon by their Counsel, if they think fit.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Mistery of Bakers, in the City of London, was referred.

And the lame, with the Resolutions thereupon, were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the Allegations, contained in thelaid Petition; it appeared, that in the Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, for regulating the Price and Assize of Bread, there is a Penalty of Forty Shillings, wholly given to Informers, for Accidents, which are unavoidable; for which several of the Petitioners have been punished, and paid the said Penalty, because the Mark on their Bread hath accidentally been imperfect, although the same was full Weight, and have often fulfered by a Loaf wanting a (null Matter in its Weight, which sometimes is not to be avoided, by reason of its being over-baked, or Hale, or by some other Accidents, incident to the Trade.

It appeared also to the Committee, that common Informers, as Soldiers, and such-like loose Sort of People, have often gone, and do go, from House to House, to buy a crusty or Hale Loaf, on Purpose to ground an Information upon.

That, to prove which Allegations, several Persons were examined , viz.

Bartholomew Marsh said, that he was fined Forty Shillings, because the Letters of the Mark did not plainly appear on a Peny Brick, although the Impression was very plain, before it was baked, but, in baking, it became imperfect: He was convicted before Justice Fuller, and compounded with the Informer lor 20

John Butler said, he was fined Four Pounds, for want of a Mark on Two Peny Bricks, which were full Weight: He was convicted before Justice Fuller, And compounded with the Informer for 30*.

Joseph Booth laid, he was fined, and paid, Forty Shillings, for want of a Mark on a Half Peck Loaf.

Robert Hubbard said, he paid 20*. for want of a Mark on a Peny Brick.

'Robert Gijbiirn said, that an Informer came to his Shop, and bought a Six-peny Loaf, and kept it F<5ur Days, and then informed against him, that the Loaf wanted Half an Ounce; for which he was convicted before the late Lord Mayor, and paid 40*.

'Thomas Cove said, that he paid 40 s. on Account of a Six-peny Loaf, Four Days old: The said Loaf, after it was bought, was dimimlhed, by having a Piece pulled out; the Informer (who was a common Soldier) after he bought it, carried it to a Justice, and procured a Warrant of Distress, which was levied, and paid: Mr. Cave afterwards brought an Appeal at the following Quarter 7 K Sclfions,

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of St. Olave in Southwark, in the County of Surrey, together with the principal Inhabitants of the adjacent Parishes, was referred; and who were to enquire upon what Invitation, or Encouragement, the Palatines came over, and what Moneys were expended in bringing them into Great Britain, and for maintaining them here, and by whom paid.

And the said Report was read, and is as follows; viz.

That they have examined the Matter, and, upon the Examination of Mr. Wig one of the Churchwardens, find.

That in September, or Oftob 1709, near a i,ooood Palatines came into their Parish, and were entertained in Sir Charles Cox's Warehouses,' although Sir Charles Cox was desired by the Parish Officers not to receive them, for fear of Expence, or Infection, they being very numerous, and sickly.

Mr. Walter Cock fays, the Palatines were removed from their Camp at Black-heath by Order of the Commissioners, appointed to distribute her Majesty’s Bounty, and other Charities to them, and Places were hired for their Reception; but he did not hear of any Security given to the Parish.

Mr. Meggott and Mr. Lade said, the Palatines were at

that Time received into Sir Charles Cox's Warehouses, though the Parish Officers had applied to him, to prevent their being received into the said Parish.

Mr. Bendyjb, Secretary to the Commissioners for the Palatines, said, that, when the Commissioners had it under their Consideration to dispose of them in the Autumn of 1709, the cold Weather approaching, the Commissioners never consulted the Parishes about receiving them, but where they found room, they contracted for it; and then it was, that Sir Charles Cox offered his "Warehouses for Two Months, gratis, with Condition to be paid for the whole Time, if they flayed any longer: And it appears by the Minute Book of the general Meeting of the said Commissioners, that on the Eighth of February, 1709, Sir Charles Cox, on his Application to the said Commissioners, had a Warrant on the Chamber of London, to pay him 100 Guineas for the Hire of the said Warehouses, upon Condition, the poor Palatines should flay there, till they were sent to Ireland; which Sum he received the Ninth of February, 1709, as by the Chamberlain of London's Book.

Mr. I ho. East said, there was an Order of Vestry, to apply to the Commissioners for the Palatines, to get rid of them about the End of October, 1709, when they appeared to be about 1,400 Persons; and that about the Beginning of February after they were removed.

It appeared to the Committee, that Three thousand Palatines were sent to Ireland in August, 1709, pursuant to an Address to her Majesty from the Lord Lieutenant and Council in Ireland, desiring as many Palatines, as her Majesty should think fit to fend thither, and giving 20

furances of their being received and settled in that Kingdom; and that the Commissioners for the Palatines here bore their Charges thither, which amounted to the Sum of £.3,498. 1 6s. 6d.and, to complete their Settlement

in Ireland, a Warrant was signed by her Majesty, and directed to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, appropriating ,£.15,000 out of her Majesty’s Revenues in that Kingdom, to be paid in Three Years, at 5,000 a Year.

In February, 1709, Eight hundred Palatines more were sent into Ireland, upon a Representation from the Lord Lieutenant and Council of that Kingdom (the Commissioners here bearing their Charges, as before) and a Second Warrant was granted by her Majesty, and directed, as before, appropriating £. 9,000 of her Majesty’s Revenues in that Kingdom, to be paid in Three Years, at £. 3,000 a Year, to complete the Settlement of these 800.

In some short time several of the Palatines being returned out of Ireland, and more ready to follow, the Commissioners for the Palatines here sent Mr. John Crockett to Ireland, to prevent the Return of these People to England: And the Committee being informed, that John Crockett attended, he was called in, and said,

John Crockett. Upon his Arrival in Ireland, he found Twenty Families going on board, to return to England, with a Pass for 15 Families, to this Effect: " Permit to pass into England Five-and-twenty " Families of Palatines, it being by my Lord Lieutenant’s " Leave:" Directed to the Sutveyor of Ringsend: Signed John Smalles, who was Steward to the Lord Lieutenant,

and Secretary to the Commissioners for the Palatines in Ireland: Which Pass Mr. Crock opt, and, on applying to the Lord Lieutenant, the said Pass was recalled; but that several Families had returned before he came to Ireland: and that, upon further Application to the Commissioners for the Palatines in Ireland, to prevent any more of them returning to England, he was answered by my Lord Chief Justice Broderick, who was in the Chair, that they had no Power to flop them, they being a free People: Since which several Families are returned: so that there are now 232 Families, one with another, he believes, of Five in a Family, most of them now at the Bridge-house in Southwark.

Upon the Examination of John Henrick Hind, Frederick Rose, John Umpack, and John Peter,

Palatines.

It appeared, they were of the Number of those, who had gone for Ireland’, and were since returned to Southwark, as are the rest, there, to the Number of 232 Families.

That the Reasonsof their leaving Ireland was, the hard U sage they received from the Commissary Hinch, Mr. Sweet, and others, who did not pay them their Subsistence; on which they applied, to the Lord Lieutenant, who ordered it for them; but they never received but one Week’s Allowance. They said, they paid their own Passage to England, though they were told by Mr. Hinch, that they should have Ten Shillings per Head, to leave Ireland: That they wrote Letters to each other, to meec at Dublin;and that Seventy-five Families returned with the said Nonius.

That the Palatines are in a starving, miserable, and sickly, Condition, was proved by

Mr. Wignall; who said, they were all lodged in one House, which was become very nauseous, and they sickly, and the Parish fearful of some infeClious Dillcmper.

Mr. Amy also said, that he lives in the Parish of St. Olave's, near an Apothecary’s, who, with Doctor Mead, had the Care of a Family, who were sick, near the Place, where the Palatines were lodged; who said, the Places adjacent are in Danger of Infection from a very ill Distemper among them, of which many died.

As to the Apprehension of Charge to the Farifli;

It appears, the Palatines have no Subsistence, but what they get by their Wives begging for them in the Streets,

Great Endeavours were uled here to dil'perse and settle the Palatines in several Towns in England. My Lord Sunderland wrote a pressing Letter to the Mayor of Canterbury, to receive some of them into that City, which, upon communicating the Letter to the rest of the Magistrates, they refused to do, because of the Burthen of their own Poor, they already laboured under.

Several Proposals were likewise made by private Per-fpns to receive some, and many were received, the Commissioners allowing 5 per Head, and travelling Charges,

with them; but in a very short time most of them returned, and were afterwards otherways disposed of.

Mr. Secretary St. John acquainted the House, that he Messagefrom had a Message from her Majesty, signed by her Majesty: the Queen-And he presented the same to the ?House; which Mr. 8

Speaker read; and is as followeth; viz.

ANNE R.

HER Majesty is pleased to acquaint this House with the ill News she hath received of the Emperor’s Death:

And being sensible of the Consequence, this great Loss may be to the Allies, how disheartened some of them may be on the one hand, and how diligent France will be on the other, to improve every Accident to their own Advantage, her Majesty is desirous to let you know, that, immediately on the first News of the late Emperor's Sick-ness, she came to a Resolution to support the Interest of the House of Auftriain this Conjuncture, and to use her utmost Endeavours to get the King of Spain made Emperor, in which the States General have likewise concurred with her Majesty; and, since that, her Majesty hath taken the most proper means to engage all those (who have a Share in this Election, and are in the Interest of the common Cause) to join with her in bringing this great Work to a good Issue: And she hath an entire Confidence in the Affection and Duty of her Parliament, that, with their Assistance, under the Protection and Blessing of Almighty God, flic shall be enabled to make a happy Conclusion of this War, in a safe and honourable Peace.

The Season of the Year, and the Length of Time, that hath past since your meeting, will make you all wish, that you may be at Liberty to attend the publick, as well as your own private Affairs, throughout the Kingdom; and therefore her Majesty does recommend to you so to hasten your Consultations about all the publick Concerns, that her Majesty may put a speedy End to this Session.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, to return her Majesty the humble Thanks of this House for her Majesty’smost gracious Message; and to assure her Majesty, that this House is truly sensible of the great Loss, the Alliance has sustained by the Death of the Emperor, and of the early and wife Care, her Majesty has been pleased to take, to prevent the ill Consequences thereof, by resolving to flip-port the Interests of the House of Austria, and by endeavouring to get the King of Spainelected Emperor: And farther to assure her Majesty, that Ihe may safely place an entire Confidence in the Duty and Affection of this House, which cannot bediscouraged, by this Misfortune, from supporting her Majesty in all those Measures, (he, in her great Wisdom, shall judge proper, to bring this War to an happy Conclusion, by a safe and honourable Peace; and that this House will give all possible Dispatch to the publick Business depending before them, that foher Majesty may put a speedy End to this Session.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address, upon the said Resolution.

County of Suffolk, as well on behalf of themselves, as on behalf all their suffering Brethren within her Majesty’s Dominions of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that whereas your Honours have been so gracious, as to order a Bill to be prepared, for the releasing us out of our lamentable Condition and Confinement, and have caused the same to be directed to a Committee thereupon appointed, to settle the Conditions and Limitations thereof, and granted to them their Redemption from this their dismal and tedious Confinement, and that they may obtain their ancient Freedoms, and be thereby rendered capable of providing for, and taking Care of, their poor suffering Families, who are now under the greatest Wants and Distress.

A Petition of Robert Kerby, Gentleman, Bailiff of the Bishops Town of Bishops Waltham, in the County of Southampton, Waltham, and of I/aac Moody, Gentleman, Bailiff of the Town 4,c> Market of Havant, in the said County, and of James Lacy, Gentleman, Bailiff of the Town of Hambledon, in the said County, and also of ‘Thomas Aubery, Gentleman,

Bailiff of the Town of Fareham, in the said County, on the behalf of themselves, and other Inhabitants of the said several Towns, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said several Towns are ancient Market Towns, and are situate above Five Miles From each other, and from any other Market Towns: That, by reason they lie in the Roads, leading to the Garison of Portsmouth, in the said County, they have been greatly burthened with Soldiers on their Marches; and by reason, that the common Trade of buying and selling of Corn is now done by Sample, and not brought into the Markets, and Cattle are bought up and down in the Country, out of Market, the Markets of the said Towns are gone almost to utter Decay therein: And praying, that lbme good and effectual Law may be made for the Support of the said Markets, and ascertaining of the Toll therein, and that both' Seller and Buyer may be under some Penalty for felling and buying out of Markets.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

The Committee proceeded to enquire into the Nature of the Exchequer Process against Accomptants, and the Methods ot i(Tiling the fame.

Mr. Stephan, late Deputy of the Queen’s Remembrancer’s Office, informed the Committee, that the present Practice was, to issue a ad

then an Altai, and a Plures against such Accomptants, as were certified to be behind in their Accounts, and by the Auditors of the Imprefts in their half-yearly Ceuifi-cates; which Process was continued to be issued every iftuable Term, unless the same were ft.ryrd by Warrant from the Treal’ory, or Order of the Court of Exchequer: Which Process, he said, had very little effect; for that the Sheriffs for the most part returned no Issues, and (ometimes the Process was issued into wrong Counties, for want of due Information, there being no Solicitor appointed, to take Care of the due ilfuing of Process, and of the due Execution thereof.

He further said, that, upon looking into some of the old Entries, he found, that a Capias ad compu/andum had formerly ill'ued j bat this had been diluted for many Years.

Mr. Morgan, the present Depofy Remembrancer, produced the Roll of Process against the several Person9, set tnfuper in the Account of the Lord Coningsby and Mr. Fox, late Paymasters in Ireland; which it appeared, that, tho* Process had issued open the said (or

many Years, yet very few, or no, Issues had been returned; lb that a very great Sum (till remained upon the fame, for which no Account was rendered j whic h was the Cade in many other Accounts.

ReJo/veJ, That it appears to this House, that of the Moneys, granted by Parliament, and issued for the publick Service, to Christmat, 1710, there are Thirty-five millions Three hundred and two thousand One hundred and Seven Pounds, Eighteen Shillings, and Nine Pence, for a great Part whereof no Accounts have been laid before the Auditors, and the rest aot prosecuted by the Accomptants, and finished.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer,

When the barbarous and villainous Attempt, made upon you by the Sieur De Guiscard, a French Papist, was communicated to this House, they immediately declared, they were moll deeply afflfted, to find such an Instance of inveterate Malice against you; and ^observing how you have been treated by some Persons, they concluded, they had Reason to believe, that your Fidelity to her Majesty, and Zeal for her Service, had drawn upon you the Hatred of all the Abettors of Popery and Faction.

In this Opinion they moll be abundantly confirmed, since the Lords, and the Queen, have concurred with them.

Sir,

If your Fidelity to her Majesty, and Zeal for her Service, cou'd ever be doubted, and wanted any Teflimo-nials, to prove them, you have now the moll honourable, the moll ample, and the moll undeniable, that can be given; and, after these, it would be an unpardonable Pre-fumption in me to imagine, I could add to them, by saying any thing of your faithful Discharge of those great Trulls, you have been honoured with, to which your eminent Abilities at first recommended you, and your distinguishing Merits have since justified her Majesty’s wife Choice.

Your [very Enemies, Sir, acknowlegc this, by their unwearied and restless Endeavours against your Person, and Reputation.

God be thanked, they have been hithertodisappointed, and have not been able to accomplish, what their inveterate, but impotent, Malice had designed against both.

And may the same Providence, that has wonderfully preserved you from feme unparalleled Attempts, and that

Sir,

A Petition of the Governors and Directors of her Ma- Greenwich jetty’s Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, was presented to lie House, and read; setting forth, that in pursuance of her Majesty’s Commission, for carrying on and perfecting the said Royal Hospital, for Relief of disabled Seamen, the Petitioners have perfected a considerable Part of the Building thereof, so that for some Years pad Men have been received in, and maintained there, the Number of them being yearly encreased: That at present there are Four hundred Pensioners therein, provided for with all manner of Necessaries, besides Nurses, for tending them, and cleaning the House, all Widows of Seamen, with other Servants needful, being seafaring Persons; That the for-gent Necessities of many more poor disabled Seamen are such, that the Petitioners mutt be obliged to take them in, so soon as the Debt for the Building, already erected, can be paid, which, they presume, may be in a Year's time:

That the Income of the said Hospital being so applied for Support of those poor and necessitous Sufferers, the Petitioners shall not be able to build a Church for divine Service, or finish other Parts of the House, unless afliffed by some Encrease of Revenue, or Donation thereto: And praying the Consideration of this honourable House on the same of the said Hospital, that, among the Provision, they are making, for building Churches, they will give some Allowance for building a Church for the said Hospital, and for further Advancement of the other Buildings of the House, begun, and now lying unfinished.

A Petition of the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace,. Grand Jury, and other Freeholders, and Farmers, of the County of Gloucester, at the Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held the 9th Day of January, 1710, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners being truly sensible, that by reason of the great and unlawful Measures Corn is sold by in this and other Counties, by which not only the Poor are deprived of great Part of their Bread, but the Farmers are also Sufferers, for want of Standards, publickly kept in all Markets; and notwithstanding we have used our utmost Endeavours to have the Laws put in Execution, for regulating the Measures, and prosecuted Offenders by Indictments and Informations; yet it hath little Effect, by reason the Bakers, Maltsters, and other Corn-buyers, utterly refuse to buy any Corn by the lawful Winchester Measure; so that the Farmers, who have cut their Measures, and had them sealed, according to Law, are now forced to fill their Corn by the large Measure again, and run the Hazard of forfeiting the fame, as well as the other Penalties of the Statute of the 22d and 23d of King Charles the lid: And praying the same may be remedied.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are informed, there is now in this House a Bill depending, intituled, A Bill for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Fishery within the River of Thoms, and for regulating and governing the Company of Fishermen of the said River; which (if the same should pass into a Law) will be highly prejudicial to the Rights, Liberties, and Privileges, of the said City: And praying, that they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, before the same do pass.

Ordered, That the Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Fishery within the River of Thames, and for regulating and governing the Company of Fishermen of the said River, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the Committee, if they think fit.

A Petition of several Inhabitants in and about Billingsgate Dock, within the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that whereas the publick Stairs at Billingsgate aforesaid is the Place, where common Ferry-boats take in and land their Passengers, who are carried to and from the Villages, which lie betwixt London and Gravesend; that, since the making Billingsgate a free Market, great Numbers of Fish Vessels, which ought, of Right, to have Access to the said Dock, are forced to lie at the said Stairs; by which means the Way is so block’t up, that Passengers cannot, without Danger of their Lives, take Water, or land, at the said Stairs; which has occasioned several of her Majesty’s Subjects to be drowned, and is also a very great Detriment to the neighbouring Inhabitants, and the Petitioners: And praying, that the said Abuses may be prevented by some proper Clause, or Clauses, in the Bill, now depending, for the Preservation of the Fishery of the River of;

and that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Fishery within the River of Thames, and for regulating and governing the Company of Fishermen of the said River, is committed.
