Mr. Conyers reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed Kim to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where they were once read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That ayearly Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Forty thousand Pounds, for Thirty-two Years, out of the weekly'Sum of Seven hundred Pounds, arising out of the Poll Office, and out of the Duties upon Hides, Skins, Vellum, and Parchment, granted in this Session of Parliament, be set apart, and appropriated, for raising a Sum, not exceeding One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, by Contributions for encreasing Annuities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Fund be granted to her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, for Payment of the Interest, after the Rate of Six Pounds per Centum per Annum, from the 24th of De-

tember, 1711, for the several publick Debts, and Deficiencies, for which a Supply was granted, by the Resolutions of this House the 10th of March last, and also for the Interest of the said Debts, and Deficiencies, to the 125th of December, 1711; and that such Fund be made redeemable by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the said Fund, the several Impositions, and additional Impositions, Rates, and Duties, and Sums of Money, which, by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, (amongst other Things) An Act for continuing several Impositions, additional Impositions, and Duties, upon Goods imported, to raise Money by way of Loan, for the Service of the Year 1710, were granted, and continued, or applied, for the Payment of the Principal Money, to be lent, or advanced, by virtue of the said Act, or the Interest thereof, shall be granted, and continued, to her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, from the several Days and Times, for which, by the said Act, they are so granted, and continued, or applied, for ever, redeemable by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to make the said Fund more effectual, all such Tallies and Orders, as have been made out, by virtue of the said Act, made in the Eighth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, shall be engrafted into and upon the said general Fund; and that the several Impositions, additional Impositions, Rates, and Duties, and Sums of Money, by the said Act granted, continued, or applied, for Payment of the said Tallies and Orders, shall be made Part of the said general Fund, for paying the said Principal, and Interest Money, during all such Time, as the same are, by the said Act, granted, continued, or applied, as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the said Fund, the Duties upon Candles, and Rates upon Money to be given with Clerks and Apprentices, which, by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, were granted to her Majesty from the First Day of May, 1710, for the Term of Five Years,

be further granted, and continued, to her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, frefrn the last Day of April, 1715, lor ever, redeemable by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Proprietors of the said Debts, and Deficiencies, be incorporated to carry on t he Trade to the South Seas.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That what the said Rates and Duties, before agreed to be Part of the said Fund, for Payment of the said Interest, shall fall short of paying the said Interest, such Deficiency shall be annually paid out of the first Aids that shall from time to time be granted by Parliament.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " encreasing Annuities," and to insert " Exchequer Orders, payable in Course, with a certain Encrease of Principal and Interest, according to several " classes, with the addition of Chances."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the Floufe.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, so amended, that a yearly Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Forty thousand Pounds, for Thirty-two Years, out of the weekly Sum of Seven hundred Pounds, arising out of the Poll Office, and out of the Duties upon Hides, Skins, Vellum, and Parchment, granted in this Session of Parliament, be let apart, and appropriated, for raising a Sum, not exceeding One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, by Contribution, for Exchequer Orders, payable in Course, with a certain Encrease of Principal, and Interest, according to several Classes, with the Addition of Chances.

The rest: of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

That the Committee ordered several Papers to be laid before them by the Agents of Taxes, and examined Mr.

Clayton and Mr. Shoreditch, Two of the said Agents; who gave them an Account of what Money had been paid since the 8th of December last, for the Year 1705, 1706,

1707, 1708, and 1709: And the Committee took into Consideration the most considerable of such Arrears.

That the Committee began with the Arrears due from Mr. James Taylor, Receiver for the Queen’s Houshold,

°f£ 63>4S*' ts. 2d.

And the Agents for the Taxes acquainted the Committee, that the said Taylor has paid, during his Examination, £. 3,246. 19 a. 6d. which reduces the Debt to £.60,211. ts. 8id.

As to the Occasion of this Arrear, the Agents said, that in the Year 1705 there was laid upon the Queen’s Houshold Three times more, than in former Years; and they, upon Complaint to her Majesty, that the Tax was more, than they were well able to pay, the Queen promised, Ihe would piy One-third of the Sum; so they were never assessed, in any one Year, but Two-thirds of what was given by Parliament, but have, every Year, been charged with the whole Tax; and no Part has been, paid by her Majesty, to lessen this Debt.

The Commissioners for the Stamp Duties, in Answer to Arrears, informed the Committee, that they are obliged to give the Distributors Credit, that they may have Stocks to supply the Country with stamp Parchment, and Paper, to, at least, £. 6 or 700 for a County; for which they take as good Security, as they can get:

That they have an Inspector, to enquire into the Sufficiency of the Securities proposed; who generally informs himself by the Justices of the Peace, and other Gentlemen of the Counties, within the District, of each Distributor, and where their Securities live:

That the Distributors return their Accounts upon Oath, yearly, to the Commissioners, of the Money received, and their Stock in Hand:

That they have also their itinerant Officers, whorarca Check upon the Distributors:

That the Distributors have in the Pound allowed them for what they distribute, as an Encouragement; but this is not allowed, until they clear their Accounts; and this Money, if answered, will lessen the Arrears.

The Commissioners of the Stamp Duty also repre'-fented, that this Duty is of 17 Years (landing; and that there has been received for the fame, and paid into the Exchequer, nigh a Million and half of Money; and that the whole Arrear of insolvent Persons will not be above £. 8 or 9,000, and that, by Indulgence to Distributors, and their Sureties, many times they become able to pay some Part of their Arrears.

The are several other Arrears from divers Distributors, of small Value, amounting to £. 897, of which, the Commissioners said, £. 469, will prove bad Debts; and the Remainder, being £. 428, will be paid in a short time; of which the Committee make no mention.

And the Solicitor acquainted the Committee, that the then Attorney General, being attended, was of opinion, the Plea was god: So no further Prosecution was had thereon, the Suit being in the said Attorney’s Name; and in his Power to flay Process, when be pleased.

That the Committee, observing, that the same Plea had been pleaded, and was ready to be pleaded, by several other Securities for divers Collectors, and that a great Loss had happened to the Revenue thereby, enquired, if any new Deputations had been given after the King's Death, or any new Security Bonds taken; and ordered Copies of the Bonds, taken in the Reign of King William, and her pielent Majesty’s Reign, to be laid before them.

That, uj>on Perusal of the Bonds (delivered by Mr. Cari asse. That the Obligation in the Bonds, on the Queen's Accession to the Throne, was, Regina, ribus, vel affrguat' fuis; the Condition the fame, a6 in King William's Reign:

But fmee the Pica in Clinton's same aforesaid, the Bonds have been altered; and now the Obligation is, Regina, haredibus. vel exeattoribus, fuis; and the Condition, that the Collector shall, to Jong as employed by virtue of his Deputation, or any other Authority whatsoever from her Majesty, her Heirs or Successors, well and truly collect and receive all and every Sums, arising, and payable, to her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors.

That the Commissioners of the Customs, attending the Committee, in Answer to the Matter above, said, they were very much surprised at the Plea of Sir Simon Dewes, in Clinton's Cafe, and represented the same to the Lord Treasurer; whereupon, by Advice of the Attorney and Vot. 16.

Solicitor General, in 1707 the Bonds were altered: And further said, that the Condition of the Bonds, taken in King Charles the cd, and King James the ad, Reign, were the lame, as in King William's Reign; and that it never Was the Practice of the Commissioners of the Custotns to renew Security Bonds, on the Demise of the Crown, tho’ they renewed Deputations: There were none taken on the Demise of King Charles, Abdication of King James, the Resolution, or Death of Queen Mary, as supposed need-lets: That the Commissioners acquiesced under the Opinion of the Attorney General, and did not proceed to Trial, for fear of giving Notice to other Securities; but have (ince recovered several Sums upon the like Bonds.

And Mr. Godblphiu said, he had been a Commissiontfr of the Custotns for 19 Years, and was so at the Death of King William', and produced the Commission, wherein there is a Claufr, for appointing him Register of all trading Ships, and to excuse his Attendance at the Board: And laid, he was not there from Christmas, 1701, to May, 1705, but on extraordinary Occasions: And further said, he was not present at signing of the new Deputations after the Death of King William; and seldom attended the Board, but when he was sent for, on extraordinary Occasions, or when he went to present Memorials to them.

And the Committee asking the Solicitor of the Customs, upon the renewing the Bond, whether, in the Condition of a Collector's Bond, there are Words sufficient to make the Sureties liable to answer for Moneys, received by the Collector before the Date of such Bonds; he answered, that the Attorney General was of opinion, that the Condition of those Bonds did not operate by Rctrospect, so as to make the Security liable for Money, received before the Security given.

That the Commissioners of the Customs being examined concerning such Arrears;

Mr. GoJolphinsaid, that tin/ there are monthly Ab-

strafts, and quarterly Accounts, from the Collectors; yet their Debt does not appear to the Commissioners, until their Accounts are stated by the Comptroller General, which may be Two or Three Years after:

That, when they find any Collectors running confides-ably in Arrear, they press them to make Returns; on Failure whereof, they ordfcr their Solicitor to prosecute them, and their Sureties; as they did upon Saufum, and divers others, as appeared by several Letters and Memorials, produced to the Committee:

That, as to the Observation, that the Collectors Arrears often exceed the yearly Produce; they lay, it may so happen in some of the smallest Ports, by reason of a Tobacco Ship’s coming in there by Chance, which greatly augments the Customs; and by reason of the Uncertainty of Trade, during the War; as at Dover, Carlisle, Boulton, Pad/low, and- many other Places.

Mr. Freeman reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Camelford, in the County of Cornwall, and the RefoJutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed hirri to report to the House: And he read the Report, and Resolutions, in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Paul Orchard, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Henry Mamaton, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Camelford, in the County of Cornwall:

That the Right of Elect ion was agreed to be in the Mayor, chief Burgesses, and Freemen of the Borough.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel infilled, that Mr. Edward Cloake is the legal Mayor of the Borough, and ought to make the Return.

That the fitting Member’s Counsel infilled, that Mr. Godfrey White (who has returned the fitting Member) is the legal Mayor.

That, by the Charter, the Mayor, and chief Burgesses, for the Time being, or the major Part of them, whereof the Mayor, for the Time being, is to be one, are annually, on Monday after Michaelmas Day, to meet, and cleft one of the chief Burgesses to be Mayor for One whole Year then next following; and the Mayor elect is to be sworn before the chief Burgesses, or any Four or more of them, for the Time being; and after he is sworn, he is to continue in the Office for the Space of One whole Year then next following, and from thence until another of the chief Burgesses is duly elected, anil sworn, into the Office of Mayor.

That the Petitioner’s C tunlel examined Witnesses; and called,

Samuel Jackson, Samson Bond, Edward Hodge, Richard Hewgce; who said, that upon Monday after AJichae/mas Day, 1709, being the Charter Day for ciefting the Mayor, Mr. God/rey White, the then Mayor, and Four of the chief Burgesses (the whole Number of which then in being was but Six) whereof the Witnesses, Jackson, Bend and Hodge, were Three, met, upon Mr. s Summons, to elect a Mayor for the Year then ensuing: That they accordingly proceeded to elect the Mayor; and the Town Clerk called over their Names, and asked their Votes:

That Mr. White, being first asked, refused to vote; and that the other Four chief Burgesses voted for Mr. Cloake to he Mayor:

That White role from the Table, protested against their Proceedings, and declared, there should be no Election, till the Charter (which was deposited in Jackson & Hands by the chief Burgesses) was brought, to fee, if the Freemen at large had any Right to vote for Mayor, as they pretended to have:

That, before White was gone out of the Room, they had given their Votes for Cloa; and the Town Clerk was entering the m* when White went away:

That, a little while afrer. returned; and then

Cloake was sworn Mayor before and the other

Four chief Burgesses:

That the Charter being thus called for, the Town Clerk fetched an English Copy of it: And the fitting Member (who is the Recorder of the Town) put it in his Pocket, and said, there was nothing in it:

That

Camelford That all the Year 1709 held Courts, and acted,

ElectioB. as Mayor; and the Magistrates owned, and acted with, him, and protested against White:

Cloake then executed a Mandamus for filling the Common Council j was chosen and sworn Mayor for the present Year; and in Ottobt last presided, and acted, as Mayor, in the Election to Parliament; and the fitting Member then owned, and solicited, him as Mayor; and recommended to him his Kinsman, Mr. Ratcliff, who was returned by him; and the chief Burgesses elected under Cloake in 1709, have always voted, and acted, without Object ion.

That the fitting Member's Counsel insisted, there can be no Election of Mayor, without the Mayor for the Time being:

That White protested against the proceeding to elect Cloake in 1709, and went away:

That that Election was made in his Absence; is therefore void; and White continues Mayor, till another is chosen. And they called

Ralph Pike, Wm. Row, ‘Thomas Farley, Jof. Tincombe, Daniel Bridge-, who said, that 20 Years ago, by virtue of a By-law, the Freemen returned Two Persons; and out of them the chief Burgesses chose the Mayor:

That they have broke that By-law several Years, and have since elected according to the Charter:

That at the Election of Mayor in 1709, some of the Freemen claimed this Privilege; and Mr. White insisted to have the Charter, for their Satisfaction; and declared, be would not proceed to cleft a Mayor, till he had it.

That he protested against the chief Burgesses proceeding to the Election; and went out of the Room, when Two of them had given their Votes, and before the Town Clerk had entered the Second Vote; and the other Two voted, after he was gone.

And the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Mr. Edward Cloake is legal Mayor of the Borough of Camelford, in the County of Cornwall; and ought to

make the Return of a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough.

The Poll, taken by Mr. Cloake, was thus:

12 for the fitting Member:

21 for the Petitioner.

That the fitting Member’s Counsel declared, they were not instructed to object to this Poll.

And the Committee came to these Resolutions: Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Henry Manaton, Esquire, is not duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Camelford.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Paul Orchard, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

And he was called in; and, being examined at the Bar touching the said Indenture of Return, he said, that he had made the same at the time of the last Election for the said Borough; and that he tendered it to the Sheriff.

And, having delivered the same into the House, he withdrew.

And the said Report was read, and is as follows;

Mr. Patrick Hurley; who said, that upon his acquainting Mr. Murphy, Marshal of the Guards, with his being much in Debt, he was told, that for Two Guineas he should be lifted, and protested from his Creditors; and might be discharged, when he plealed, on the Payment of Five Pounds, and finding a Man in his Head:

That, on the 2 tft December, 1 709, he, and Two of his Friends, Whom he brought for Witnesses, met Murphy, and Two Serjeants, at an Alehouse; where he lifted himself regularly in Sir Robert Rich’s Company of the Foot Guards: He then received £.1 as Bounty Money, and for a Week’s Subsistence, and gave his Receipt for it; but immediately returned the Money to Murphy, proposing no other Advantage by his lifting, than the Protection:

That, about a Month after, he was mustered in the Company; and has since appeared at some, but not at all, Musters:

That Colonel Charteris, having obtained the Command

of the Company, sent for Hurley, to let him know, he had paid a great Sum for it, and was not bound by Sir Robert Rich's Bargain with Hurley; and would therefore neither protest him from his Debts, nor exempt him from his Duty, without a farther Gonfideruion; and demanded ot him Five Pounds: Which he paid, and procured him an effective Man, to do constant Duty in his stead; but was, notwithstanding, forced to pay a Week for his own being excused from it:

That he had twice done Duty; first, by Handing a Quarter of an Hour in regimental Cloaths, under Arms, in Murphy's House, which is the Prison in the; and a Second time, in the dark, at St. James’s, he changed Coats with the Centinel, and took his Arms, and his Place, which he kept for Six or Seven Minutes, while a Serjeant, and fume of his Friends, came thither to lee it, and bear Witness of it:

That he had been committed to the Savoy for Neglect of Duty, though never called to it; but was not then long confined, or used with any of the Severities, which other Prisoners are: This was done, that his Commitment might appear on the Prisoners Books, when he should have Occasion to produce them in Proof of his being a Soldier, in order 10 defraud his Creditors:

That he never received any Pay; but constantly signed the Books, as if he had received it.

That when he was arrested by his Creditors.and carried to the Compter, and thence removed to the Fleet, he made several fruitless Applications to his Colonel for his Protection; who would not relieve him, though he agreed first with Mr. Murphy to find Six Men, or pay till he had

That Broughton, being thereupon arrested, applied to the Judge, whose Summons was produced.

He said further, that Toon, a Butcher in street, had been twice arrested, and discharged, being lifted in the Guards; and named several others, whose same was the fame.

Mr. Macmorran said, that Thomas Marreck owes him £. 87, for which he was arrested, and put in;

and discharged, being in Colonel Wheeler's Company.

That Marrock owned before the Lord Chief Justice, that he owed many more considerable Sums, but still carries on his Trade, and pays ready Money for what he buys.

Robert Corruther said, that

Charles Iwinowes him £. 36.

Andrew Bean - - 15.

Cha. Tunnab - - 52.

Edward Duke - - 181.

But all bid him Defiance, being all lifted for the Guards.

Mr. Fulkes said, that John Longden, an Apothecary at Worcester, owes him £. 63, and was arrested, and put in

Worcester Gaol; but was discharged, being lifted in Colonel Charteris'Company:

That he offered to take Lons Effects, and pay all his Debts, and give him £. 100 in his Pocket:

That Longden offered £. 300 for a Commission, whilst he made use of his Protection of the Guards to defraud his Creditors, and now lives like a Gentleman.

-' The Committee observing, that the Complaints of this Kind were very numerous, and being informed by Mr. Billers, that he could furnish them with many Hundreds more, thought it not proper to extend their Examination to such a Multitude of Facts of the same Nature, which only serve to shew the ill Use, that had been made of the Encouragement given to Volunteers in the Act for recruiting the Army; but this Complaint seemed to be made with great Earnestness, as being attended with no less mischievousaConsequence, than the utter Destruction of all Credit in Trade, and consequently of Trade itself.

Richard Seddan, a Painter, lifted in Colonel Swan's Company, said, that he returned the Bounty-money, and never received any Pay; but has been forced to hire one to do Duty for him, and pay i$d. i Week for his own being excused:

That be was put into the , for not doing Duty, and released out of it, upon Payment of Two Guineas.

John Ackland, a Harncfs-maker, lifted in the same Company, and Manner, said, he was to be discharged at any time for Three Guineas; which will not now be taken, unless he also provides another Man in his stead:

That he never received any Pay, tho’ he has demanded it, and done Duty.

Colonel Swann laid, in his own Defence, he had been a Prisoner in France Two Years, and could not answer for the Management of his Company in his Absence; but had endeavoured, Cnee he came over, to have none but effective Men in it, and was therefore willing to part with Seddan for another Man; of whom he owned he had received the Two Guineas, which he would return, if he found him a Man, or discharge him for Two more, which another Man would cost him.

Remark Burnt orth said, that several Persons, pressed by Constables, and turned over*by the Commissioners, were d ifeharged for Money by Murphy, the Keeper of the Savoy

Prison; and that other Persons, who have been in the Service, and are discharged, were sent over in their room; by which Means the same Person is fold several times over; and instanced in one

Mr. Thomas Murphy, Keeper of the Savoy Prison, laid,

that Langton, being pressed, and turned over, as above,

had expressed to him his Unwillingness to go beyond the Seas; upon which Murphy offered to fend another in his room for £.4, but Langton, not being able to perform that

Condition, was at last himself sent into Flanders; but being too low of Stature, and too old, was discharged by the commanding Officer of the Regiment, to which he was sent.

Langton confirms his being pressed, and turned over, and his Promise of £. 4 to M, that he might flay behind, which he was not able to perform; but laid, that when he was sent over, it was to save another, who, no doubt, had paid for his Redemption, as be had promUed to do:

That he was indeed discharged by the commanding Aborts hr Officer of the Regiment he was sent to, and brought back paying tbs into England, but not to enjoy his former Liberty; for Guards,

the Minute he landed at Harwich, he was secured by the Serjeant, that came over with him, to be returned to his old Confinement in the Savoy, till Mr. Murphy might have another like Opportunity to fend him over again in the room of some other prest Man, better able to pay his Ran lorn.

It appeared to the Committee, that his Discharge (which was produced) was not in his own Custody, but Mr. Murphy's.

Mr. Hurley and Mr. Bamfordproduced Serjeant and others', in relation to Cheifca Hospital; who said, there were great Numbers, belonging to the Hospital, out upon Furlows; but did not seem to have any thing material to complain of.

They said, that Thomas Hicks, an Oilman near Charing Grofj, was admitted as a Comoral of Horse in the Hospital, tho’ neither want of Health, his.Age, his Circum fiances, nor Time of Service, entitled him to any Share in that Charity.

Mr. Crisp, Mr. Ithell, and Mr. Evans, said, as to the great Numbers, belonging to Cheifca Hospital, that are out upon Furlow, that it was what had always been, and must be; because they had no Power to find them Quarters; and because it was for the Benefit of the Men to be allowed those Furlows, without which, at some times, they would not be able to subsist:

That no Person was ever admitted into the Hospital without a Certificate, signed by the commanding Officer, under whom he had served, or by the Queen’s Order, signed by the Secretary of War, which was never dif-puted; and that Hicks's Admission was on the latter Account.

Thomas Hicks said, he had been 14 Years in the Service, but a good Pact of that time more as a Sutler, than a Soldier: That he had lodged a Petition in the Secretary of Wat’s Office, for the Queen’s Older to be admitted into Chelsea Hospital; which he succeeded in by the means off. 5 given Mr. Arnold, an Under Clerk.

Mr. Hurley said, Charles Domfey was muflered in the Hospital ia December last, though.he died in February before.

Mr. Crisp, Mr. Ithell, and Mr. Evans, owned him so entered on the Roll, but shewed by the Books, that no Pay was allowed him; and said, that no Person is allowed Pay, unless he appears, or a Certificate be produced of his being alive, signed by the Minister and Churchwardens of the Parish of his Abode.

Col. Charterss acquainted the Committee, that at the last Muller Mr. Hurley used him with great Inference at the Mead of his Company, and insulted him to that degree, before a great Number of the Officers of the Regiment, that nothing could have induced him to bear it, but the great Regard he had for the House, and the Committee, whose Authority Hurley pretended on this Occasion, to countenance his ill Behaviour: This he proved by Witnesses; viz. Serjeant Cook, Corporal Corbett, and Mr. Caddell.

Major General Fat ton said, that he was among the Officers at the Mutter, and saw Hurley insult Colonel Chartris, and heard his insolent Language, which was such, as amounted to a Challenge, and what he wondered, the Colonel would bear: He said also, that Colonel Charteris had brought Men out of Scotland, and (pared no Care or Expence to have a good Company; and that his appeared to be so: He confirmed what was before said of his deciding the Difference between Colonel Charteris, and Williams, his Serjeant.

Colonel Cathcart, said, in his own Defence, that he was

H

so very much indisposed, when he obtained the Command of his Company, that he was not able to appear abroad to be presented to it.

That, as soon as he was able to bear the Journey, he went into Scotland j where he had continued in the same ill State of Health, till he heard, his Name was mentioned in this Complaint:

That he was in Scotland, when the Court Martial fat upon the Complaint of Birkett and and knows

nothing of that whole Affair, but by the Account, which his Lieutenant gave him; who wrote him word, that Birkett and Bunworth were imprisoned, and sent abroad, as a Punishment for their Perjury and Ingratitude: To which he had returned this Answer, that he was sorry they were sent abroad; for that he thought, if they had done imifs, they ought to have been punished according to Law:

That he never paid fewer Men than the Complement, which the Queen allows:

That he had indeed desired Mr. Rockett to manage the Affairs of the Company, when, by reason of his

Lords, for disagreeing to the Amendment, made by them to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways between Dunstable and Hockley, in the County of that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table j where they were twice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House j and are as follow; viz.

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between Dunstable and Hockley, in the County of Bedford, Skin the id, Line the 13th 9

Because the Persons, appointed tobe Trustees, should be proper Persons for the Execution of the Trull reposed in them by this Bill, and free from all manner of Objec- . tions, which, the Commons conceive, the Persons, added by your Lordships, are not.

For the Commons are informed, that Symon Taylor, le-nior, is the chief Manager of the Toll, appointed by an Act, of the 5th Year of the Queen (intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between Hockley and Wooburn, in the County of Bedford) is Surveyor of the Highways to be repaired by the said Act, and receives and disposes of the Money, arising by the said Toll, accountable only to the Quarter Sessions $ and as the said Toll, and that granted by this Bill, lie contiguous to each other, if the Interest of one should in anywise prove' inconsistent with that of the other, Symon Taylor, senior, who is lb nearly concerned in the Interest of the first, cannot be thought a proper Person to determine Disputes, that may arise in the Management of the last.

And Symon Taylor, junior, is the Son of Symon,

senior, and therefore, it may reasonably be supposed, will always aft under his Influence and Controul.

The Commons dedine at this time offering any other Reasons, believing, what has been said may be sufficient to prevail with your Lordships not to inGft on the Amendment, that a Bill, so necessary, may not be loft.

MR. Monekton reported from the Committee, who pin(

were appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered Am to the Lords, for disagreeing with their Lordships in an Amendment, by them made to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Preservation of white Pine Trees, growing in her Majesty’s Colonies of New Hampshire, the Bay, and Province of Main Rhode Island, and Providence Plantation, the Narraganset Country, or King's Providence, and ConneSUcut, in New England, New York, and

New Jersey, in America, for the mailing her Majesty’s Navy; that they had drawn up the Reasons accordingly, which they directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk's Table; where they were twice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon (with an Amendment) agreed unto by the House, and are as follow; viz.

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships, Pr. ill. Line the 30th, by adding, after the Word " Earth," " within Five Miles " of the Sea, or the navigable River Because the Sea-coasts, and Lands lying on Rivers, are the Parts first planted, and moll coveted, both for Fertility, and Convenience, and are now, by the great Increase of People, generally cultivated, and the Trees destroyed: and where the Ground is not cleared, yet the Lands within the Compass of Five Miles are for the moll part taken up, and become the Property of private Persons therefore, if this Restraint should be fixt to those Limits only, it would preserve very few Trees, fit for the Service of the Navy.

io° Mail.

Moggie ft on's ElUte.

Tyih* of Hops.

Standard of Plate.

And the Commons conceive, that, should this Bill pass with this Limitation, it would rather encourage, than prevent, the Mischief complained of; since it might from thence be inferred, that the Inhabitants of those Colonies bad thereby a licence, at lead implicitly, granted them to destroy the bed Trees growing beyond those Limits: And since it was thought necessary in the late Reign to prevent thisAbufe, by establishing an Officer, to take care of such Trees, as were fit for Mads, and to keep an exalt Regiderof them, in all the Colonies, mentioned in the Bill, who has ever since been continued at a great Expence, and condant Salary; therefore they cannot think it proper to redrain the Bounds of that Officer’s Charge, and make them less, than the Extent of his Commission now is.

And since all the Mads for Ships of the id and 2d Rate, and the greated of the 3d Rate, are now brought from her Majesty's Plantations, and dand from 24 to 39 Inches Diameter in the Navy Contrail, and Length proportionable, whereas those from , and th z Baltic,

are only from Seven to 28 Inches Diameter; and few Countries producing any l'o large, and tall, as that Part of America belonging to the Crown of England; but such Trees, fit for Mads, and of the larged Dimensions, being very scarce in those Plantations; the Commons conceive, it is both reasonable, and necessary. that the Licentiousness of those Inhabitants should be redrained, and they not lufil-red to cut such Trees on her Majesty’s I^nds for Lumber, when there is Plenty of others, fit for that Pur-pote, that are allowed them.

And therefore the Commons hope, your Lordships will agree, that the Officer, appointed for that Purpose, may (by the Provisions in this Bill) be enabled to preserve the Trees of the Dimensions specified, and not infid on that Amendment.

Ordered, That the said Reasons be delivered to the Lords at a Conference.

Ordered, That a Conference be desired with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the said Amendment.

Ordered, That Mr. Monckton do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

prefen ted to the House, and read; letting forth, that whereas the Improvement of the Fishing in all Parts of North Britain is of the greatest Importance, being the most considerable Branch of Trade and Export from thence, and fubfllls divers Thousands of poor People, who are employed therein, and they are obliged to cure all Fish, exported, with foreign Salt only, which at present we have not, although divers Ships have been loaded outward for Portugal, up >n Design to bnng Salt from thence; vet several of them have been call away, or taken by the Enemy, and some detained by cross Winds, and all so late in going out, and so uncertain of arriving at their outward Port, by reason of the Numbers of French Pri-vatv ers and Crullers on that Coast, that we cannot have any Quantity of Salt returned in time, to answer the Fishing; whereby the same is in danger of being utterly ruined; and the foreign Salt, imported before the Union (which we depended would be sold for the Use of the Fishing) is otherwise disposed of, viz. the French Salt transported for the Viol ualing, the and Portugal sold by

the Commissioners of the Cutloms to some private Merchants, who are to export the fame, and to return Certificates of its being landed there; by which we arc deprived of our Exnctftntions that way: And praying to be allowed flie Spatrjband Po tugal Salt, bought for Exportation, to

Sir Thomas Haunter reported from the Corntnitter, ap* Representa* pointed to draw up a Representatiort to be made to b*r in’\7ifw- Majesty upon the Reports, and Resolutions of this House* uageinent relating to the Imprest Accomptants, the publick Debts, and Abuses.1 the Arrears of Taxes, the Abuses of the Victualing Office, the bringing over the Palatines, and the Chart ft imposed upon the Corporation ot Btsvdky, in the County of IFore ester, and upon the Debate of the House; thwc they had drawn up a Repreleritation accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And hte read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it ih at the Clerk’s Table; where the fartie was twice read, and is as follows;

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s mc& dutiful and foyd Subjects, the Commons of Orfat Britain, in Parliament atlembled, have with the utmost Zeal and Unanimity applied outdrives to the Dispatch of those great and important Affairs, which your Majesty Was pfeased to recommend to us from the Throne , and we humbly hope, that we have in every rdjxft answered your Majesty’s Expectations in calling this Parliament.

In making suitable Provision for the publick Service, we have met with great Difficulties, from the Anticipation of Funds, and the large Suras, with which the publick Revenues (land charged for long Terms of Years to come: However, we have not been discouraged; but have, with greater Diligence, carried on our Endeavour* to raise such Supplies, as, we trust, will be effectual, not only for the Service of the prefect Year, but also for the Discharge of the heavy Debts, so long and fojuftly complained of i and, as the absolute Necessity of carrying on the War, and our Resolutions to support the publick Credit, and maintain the Honour and Justice ot Parlia-' ment, hare obliged us to increase the Burthen of Taxes upon our Fellow-subjects, so we are perfoaded, that thfe same Reasons will induce them to pay those Taxes with Chearfulness and Satisfaction.

At the same Time we have thought it another Part of our Duty to enquire into the Causes of the heavy Debts we laboured under, and to trace the Source of that great Evil, as what, wc thought, would, in some Degree, satisfy the Minds of your People, and prevent the like Mischief lor the future.

This was a Promise and an Assurance, which we presumed to give your Majesty at the Beginning of this Sese fion; and now, at the Conclusion of it, we beg Leave to lay before your Majesty the Result of our Enquiries, which, we hope, your Majesty will not judge to be unworthy of your royal Consideration.

Ih examining into the State of the War, and looking back from the Beginning of it, we find, that in several. Years the Service has been enlarged, and the Charge of it increased, beyohd the Bounds prescribed, and the annual Supplies granted, by Parliament. To this new and illegal Practice wc mu ft, in great measure, ascribe the Rife and Growth of the heavy Debts* that lie upon the Nation: Nor does the Consequence of it end there: For We must also reptefent it to your Majesty, as a dangerous Invasion of the Rights of Parliament. The Commons must ever assert it as their foie and undoubted Privilege to grant Money, and to adjust and limit the Proportions of it; and, when your Majesty has recommended to them, to consider of Supplies, and they have deliberated upon the several Estimates for the annual Services, and considered, and determined, what tire Nation is able to bear, their Proccedr ings would be very vain and ineffectual, if, aftet the respective Shms are dated, and granted, those, through whose Hands the Disposition of them passes, are allowed, in any measure, to alter and enlarge them.

This is an Attempt, which very little differs from levying Money without Consent of Parliament, as will appear to your Majesty from this one Consideration; That a Charge of that kind, once incurred, and laid as a Debt upon the Navy, or any other publick Office, is so far binding upon Parliament, that, how little soever they

This also has been an Occasion, why great Sums of un* of the publick Money had been regularly puffed; but, to appropriated Money, arising from the Exceedings and our great Surprize and Concern, we find, that they, who' Surplusages of some of the Funds, granted by Parlia* of late Years have had the Management of your Ma-ment, have not been applied, as they ought to have been, jetty’s Treasury, and ought to have compelled the several in Aid of the Deficiencies of other Funds: Had this just Accomptants duly to pass their respective Accounts, have Care been observed, the Debts of the Nation could not been guilty of so notorious a Breach of Trust, and of so

have increased to so exorbitant an Height: But other Uses were found out, such, as were neither voted, nor addressed for, by Parliament; which, therefore, we ad* judge to have been a Misapplication of publick Money.

With regard to the Debts of the Navy, we find, that one great Discouragement and Burthen, which that Part of the Service has lain under, has been from a Liberty, that has been used, of diverting several Sums issued to that Service, and transferring them to other Purposes, for which they were not intended; particularly, that the Sum of £.606,806. 7 s. yd.belonging to the Navy, has been paid for Provisions supplied to Land Forces, lent to Spain and Portugal, and for the Garison of , for which

no Deductions have been made from the Pay of those Forces, nor any Part of that Sum re-assigned to the Victualing, notwithstanding the several Acts of Parliament provided, and the many Letters, and Representations made, to the Treasury, in that Behalf. This unjustifiable Proceeding has been a Discouragement to the Seamen, occasioned the paying extravagant Rates upon Contracts, and has very much contributed to fink the Credit of the Navy.

Tothiswemuftadd the many notorious Imbezzlements; and foandalous Abuses, which appear to have been practised, as well in the Management of your Majesty’s Brewhouse, as in the Contracts for furnishing the Navy with Beer. We have already presumed to addrels your Majesty, that several Persons, whom we discovered to have been guilty of those Frauds, should be prosecuted at Law for those Offences; and we intirely rely upon your Majesty’s most gracious Assurance, that thofeProfecutions shall be effectually carried on; but we must also (upon this Occasion) beg Leave farther to represent to your Majesty, that the Commissioners, appointed to take care of the victualing your Majesty’s Navy, have been guilty of great Negligence and Remissness in their Duty: For the Instructions, which go along with that Commission, are so well adapted to the preventing those very Abuses, which have been committed, that nothing but a notorious Mismanagement in that Office, and an inexcusable Ne-gleet in pursuing those Instructions, could have given way to the great Loss, the Publick has sustained in that Part of the Service.

The evil Effects of this Mismanagement in publick Offices, and Misapplication of parliamentary Supplies', have been increased by the very Methods of bringing in the publick Money: For it has appeared to us, that the Receivers of the Land Tax, and of the other Revenues, have not been called upon to pay in the Money they had received, in due Time, as the Law requires. Such has been the extreme Remissness, and unaccountable Indulgence, of those, whose Duty it was to oblige these Receivers to due and punctual Payments, that on the 8th Day of December, 1710, there was an Arrear of the several Land Taxes for Five Years, ending the 24th of March, 1709, amounting to the Sum of £.272,596. is. id. some Part of which was paid into the Exchequer, after the Commons had ordered an Enquiry into that Matter; so that the Sum (landing out at the Beginning of April, 1711, was £. 180,439. 7 6

From these Omissions the Publick remains long under the Load of Interest, for want of that Money, which lies in the Hands of Receivers; so that the Supplies granted to your Majesty, however large, or well proportioned to the Occasions of the War, could never prove effectual to prevent the Incumbrance of DebtSj whilst they were neither collected, nor disbursed, faithfully, according to the Ends and Methods designed by Parliament.

Thu* hit have we proceeded in difoovering some of 16

high an lnjustice to the Nation, that of the Moneys granted by Parliament, and issued for the publick Service, to Christmas, 1710, there remains unaccounted for the Sum of £-35,302,107, for a great Part of which no Accounts have so much as been laid before the Auditors; and for the rest, tho’ some Accounts have been brought in, yet they have not been prosecuted by the Accomptants, and finiftied. This has made it impracticable for us to arrive at so exact Knowlege of the State of the Nation, with regard to the publick Money, as we with, and might have expected; and your Majesty will please to consider, in such an immenseSum unaccounted for, how many Imbezzlements may be concealed, and how justlf it is to be suspected, that so foandalous a Remissness has been allowed with no other Design.

We humbly beseech your Majesty, that you will give immediate and effectual Directions, for the compelling the several Imprest Accomptants speedily to pass their Ac -counts; and in the mean time we humbly hope, your Majesty will approve the Resolution of your Commons, that such of the Accomptants, who have neglected their Duty in prosecuting their Accounts, ought no longer to be entrusted with receiving the publick Money.

We cannot omit taking Notice to your Majesty of an-otherextraordinary lnltance, in which the publick Money has been misapplied, by bringing over the poor,

to inhabit and settle themselves in this Kingdom. This was not only an extravagant and an unreasonable Expence in itself, but many other ways uneasy and grievous to your People; for, as it was visible, that such Numbers of ne-cefiito'us and useless Foreigners must unavoidably tend to the Increase and Oppression of the Poor of this Kingdom; so being a Mixture of People of all Religions, it was evident, how dangerous they might prove to the Quiet of our Government, and the Constitution of our established Church. Upon what Encouragement and Invitation they came over, we have not been able to discover; but we look upon it as certain, that the calling over so many Families from' a Country so remote could not be brought about without Industry and Contrivance; and those, who were concerned in it, seemed to have been conscious of the Evil of their own Designs, by the Secrecy, with which they pursued them. Your Majesty, in your great Wisdom, will best recollect, from whence this Attempt and Advice proceeded; and we humbly represent it as our Opinion, that the Authors of it were Enemies to your Majesty, and your Kingdom.

W© beg Leave to offer to your Majesty’s Consideration but one thing more, which has alarmed your People with just Fears; the arbitrary Attempt of new-modelling Corporations, by imposing a Charter upon the Borough of Bewdley; a Charter void, and illegal, not being accepted by the Corporation then in Being; destructive of the Constitution of Parliament, in transferring the Rights of Electors to others; and injurious to your Majesty’s Subjects, in divesting them of their Franchises and Freeholds, even after they had been affirmed by Judgments upon the rigorous Prosecutions of Quo Warrantos.

We return your Majesty our most humble Thanks for putting a Stop to so pernicious a Precedent, by ordering the proper Methods to be taken for repealing the said Charter, and quieting the Borough in the Possession of their ancient Privileges. We are truly sensible of your Majesty’s tender Regard to the Rights of all your People; and we cannot without Indignation reflect upon the oppressive Designs of those evil Counsellors, who endeavoured to have brought a Blemish of this Kind upon your Majesty’s most just and gentle Reign.

Your People could with greater Patience have suffered the manifold Injuries, done to thrmselves by the Frauds and Depredations of such evil Ministers, had not the same Men proceeded to treat your sacred Person with Undutifulness and Dif-regard; but, as the Interests of your Majesty and your People are inseparable, and are by your Majesty and your good Subjects inieparabiy pursued, the Wrongs, which these Men had done to the Publick, drew upon them your royal Displeasure; and their Irreverence towards your Majesty justly exposed them to the Indignation of your People.

Your Majesty had, from the Beginning of your auspi-cious Reign, expreli'cd a true Christian Moderation, by Promises of Lenity and Protection to all your peaceable Subjects, and of Countenance and Favour to those, who should most recommend themselves by their Zeal for the established Government in Church and State; but these Ministers framed to themselves wild and unwarrantable Schemes of balancing Parties, and, under a fallc Pretence of Temper and Modciation, did really encourage Fastion, by discountcn tncing and depressing Persons, zealously affected to your Majesty, and to the Church, and by extending their Favour and Patronage to Men of licentious and impious Principles, such, as (hake the very Foundation of all Government, and all Religion.

Out of our unfeigned Zeal for your Majesty’s Honour and Service, and our faithful Affcdion to the publick Good, we cannot forbear with all Humility and Earned-nets to beseech your Majesty, that you would avoid, as the greatest Enemies to your royal Dignity, and to your People’s Safety, all Persons, who shall endeavour to engage you in such pernicious Measures; and that you would employ in Places of Authority and Trust such only, as have given good Testimonies of their Duty to your Majesty, and o( their Affcdion to the true Interest of your Kingdom.

These are the humble Desires of your faithful Commons, and thcl’e we know to be your Majesty’s gracious Intentions. From your tender Concern for this Church and iN'ation, and from what you lately have done, and are going on to do, for the Happiness and Satisfaction of your People, we promise ourlclves a favourable Acceptance of this our Application; and from our Duty to your Majesty, and our Fidelity to our Trust, your Majesty may confide in us, that wc will, upon all Occasions, defend and support your Majesty, and our happy Constitution, against all Enemies and Oppoiers whatsoever.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom it was referred to examine the Matter of the Reports of the Auditors of the Iniprcfts, and others, relating to the Method of computing the Duties on East India unrated Goods.

And the Report, and Resolution of the Committee, were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee have (pursuant to the Order of the House) examined the Matter thereof, and find the same to be as follows; viz.

Peter Garde laid, that upon the Commencement of the Art, of the zd «nd 3d of Queen Anne, which prescribes . Vot. It).

the Method for adjusting the Values of uncated East India Goods, he was then a Clerk to Mr. Carkefs, one of the Computors, or Collectors, in the Custotn-house, London, and now Secretary to the Commissioners.

That in a iliort Time after the passing the said Art, Mr. Carkefs delivered to several Officers, concerned in the inward Receipt, a Scheme to be purlued in the Application of the said Art, exemplified by the Instance of China Wares; which Scheme was imitable in adjusting tho Values of all other unrated East India Goods, Regard being had to the Duties they are respectively charged with. ’

That by the Art 3 id 4" Anna Regina, a Duty was imposed on China Wares, of 12 Cent, and by the Art 3,u et 4" Anna Begin*, a further'Duty of £.5 p& Cent, being laid on that Commodity, for the Two-third Subsidy.

That upon one of the first Entries of China Wares, liable to those new Duties, he privately discovered to Mr. Carke/s, that, notwithstanding the Accefllon of the said new Duties, no Increase was made in the general Amount of the Customs on that Commodity; and he told Mr.‘ Carkefs, that' China Ware upon Exportation drawed back more Money, than it did before the Commencement of those Duties. Mr. Carkefs answered, he believed, he wai mistaken; but, if not, 'twas o.wing to some Fault, or Detert, io the Art.

That a few Days after, having conferred with Mr. Mitchell (one of the Examiners of the Out-perts Cob lertors Accounts) he repeated to Mr. Carkefs his Stifpi-cions, that the aforesaid Scheme was erroneous; and prevailed with Mr. MttcbeU,(who is esteemed a Person very capable in Figures, and in the Business of the Customs) to accompany him to the said Mr. Carkefs $ but what Discourse passed between Mr. Carkefs and Mr. Mitchell, he can’t fey.

That about the same Time the said Mr. Carkefs gave him ftrirt Commands, not to concern himself any furthef in that Affair.

That, upon Mr. Carkefs'$ Removal to another Employment, be was succeeded in his Office, as Computor, or Collector, by one Mr. Charles Mein, with whom he continued for some Time; and that he frequently advertistd Mr. Mein of this Error.

'Fhat, while he was under Mr. Mein, he frequently hinted to him, that the Exemption of those Goods, fold under the Denomination of Wrappers, from paying the Duties, was not justifiable.

That, finding all his Remonstranees to Mr. Carkefs, and Mr. M’», concerning the Error in adjusting the Value of the unrated East India Goods, ineffectual, he sent a Letter (about Two Years Three Quarters since) wrote in an unknown Hand, to the honourable the Commissioners of the Customs; wherein he acquainted the Commissioners with many Absurdities, proceeding from the erroneous Method of computing the Duties on the said unrated Goods; but what Report the Officers, to whom it was referred, made, he cannot lay.

That about Half a Year since he wrote to Mr. Score, Collector of Exeter, in this Affair, and desired him to exert (himself in it for her Majesty’s Service; but Mr. Score, contrary to his Expertation, shewed his Letter to Mr. Carkefs, who he had therein taken Notice of, under the Name of a certain great Man, as an Opposer of this Affair; upon which being informed, that he must expert no Favour from Mr. Carkefs, he relblved to go to Sea.

Richard Score said, that he has been concerned in the Customs about 16 Years, and is now Collector at Pen-zance. '

That in March was Twelve Months (being at Exeter) his Father, the Collector of that Port (who had been an Officer in the Customs about 40 Years) observed to him the erroneous Practice of the Officers in the Port of London, in reducing the Values, and computing the Duties upon unrated Goods, and particularly East India unrated Goods.

That thereupon he told his Father, it appeared very' plainly to be a very great Abuse: That therefore he,

was

unrated

Goods.

688 i° Junii.

was of opinion, it ought to be laid before the Publick; and that, in order thereto, he was resolved to use his best Endeavours and Interest.

That his Father transmitted some Papers thereof to Mr. Godolphin, who was pleased to encourage the Prose-

cution of it.

That he came to London in April, 1710, and about the latter End of that Month he, with Mr. Foote (then a Member of Parliament) waited upon Mr. , and

left with him Papers, contained several Instances thereof, one, particularly, of £. 100 China Wares.

That the 8th June, 1710, at the Rose Tavern without Temple-bar, he acquainted Mr. therewith; who

appointed to meet him the next Day, and confer about . it.

That the 9th June, 1710, at the Queen's Arms Tavern in St. Paul's Church-yard, they met accordingly, and Mr. Carkefs brought with him Mr. , Mr. Terrill, and Mr. Andrews, Officers concerned in the Computation; who endeavoured to justify their Practice, telling him, that the Duties payable, and the Duties to be paid, had not the same Meaning, but were different Things.

That this Affair of unrated East India Goods was represented by his Father to Mr. Godolphin in last,

who was pleased to lay it before the Commissioners, being of opinion, that his Father was right in his Observations upon the Practice, and that the Officers Answer was mere Cavil.

That Mr. Towers (one of the Officers concerned) was very angry with him for what Information he had given about the Computation, and for making of it publick.

That, upon his particular Application to Mr. Shute, one of the Commissioners (who happened to be in the Chair at the Time of his Father’s Death) Mr. Shute was pleased to tell him, that the Commissioners took it much amiss, that he had been endeavouring to expose the Praft ice of the Officers in the Business of unrated East India Goods, thereby reflecting upon their Management.

That thereupon he signified to Mr. Shute his Readiness to wait upon the Commissioners; and told him, that, if the Commissioners would be pleased to hear what he had to offer upon that Subject (in the Presence of all the Officers concerned) he would undertake to convince every Gentleman at that Board, that the Officers had been wrong iu their Practice, and that they had milled the Commissioners in a Report, made some time ago to the Trca-lury upon that Occasion; with more to the same Purpose,

In Answer to which,

Mr. Shute, one of the Commissioners, said, that ha had feme Discourse with young Score about the Computation, and was so far from being angry for concerning himself therein, that he recommended him to the other Commissioners, and he was minuted down for Collector at Pool, which is £.30 per Annum better than his present Collection; but he, being all'o an Officer for the Salt Duties, did not think fit to accept of Pool, one Chamberlain (whose Services the Commissioners thought preferable to Score's) uaving been made Collector at Exeter.

That Score, the Father’s, Papers were referred to the principal Officers of the Customs, in order to confer with Score, the Son, who was directed to answer their Objections in Writing; but he doing nothing the rein, the Commissioners took it for granted he couid not; and believes, the Commissioners might take it ill, that Score ta'k’d of the Mistake all about Town, without applying himself to them.

That their Officers marie Application to the Board, to know, what should be done by the Computation, and went to the Attorney General therein.

That he does not luppoie, all Custom-house Officers are Algebraills; but, it they were, the Merchants are not; and thinks, the Merchants ought to be satisfied in the Manner of accounting; for to account out of the common Way, and by Ways unknown, will cause great Clamour amongst the Merchants, and discourage Trade, and also will discourage prompt Payments, and consequently create more Bonds.

1711.

Mr. Mitchell, one of the Examiners of the Customs, said, that about Seven or Eight Years since Mr. Carkefs sent for him, and told him, he heard, that Mitchell had said, the Computation was wrong; and shewed him wherein.

That, according to the now Method used in the Customs, all the present Duties on unrated Goods may be taken off; and that Mr. Godolphin referred old Score's Papers to his Confederation; and he thought. Score was in the right, only in some small Mistakes: This was Seven or Eight Years ago.

That the Drawback on Tobacco in the Out-ports is by way of Interest, but has seen it done in London by way of Deduction.

Mr. Carkefs said, that he did not prepare the Scheme of Computation upon his own Head, buc in Concert with other Officers of the Customs, which was pursued; but he had no Information of any Error on the First Act, nor before what he had from Garde; and believes, he might lay, the Custom-house Officers were of Opinion, Garde was mistaken; and that he was not concerned in the Computation at the Time Garde charges him.

Mr. Tyrrell said, be has been an Officer in the Customs above 23 Years; and that, upon passing the said Act, in the 2d Year of her Majesty’s Reign, Mr. Waterson (who had been a Computor at the Custom-house for 50 Years) and other Officers, confulced Mr. Lozvndes about the Scheme of Computation, now practised; and all were of Opinion, it was right: That afterwards, upon an anonymous Letter, sent to the Commissioners in 1708, representing, that, notwithstanding the new additional Duties of the -jd Subsidy, and 12 per Cent, on China Wares, the Customs were nothing advanced, but a Diminution of the Revenue-upon Exportation, that Matter was referred to the principal Officers of the Customs, who made a Report thereof in Writing to the Commissioners; and on the 3d of,

1708, the Commissioners reported to the Treasury, that the Method and Practice of their Officers, in computing the Duty of Goods paying ad valorem, was agreeable to the Rule of Law, and their ancient Usage; and be never heard, there was any Direction from the Treasury for altering the Method; and believes, no Advice was then taken in the Law upon the Conftroftion of the said Act, the Law being plain, as they apprehended.

And he agrees, that the more Duties are laid, the less will be paid, by reason of the Absurdity of the said Act; for that the Seller may allow what Discount he pleases.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to the Committee, that there has been a very great Loss to the Revenue of the Customs upon unrated East India Goods, and other unrated Goods, by the Method, practised in the Custom-house, in computing the Duties on the said unrated Goods, whereby, when there has been no more than £. 18. 8 s. 9 \d. per Centum received for Duties, there has been allowed for the (ameDuties to the Importer £. 52. 2 j. 6 by which Method it appears, that, notwithstanding an additional Duty of £.12 per Cent, was laid on the said Goods, yet no Ad-

vance was made to the said Revenue by the said Duty.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that, by the Method of calculating the Duties upon China Ware, in every £. 18. 8 s. 9^ d. received, there has been loft to the Publick the Sum of £. 11. ror. to

Ordered, That the said Reloiutions be laid before her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, Went up to attend her Majesty in the House of Peers; where her Majesty was pleated to give the Royal Assent to several publick and private Bills.

After which, her Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament.

And afterwards the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, by her Majesty’s Command, laid.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is her Majesty’s royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament Parliament should be prorogued until Tuesday, the Tenth Prorogue Day of July next» and this Parliament is prorogued accordingly until Tuesday, the Tenth Day of July next.

Martisy 10* Julii;

Anno 10° Annae Reginae, 1711.

[Parliament further prorogued.]

Mr Speaker being in the Country, and several Members of the House being met;

A Message was broughi from the Lords by Mr. Davit, Deputy Gentleman L'lher of the Black Rod: Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly the Members present (with the Clerk) went up to the House of Peers; where the Commission was read, for proroguing the Parliament until the Onc-and-twentieth Day of next; and the Parliament was prorogued accordingly until Tuesday, the Ono-and-twentieth Day of August next.

Anno 10° Annae Reginae, 1711.

[Parliament further prorogued.]

Mr Speaker being in the Country, and several Members of the House being met;

A Message was brought from the Lords by Sir Wm. Oldes, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly the Members present (with the Clerk) went up to the House of Peers; where the Commission was read, for proroguing the Parliament until the Ninth Day of October next; and the Parliament was prorogued accordingly until Tuesday, the Ninth Day of October next.

Martis, 9° die Octobris;

Anno 10° Annae Reginae, 1711.

[Parliament further prorogued.]

THE House being met;

A Message was brought from the Lords by Sir Wm. Oldes, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers; where the Commission was read, for proroguing the Parliament until Tueday, the Thirteenth Day of November next; and the Parliament was prorogued accordingly until Tuesday, the Thirteenth of November next.
